items.title: A metal-heavy newsletter, from a mirror by a female welder to a Graves-inspired butter dish
items.summary: Plus: Interiors from a bakery, a showhouse, and a tech office.
items.text: 11.07.26 The Weekly A metal-heavy newsletter, from a mirror by a female welder to a Graves-inspired butter dish by Monica Khemsurov Welcome to the new Sight Unseen, a weekly newsletter that delivers the best of the design world — news, trends, shopping advice, interviews, travel recs, and more — straight to your inbox. If you’re not subscribed, follow this link to sign up . Want to partner with us, advertise, or submit your work ( guidelines here )? Email us at hello@sightunseen.com . A Minimalist Conversation Pit and a Maximalist Lounge Were Our Faves at the Brooklyn Heights Showhouse Top and middle left, Llewellyn Chupin’s room at the Brooklyn Heights Designer Showhouse; middle right and bottom, Max Aboody’s. Photos: Tori Sikkema The biennial Brooklyn Heights Designer Showhouse wrapped its latest edition this past weekend, having invited 19 designers to take over a landmarked 1852 mansion on Monroe Place. The results ranged from classic, antique-filled rooms (as we all know, most showhouses skew pretty trad) to a couple of wilder decorative experiments, but two of our favorites happened to occupy opposite ends of the aesthetic spectrum: a serene, almost minimalist gathering space by Llewellyn Chupin and a dark, Space Age–inspired lounge by Max Aboody Interiors. We’ve been following French-born, New York– and Paris-based designer Llewellyn Chupin since naming her to our American Design Hot List last year , with a furniture collection that paired architectural forms with jewelry-like details. For the showhouse, she transformed a small cellar-level room into the equivalent of a chic conversation pit. A continuous, cream-colored banquette wrapped around three sides of the space, facing a low travertine coffee table, while floor-to-ceiling curtains and strategically placed mirrors made the room feel taller and more expansive. In addition to the table, the sofa’s frame and arms acted as pedestals for a smattering of vintage objects. The overall effect evoked an intimate Parisian salon with a Japanese sense of minimalism. Upstairs, Brooklyn designer Max Aboody drenched a room in color and pattern. Aboody — who studied fashion at Parsons and worked in couture before turning to interiors — created a lounge that was almost too rich and layered for its stated inspiration source of “retro space-age design.” Walnut-paneled walls were punctuated by lighted circular openings and perforated shutters, while the rest of the room was swathed in blue carpet and upholstery, offset with a painterly wallpaper from Arte . Perfectly placed objects like a chainmail stool from Mexican studio Panoramma and a vintage tramp art frame from Freaks NY completed the scene. If Chupin’s space invited you to settle in and chat for hours, Aboody’s made you want to pour a drink and put on a record. It’s kind of a bummer that both were only temporary in the end. Of: Enso Fills a New York Office With Vintage Finds and a Painting-Adorned Daybed The new Cosmos offices by Of: Enso include the studio’s own objects as well as vintage ones, but my favorite is a painting hung on the side of a daybed. Photos: Marco Galloway Considering the founder of Cosmos — the visual inspiration platform intended as a Pinterest alternative for high-brow creatives — was also a co-founder of the New York vintage furniture gallery Galerie Was, it tracks that his company’s new headquarters in Tribeca is object-laden and curated to a tee. He invited interiors studio Of: Enso to create a space that feels less like it was furnished all at once than assembled lovingly, piece by piece, over time. We’ve covered more than our fair share of offices that look like living rooms lately, but this one feels particularly appropriate given the client’s obsession with images, objects, and the way people collect and organize them. Occupying the 19th floor of a 1930s building, the office has the kind of architectural bones that don’t need much embellishment: high ceilings, concrete floors, and enormous original windows overlooking the city. Of: Enso used that envelope as a clean backdrop to the furnishing scheme, which mixes vintage finds with their own custom designs like a cherrywood screen with leather-rope detailing, and a mustard-yellow silk pendant with a hand-painted floral motif. Elsewhere, vintage Japanese objects, leather sling-back chairs, and a hanging Indian Kantha quilt give the space texture, in addition to my very favorite part of the scheme: a tiny landscape painting hung on the back arm of a Judd-like daybed, which plays to my ongoing obsession with artworks displayed in unconventional ways . The designers made a point of choosing furniture that could be moved around as the company grows — a practical consideration that thankfully doesn’t seem, in this case, to have come at the expense of aesthetics. Jialun Xiong Explores Her Cozier Side For a New Bakery in L.A. Jialun Xiong’s interiors for the new bakery Dear Guest in L.A.’s Silverlake neighborhood. Photos: Elizabeth Carababas The early work of L.A. designer and Hot List alum Jialun Xiong was almost exclusively monochromatic, angular, and heavy on metal; her 2023 restaurant project, 19 Town , introduced a little more warmth and texture, but still relied on a neutral palette and rigorous architectural forms. We love to see a designer’s practice expand and shape-shift, and Xiong’s newest project — the interiors for a bakery called Dear Guest in L.A.’s Silverlake neighborhood — tests the boundaries of her aesthetic, trading some of that restraint for buttery yellows, reddish-brown wood, polka dots, and a sunnier take on Art Deco in general. The interior combines elements of a vintage hotel lobby with a hint of inspiration from Japanese ryokans; wood trim divides the walls into geometric panels, punctuated by circular mirrors, while overhead, custom lantern-like pendants pair metal frames with silk shades. In addition to those lights, Xiong designed much of the furniture herself, including the upholstere
designers: Monica Khemsurov Welcome to the new Sight Unseen

items.title: Our new, go-to ceramics talent + the best interiors book we’ve read in years
items.summary: Plus: An iconic 1960s lamp gets a long-overdue reissue.
items.text: 10.22.26 The Weekly Our new, go-to ceramics talent + the best interiors book we’ve read in years by Jill Singer Welcome to the new Sight Unseen, a weekly newsletter that delivers the best of the design world — news, trends, shopping advice, interviews, travel recs, and more — straight to your inbox. If you’re not subscribed, follow this link to sign up . Want to partner with us, advertise, or submit your work ( guidelines here )? Email us at hello@sightunseen.com . Su Wu’s Mesoamerican Modern Made Us Rethink the Meaning of Home Casa Amalia, designed by architect Agustín Hernández for his sister, is one of the 16 homes in Mesoamerican Modern by Su Wu. Photos: Luis Garvan Admittedly I’ve only been to Mexico a few times — an Acapulco wedding, a trip to Tulum at the height of its reign, a whirlwind jaunt photographing homes for How to Live With Objects — but I don’t think I’ve ever learned as much about a place from reading an interiors book as I did with Mesoamerican Modern by Su Wu, the California-born curator and artist who moved to Mexico more than a decade ago and began inhaling the country’s customs and culture. Wu has always been a wonderful thinker; it’s what led us to her work all those years ago . Here she’s thought deeply about her adopted home and how its nuances have often been flattened or erased in our post-colonial world, but she’s also exposed how slippery a beast the very concept of home can be. The book is separated into unexpected rubrics — there’s a whole section devoted to “Unsquared Rooms” — but at its heart is a willingness, almost an imperative, to embrace different ways of living. In one section, there’s a circular house sunk into the ground, whose windows look out onto an interior courtyard; in another, there’s a house that remains forever unfinished, as its owner chips away at stone, forming sculptural reliefs. The book encourages painting everything pink, or allowing a tree to grow through the wall, or emptying a house of nearly all its furniture, leaving a bed that can be moved from room to room, depending on the season. One of our favorite projects in the book (featured in the photos above) is Casa Amalia, which the architect Agustín Hernández — widely regarded as the progenitor of contemporary Mesoamerican architecture — built in 1973 for his sister. The house takes its form from the aquiline profile of an indigenous person; “the cranial area… holds the radiating bones of the house, leading up spiral stairs to an eye-shaped window peering out across the valley.” It’s an old pre-Hispanic idea, that a space ought to look towards the cosmos, mixed here with elements of modernism, like Hernández’s use of reinforced concrete. In other words, it’s a perfect encapsulation of the idea of the book itself. An Iconic 1960s Lamp, Notoriously Difficult to Produce, Gets a New Lease on Life The retooled Lotus lamp by Carlo Nason, reissued by Gubi and available through Design Within Reach. Did you know that the iconic Lotus table lamp, by the late Italian designer Carlo Nason, once had a much more technical name? It started life in 1969 as the nominally challenged LT305, and it was only after early collectors — whom I’ll heretofore refer to as “Lotus-heads” — began poetically referring to it by the flower it resembles that the name took hold. Despite its initial popularity, the Lotus lamp soon went out of production and remained so for nearly 50 years — until now. As of this week, the Lotus is available once again through Design Within Reach as a reissue from the Scandinavian furniture company Gubi, who have retooled some of the light’s peskier parts but retained its ineffable beauty. The futuristic light, which nestles four graduated “petals” of mouth-blown glass inside one another, has always been challenging to make. Fabricated by expert artisans in Murano, each layer undergoes a traditional “pulegoso” process, in which hot glass is rolled in fine granules, initiating a reaction that suspends thousands of microscopic air bubbles inside the glass’s clear layers. Each layer is then carefully mouth-blown to ensure the same thickness, clarity, and bubble distribution; even in their uniformity, however, no two layers are alike, making the light an interesting early example of how to produce something on a mass scale yet still retain the hand of the maker. When illuminated, the glass becomes increasingly transparent, bringing the lamp’s lotus-like form into sharper focus, layer by layer. Garrett Morin’s Fledgling Ceramics Practice is Our Favorite New Source for Smalls A few favorite pieces by Garrett Morin, our new go-to for excellent, under-the-radar ceramics. Photos: Joanna McClure Do you know — like really know — what your friends do for a living? Sometimes you think you do and then they pull out a talent you didn’t even see coming. That’s how it was for me with Garrett Morin , who I first met as curator of the excellent design week exhibition The End is Now but know primarily as one-half of the graphic design duo behind the branding of my Substack, Counter Space . In April, Morin started dropping images of his fledgling ceramics line on Instagram and while my first question to him was How many of these can I reasonably buy?, I soon began to wonder, Is the goal to have a fully sustainable art practice? “I’ve had an art practice for a very long time,” says Morin. “Drawing is the foundation: It’s a gestural, stream-of-consciousness approach to mark-making that hints at figuration but is often simply expressive. From there, I’ll often see an opportunity to explore an idea through another medium. When I started working with clay, I quickly realized how close it felt to drawing, with the added benefit of the material having a will of its own, which I often let take over. There’s a kind of energy transfer that makes the work feel intuitive and deeply gratifying.” For now, Morin has been riffing on a few different forms — vases whose long necks erupt and flop open like a cardboard b
designers: Australian designer Anna Varendorff of ACV Projects
Gubi and available through Design Within Reach
Jill Singer Welcome to the new Sight Unseen

items.title: An Edgy London Interior by Max Radford, Three Experimental Design Exhibitions, and More
items.summary: Plus: Two Parisian apartments with really good art.
items.text: 10.19.26 The Weekly An Edgy London Interior by Max Radford, Three Experimental Design Exhibitions, and More by Monica Khemsurov Welcome to the new Sight Unseen, a weekly newsletter that delivers the best of the design world — news, trends, shopping advice, interviews, travel recs, and more — straight to your inbox. If you’re not subscribed, follow this link to sign up . Want to partner with us, advertise, or submit your work ( guidelines here )? Email us at hello@sightunseen.com . A London Couple Asked for “Edgy and Raw.” Max Radford Delivered. We’re gagging over this London townhouse, from the teal-and-steel bathroom to the vintage paintings in the dining room to how Italian classics meld perfectly with works by up-and-comers. Photos: Michael Sinclair In one of the best interior briefs I’ve heard, the clients of this late-Victorian home in London wanted something “edgy, contemporary, and a little bit raw” — the diametric opposite, basically, of the Pinterest aesthetic. They certainly came to the right person: Max Radford , who not only runs an eponymous gallery for new talents working under pretty much the same directives, but also designs interiors as such, often incorporating pieces from his roster. Likeminded clients are every designer’s dream, but the project has me thinking with pride about how far our little world has come. It’s hard to imagine clients with-it enough to hire a decorator this way 15, or even 10, years ago. Or if they did, to give them both carte blanche and a budget (rather than either/or). Working atop an existing renovation by Atomik Architecture, Radford came through in spectacular fashion, but took care not to abuse his mandate; he added in the requisite 20th-century icons like sofas by Pierre Paulin and Alessandro Becchi, lights by the Castiglionis and Mario Botta, and a bed by Carlo Scarpa before wilding out with more directional new British talents — and that scrumptious teal-walled bathroom. The living room features a zigzag steel chair by Grace Prince, the entry hall a custom radiator cover by Radford himself, the bedroom a cabinet by EJR Barnes, and the bathroom a chair by LS Gomma as well as a mirror by Radford and Eddie Olin. The best thing about projects like this one is how they can help make a case for both next-gen furniture design as well as what a contemporary interior can (and should!) look like. As Radford puts it, “you have all these quite hardcore, radical pieces of design. But when they’re set within a beautiful London family house, they’re softened down a lot and become much more liveable.” Preach. A Former Government Chamber Became a Parliament of Experimental Design in Belgium The long desks of Ghent’s former Government House became exhibition plinths during last week’s Cavea exhibition (lamp by Charlotte Jonckheer). Photos: Alexander Popelier Last week in Ghent, Belgium, BRUT Collective and the curatorial platform DesignUnDisciplined took over the historic council chamber of the city’s former Government House for Cavea , an exhibition that imagines the room as a kind of “non-conformist parliament” for people and objects. The name refers to the tiered seating of ancient amphitheaters, which was historically divided according to social class; here, instead, everyone — and everything — gets an equal seat at the table. (In one indicative piece, by Guillaume Slizewicz, a lamp decides whether to turn itself on by holding a democratic vote among five microcontrollers every ten minutes.) It’s a high-minded premise, but the work was weird enough to keep things fun. Théophile Blandet’s Fluid Dynamics lamps are made from rejected components sourced during a residency at a laboratory-instrument factory and controlled using syringes, as though light itself were a liquid. Matthijs De Block puts genetically modified bacteria into a luxury-style box for a project called Gucci, imagining a future in which genes can be designed, patented, and sold. Marie Caye stuck a sculpture made from a Michelin tire inside a volcano for four months until mineral-rich water covered it in crystals, while Studio CoPain made a vase from pâte morte, the unleavened dough traditionally used for decorations in baking competitions. There were more conventionally desirable objects on view, too, including Laurids Gallée’s cedar bar cart carved with symbols of intoxication, Linde Freya Tangelder’s rough-hewn wood furniture and glass sculptures, and a fuzzy-looking aluminum stool by Nicolas Zanoni that starts as handwoven metal wire before being cast in aluminum. In this unexpected location, it all looked not only provocative, but really nice — who knew parliament tables could function so well as exhibition scenography? Two Paris Apartments Mix French Heritage With Contemporary Design Top and middle left: The Voltaire apartment by Diettert Collet, photos: Clément Gérard. Middle right and bottom: The Cherche-Midi apartment by Claves, photos: Alice Mesguich. Considering how many Paris apartments we’ve published lately, you can’t help but start to see a recurring contemporary Parisian interior language — one in which a new generation of French designers feels comfortable drawing on the city’s decorative traditions without producing rooms that feel like pastiche. Two recent projects take very different approaches to that idea (in somewhat similar material/color palettes). For a Haussmannian apartment that hadn’t been renovated since the 1970s, the young firm Diettert Collet kept the colors restrained: cream walls and upholstery, pale stone, warm woods. The living room is anchored by a blocky custom travertine fireplace and matching vintage coffee table, and backdropped by the project’s standout piece: a vintage sculptural wood screen by Cappellini, sourced from House of Barcia , whose three panels are joined by giant zigzagging stitches. Against all those sandy neutrals, black is used almost architecturally: lining a doorway, enveloping the kitchen cabinetry, and reappearing in objects
credits: Tazy Jessett Nash After graduating from art school

items.title: An Iconic Midcentury Hotel Reborn, a Belgrade Hi-Fi Listening Bar, and More
items.summary: Plus, a shopping guide for chic fireplace andirons.
items.text: 08.10.26 The Weekly An Iconic Midcentury Hotel Reborn, a Belgrade Hi-Fi Listening Bar, and More by Monica Khemsurov Welcome to the new Sight Unseen, a weekly newsletter that delivers the best of the design world — news, trends, shopping advice, interviews, travel recs, and more — straight to your inbox. If you’re not subscribed, follow this link to sign up. Want to partner with us, advertise, or submit your work ( guidelines here )? Email us at hello@sightunseen.com . A Listening Bar Where Yugoslav Modernism Meets Japanese Hi-Fi Culture Supaform’s interiors for EJE incorporate his furniture and art, plus original London Underground textiles, vintage speaker systems, and more. Photos: Varvara Toplennikova Had you visited Yugoslavia in the 1970s, you would have seen thousands of modular structures dotting the streets, instantly recognizable by their rounded, space-age exteriors and large central picture windows. Expandable to encompass anything from newspaper stands to copy shops to small cafes, these were the iconic K67 kiosks, envisioned by the Slavic architect and industrial designer Saša J. Mächtig in 1966 and now altogether more rare in the country. It was these stands — along with Yugoslav brutalism and futurism in general, plus the aesthetic and sound design of Japanese listening bars, that inspired the interiors of Esthetic Joys Embassy, or EJE , in Belgrade. Comprising a bar, a restaurant, a DJ booth, a vinyl library with listening stations, and a dance floor that’s attached to a hotel, EJE was designed by Supaform , and features not only principal Maxim Scherbakov’s furniture designs but his artworks as well, as seen in the lower right photo above. Other key details include a pair of vintage JBL 4435 studio monitors, an iconic Japanese train station clock called the Dulton Double Face, and archival Mischa Black upholstery fabric — used on the London Tube in the 1970s — that Scherbakov’s team sourced from the original London mill that made it. The idea, he says, was to transform the space into a utopia that inspired both nostalgia and optimism; “a futuristic, autonomous station of aesthetic pleasures.” One of Athens’s Great Midcentury Landmarks Enters a New Era At top, a suite at the newly renovated Conrad Athens the Ilisian; bottom, its original 1963 facade and a shot from its Yabu Pushelberg–designed Onuki restaurant. Back in 2024 we asked the Greek design studio Objects of Common Interest to compile their 10 favorite modernist buildings from around the country . The Hilton in Athens was not one of them, but it easily could have been; Hiltons these days may not be the first thing you think of when you think “design hotel,” but this one was built in 1963 by prominent Greek architects Prokopis Vassiliadis, Emmanouil Vourekas, and Spyros Staikos, who hired artist Yiannis Moralis to adorn its front facade with an iconic, very midcentury-coded display of Greek hospitality-themed engravings. Add to that its landmark 82-foot pool, and the modernist building was long venerated both as a hotel and a piece of cultural history. Now, having undergone a four-year restoration and renovation, it has reopened to much fanfare as Conrad Athens the Ilisian , its 278 guest rooms and public spaces reimagined by AvroKo — with a restaurant by Yabu Pushelberg . While the new interiors definitely have that luxury-corporate-hotel vibe in some areas, there are lots of nice midcentury touches — both original and inspired by the original. The former are concentrated in the hotel lobby , where bronze snail-shaped fountains from the original pool, by Moralis and Bouba Lyberaki, have been repositioned into a long water feature that runs down the center of the space. At one end is a fully restored 1963 ceramic mural that Moralis created for the Hilton’s rooftop Galaxy Bar. The hotel’s suites feature elements like the Praying Mantis lamp that Francois Rispal designed in 1950, plus a newly created wood relief wall mural, pictured above, that clearly pays homage to the era. The art throughout — curated by Mare Studio — was also selected to highlight Greek and Greek midcentury artists, though guests who have stayed at the hotel since its opening in April report that none of it can really compete with the art on display through its oversize windows: sweeping views of Athens itself. This Highly Personalized Art Deco Apartment Takes Cues from Vermeer and Balkan Textiles Some of our favorite details in the Gentleman apartment by YSG include a painting by Laura Jones from Chalk Horse Gallery and a custom polka-dot ceramic planter by Remy Pajaczkowski-Russell (top), plus the most stunning galley kitchen we’ve seen (bottom right) and a dining room anchored by a vintage floor lamp (bottom left). Photos: Anson Smart Sometimes I feel like all I ever do in these newsletters is write about apartment renovations in Art Deco–era buildings (mostly in Paris), all of which look impossibly glamorous and full of sleek metal surfaces and expensive period pieces sourced from high-end dealers. I love all of the ones I’ve featured here, of course, but it’s interesting to see a project that departs from the mold a little bit. This space, a 950 square-foot apartment in a landmarked 1929 building in Sydney, was unburdened of past wayward renovations by the firm YSG in order to return to its Art Deco clarity, but then warmed up to something much more layered, colorful, and unexpected. Two points from the project description caught my interest in particular; first, that the clients, a couple, have a thing for Vermeer, so the designers painted the walls in one of the Dutch painter’s favorite colors, lead white. They also incorporated his muted yellow and ultramarine blue into the upholstery of a piano chair, and into a custom rug with ochre accents. Second, they chose some of the apartment’s other colors, along with many of its textiles and textures, as a way of paying homage to the Bosnian/Croatian heritage of one of the owners. That includes
credits: Anson Smart Sometimes I feel like all I ever do
Varvara Toplennikova Had you visited Yugoslavia

items.title: A Hotel in a 6th-Century Monastery, an Office Channeling 90s New York, and More
items.summary: Plus: The butter plate of your dreams.
items.text: 07.30.26 The Weekly A Hotel in a 6th-Century Monastery, an Office Channeling 90s New York, and More by Monica Khemsurov Welcome to the new Sight Unseen, a weekly newsletter that delivers the best of the design world — news, trends, shopping advice, interviews, travel recs, and more — straight to your inbox. If you’re not subscribed, follow this link to sign up. Want to partner with us, advertise, or submit your work ( guidelines here )? Email us at hello@sightunseen.com . Art and Architecture Find a Perfect Dialogue Inside a Modernist Connecticut Landmark Artworks made from paper layered on top of linen canvases by Kim Bartelt, on view through tomorrow at the 1960 John Landis–designed Gores Pavilion in Connecticut. One downside of taking an annual summer break from our newsletter: We sometimes miss the window for exhibitions and other time-sensitive projects. This site-specific exhibition of new work by Berlin artist Kim Bartelt is only on view until the end of the day tomorrow, but assuming most of you aren’t anywhere near New Canaan, Connecticut, anyway, we figured we might as well enable you to enjoy it from afar. For “Exhibit No. 2,” presented by Arden + White Gallery , Bartelt installed 8 of her understated-yet-colorful paper-and-linen compositions inside the Gores Pavilion , a landmarked home designed by modernist architect — and Philip Johnson collaborator — Landis Gores in 1960. The artworks resonate with both the colors and the geometries found in the home, but they weren’t so much inspired by the architecture as chosen to complement it; if you know Bartelt’s work, you know this has been her visual language for years. As the gallery puts it: “This exhibition is not about illustrating architecture, nor about placing contemporary art within an iconic building. Rather, it reveals a shared architectural sensibility, one rooted in proportion, restraint, and the thoughtful orchestration of material, light, and space.” Walker Street Market Is Turning the Berkshires Into a Contemporary Design Destination At Walker Street Market in Lenox, Mass., the craft-forward fare includes a custom counter by Brian Persico and painting by David Silverstein (top), a side table by Simone Bodmer Turner and lamp by Ashley Joseph Martin (above left), and a teapot by Akira Satake (above right), among many others. Photos: Chris Mottalini Out of all the reasons to visit the Berkshires — a woodsy region of western Massachusetts that many New Yorkers escape to in the summer — I never really considered design to be one of them, unless we’re talking about MASS MoCA or modernist architecture, I suppose. So it’s honestly a little bit wild that something has popped up in the area like Walker Street Market , a sprawling design showroom full of commissioned work from a roster of talents that could rival The Future Perfect’s. Opened in mid-July inside a 3,000-sqft early-1900s former department store building, by fashion-designer-turned-interiors-guru Matthew Ames, the project is pretty much exactly how you might imagine a Berkshires version of The Future Perfect that’s lovingly attuned to its own context: lots of gallery-level studio crafts, with a contemporary edge, culled from the best new talents who still work with their hands and venerate, as Ames does, the beauty of pieces that make that fact obvious. Since Ames is working with over 70 makers on the store’s wares — which also span flowers, jewelry, beauty products, and kitchen supplies — it’s impossible to give the full scope, but some favorite pieces when I visited a few weeks ago included a wall of multi-colored ceramic tiles by Shane Gabier, beautiful paintings by David Silverstein and Dan Bruinooge, ruffle-shade lamps by Studio Ford, textile still-lifes by Andrew Pierce Scott, glass vases by Dana Arbib, andirons and chairs by Simone Bodmer Turner, and some absolutely epic wooden floor and pendant lights carved intro trompe l’oeil frills by Ashley Joseph Martin , a name that was new to me. Obviously anyone who recognizes some of the other aforementioned names might note that not all of Walker Street Market’s designers are local to the Berkshires/upstate New York area, but highlights in that department include delicate floral lamps by Jake Coan and several monumental shelves, benches, and tables by woodworker Lily Thorne and her father Peter, some of them topped with ceramics by Natalie Weinberger. The project is so ambitious, and the work it contains so meticulously crafted, that one can only hope that if and when the good people of Massachusetts descend upon it, Ames can keep the shelves stocked. A Sixth-Century Priory Becomes Burgundy’s Most Atmospheric New Hotel (Extremely) old meets new at Les Sources de Vougeot, a hotel in Burgundy, France. Photos: Jules Focone It’s certainly true that, given the tragic outbreak of wildfires there right now, it’s a strange time to be talking about vacationing in France, in this case to a new hotel called Les Sources de Vougeot , with interiors by the Paris firm A.S.L . But at the same time, France will forever be a prime holiday destination, and for what it’s worth, this latest Les Sources — the third in a growing boutique chain, all three in different French wine countries — just so happens to be in Gilly-lès-Cîteaux, Burgundy, and thus far from the worst blazes. Anyway, whether you make plans to go or just want to join us in admiring the design, it is a very nice one; the building was constructed as a priory in the 6th century before being transformed into a country house in the 1600s, and then into Les Sources earlier this year. Because it’s a landmarked property, the hotel team had to tread carefully with their renovation, hiring historic specialists Chevalier & Guillemot to preserve original details in the process, like the indoor pool room’s stunning vaulted ceilings and a pair of fireplaces in the lobby, which used to be the priory kitchen. A.S.L accordingly focused on classical details like antique paintings, tap
designers: Jake Coan and several monumental shelves

items.title: How do you throw a party for 'flexi-drinkers'? We asked the French Bloom Founders
items.summary: Constance Jablonski and Maggie Frerejean-Taittinger, the founders of the premium non-alcoholic sparkling wine brand, share how they hosts guests in style –including on a classic British Pullman
items.text: (Image credit: Lavinia Cernau ) Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter It used to mean that forgoing booze at party meant settling for a sad glass of sparkling water or juice. This is exactly why Constance Jablonski and Maggie Frerejean-Taittinger, founded the premium non-alcoholic wine brand French Bloom . ‘In 2019, I was pregnant with my twins,' Frerejean-Taittinger says. 'I realized for the first time what it could feel like to be a little bit excluded from the culinary moment at a restaurant, but also social events with my friends or colleagues.' (Image credit: Lavinia Cernau ) So she teamed up with Jablonski, a top model and her friend since 2008, to change things. Together, the pair realised there was no premium version of a non-alcoholic drink that wasn't riddled with sugar. After a year of 70 different tests and recipes, the duo launched French Bloom in 2021. Since then, the collection of sparkling non-alcoholic wines has been incredibly well received worldwide (including in France , a tough wine clientele to please), and LVMH is now a minority shareholder. (Image credit: Lavinia Cernau ) French Bloom now includes four sparkling wine cuvées: Le Blanc, Le Rosé, L’Extra Brut, and La Cuvée Vintage 2023. To ring in the brand's fifth birthday, French Bloom recently threw a party on Belmond’s dreamy Celia carriage , a British Pullman carriage designed by Baz Luhrmann and costume designer Catherine Martin. To mark the occasion, we checked in with Jablonski and Frerejean-Taittinger to hear how they throw the perfect party where everyone, regardless of sobriety, can raise a glass. (Image credit: Lavinia Cernau ) How we Host with French Bloom Wallpaper*: Are you a relaxed host and pull it all together at the last minute, or is there careful planning? Constance Jablonski: I really wish I was a relaxed host, but I can't lie, I like planning everything. I'm such a perfectionist. I want everyone to have a good time, and it doesn't mean necessarily to have something super fancy, but I like to plan ahead. Maggie Frerejean-Taittinger: I'm like you, Constance. I'm not relaxed. The more you do before, the more relaxed you are when the guests arrive. I love planning the menu, the table, the flowers. But once the guests arrive, I want people to feel like I'm completely relaxed. So, the best evenings, in my opinion, are the ones that people don't notice how much preparation went into it. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. (Image credit: Lavinia Cernau ) W*: Can you cook? CJ: I'm a terrible cook. I never cook. I'm not the kind of person who can open the fridge and make some magic with like four or five ingredients. MFT: But Constance, I've been to some great dinner parties at your house. CJ: I order everything in! The great thing in Paris , and I'm sure in every big city now, is that you have so many great things available in épiceries and little restaurants. MFT: I do like to cook. I think being in Paris definitely raised the bar. I like to cook for family and friends. But I'm also equally happy to delegate a course or two. Knowing when not to cook is also a hosting skill. W*: What was the first dish you perfected to feed a group of friends or family? MFT: A proper roasted chicken, which is very key to Sunday lunch with family and friends here in Paris. It's simple, it's generous, it's almost impossible not to love. And then adding roasted potatoes, a nice green salad, a great bottle of wine. CJ: I do that every Sunday with my family, too. I go to the rôtisserie downstairs because they have such a great one, and I pick the potato and the chicken, and make a green salad myself. (Image credit: Lavinia Cernau ) Drinks on arrival – what’s on offer? CJ: I always have alcohol for my friends I know they love to drink, and I have French Bloom for my friends I know they will never drink. It's nice to give people the option. I think it's the whole idea also behind French Bloom, making sure everyone has something that they like. MFT: Fully agree. I've always been a sparkling girl. My husband's a Champagne maker; now we have French Bloom. I love sparkling for arrival, but as Constance says, our customers are flexi-drinkers; we are, flexi-drinkers. It's been interesting because I just moved to the US to build the market. I see that there's a big difference. In France, people start with French Bloom and save the wine for dinner because wine is culture and it's for food. In the US, I'm seeing the opposite. I'm seeing a lot of people accepting something alcoholic, and then switching to French Bloom to moderate responsible drinking without stepping down quality. (Image credit: Lavinia Cernau ) Go on and tempt us – what’s your go-to menu, from starters to afters, whether homemade or bought in? MFT: When people arrive, maybe some crudités, very French, like some radish and butter, as we stay around the couch with our drinks. And then, when we sit at the table, I want to go straight for the main course. Not only does it help my dishwasher, because, again, apartments aren’t so big, but I'm tired of the different courses. I'd do a roast chicken or simply prepared fish, maybe with seasonal vegetables and potatoes, and a green salad. I’d probably skip the cheese course and then have a beautiful dessert, maybe something chocolate; dessert's not negotiable. CJ: I'm a big fan of Greek food, so I feel like it's always like a little tomato salad or so, just something light and easy, like stuffed vine leaves, artichokes in olive oil. For the main course, I love fish; my go-to is a papillote: you place the fish in paper, add the spices, then tons of vegetables, and everything cooks together. I'll never forget about my cheese. And for dessert, I just pull out a nice box of chocolates. (Image credit: L
designers: Baz Luhrmann and costume designer Catherine Martin

items.title: A Ukrainian midcentury house finds new life as an artist-designed guesthouse
items.summary: Ukrainian artist Oksana Levchenya (Konstantinovska) is transforming three neighbouring Soviet-era houses near Kyiv into distinctive guesthouses. First up, Hata Yarova brings together salvaged materials, vintage finds and contemporary Ukrainian craft
items.text: (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter A 1960s rural Ukrainian midcentury house near Kyiv has been transformed into a rich tapestry of found materials, antiques and creative interventions. Hata Yarova, which stands out in the village of Derev’yana thanks to a mural on its facade inspired by Ukrainian modernism and Suprematism by Levchenya, is the first of three neighbouring Soviet architecture -era homes that Ukrainian artist Oksana Levchenya (Konstantinovska) is remodelling as guesthouses, turning an ordinary, anonymous typology into something distinctive and woven with narrative. (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) Inside Oksana Levchenya's Ukrainian midcentury house project The idea for the guest houses emerged during the pandemic, but the project has taken on new meaning since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. 'Continuing to build during the war is, in a way, an act of defiance against the death and destruction that Russia has brought to us,' Levchenya tells me via video call from Kyiv, her background darkened by a power cut. She relies on a small group of builders, led by a man approaching his seventies, and the goal of renting the houses is largely about covering costs and sustaining the teams’ livelihoods. 'These houses serve as places of calm and restoration for those who have remained in Ukraine. We are all working enough for three people now, and all of us need rest and comfort.' (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) Levchenya’s own childhood was another spur. After her parents’ divorce, she stayed with her grandmother and later her aunt while her mother pursued a career as a surgeon. At the age of nine, she went to live with her mother in one of the meagre apartments allotted to physicians during the Soviet era in low-cost blocks, called Khrushchyovka . 'Throughout my early childhood, I was always staying in other people’s homes, dreaming of a place of my own,' she explains. 'The Hata Yarova project was born from a desire to create a space in which time is somehow suspended – a place that does not belong to any particular period.' (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) She calls her approach 'intuitive additive architecture': an organic method of adaptation, in which the final form emerges through a slow process of interventions and additions, rather than from a fixed blueprint. Replacing the roof gave her a chance to add an attic level housing guest rooms. The original porch was dismantled, its timber planks reused as the staircase. In its place, Levchenya added an extension housing the kitchen and bathroom. Salvage is a defining feature of the project: oversized arched windows rescued from the renovation of a private residence have been cut up to suit the scale of the house and reassembled in a new composition, while an old timber platform from the former Kosmos factory was refashioned as outdoor decking. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) In the bathroom, reuse becomes even more expressive, with unglazed tiles from the 1960s and 70s mixed with rare, hand-painted pieces from Kharkiv, and contemporary Spanish ceramics. The interiors are kitted with vintage finds and pieces collected from friends, such as a stove from a restaurant. An antique wooden chest from the 1930s purchased from a fair is a poignant nod to her family history, made during the time of Soviet collectivisation, when privately owned farms were consolidated into state-controlled collective farms. (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) ‘My family has lost its inheritance and material possessions several times: first in the aftermath of the October Revolution of 1917, and again during the upheavals of the 1930s,' she explains. 'Today history has cruelly repeated itself; the elders of my family - my mother, her sister, and her brother – have once again lost their homes in Krasnopillia, a rural settlement in Sumy Oblast.' Rebuilding from these ruptures has shaped a particular understanding of value within the family: that the most enduring forms of inheritance are not material, but intellectual - one’s knowledge, skills and capacities. The chest becomes a metaphor for the limits of what can be carried through history: only what is essential, portable, and internalised. It is more than symbolic, however. 'It is an authentic domestic object, originally used to store textiles and rugs, and therefore carries a direct connection to the material culture of the home,' she adds. (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) Textiles have always had a particular emotional resonance for Levchenya, who describes them as a 'matriarchal medium' that connects women across generations. Thanks to her mother’s medical supplies, Levchenya’s favourite plaything as a child was gauze, which she used to create toys. Later, she was drawn to them again through her research into traditional Ukrainian craft heritage, but also a frustration with painting , 'which began to feel too confined and controlled,' she says. 'I wanted to have more freedom to experiment and make mistakes.' Today she creates textile sculptures and woven wall-hangings that draw from local traditions, spliced with Ukrainian modernism and contemporary imagery. 'I find a particular magic in combining opposing textures and creating structures that contain a certain paradox within themselves,' she explains. 'This can happen through visual imagery - for example, Pac-Man combined with traditional Ukrainian ornament - or through the contrast of materials.' (Image credit: Yuliia Yakubyshyna) Her own work is present in the

items.title: How Isamu Noguchi's Akari lanterns became interior design’s favourite fixtures
items.summary: The American artist’s paper lanterns are nothing short of illuminating, 75 years after he created the first designs
items.text: (Image credit: © The Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum, New York / Artists Rights Society) Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Isamu Noguchi ’s glowing washi lanterns and light sculptures have nearly become as universal as light itself. The paper lanterns glow far and wide, bringing a supremely soft warmth to homes, offices, hotels, restaurants and film and TV sets. The pioneering American artist and designer (1904–1988) created the first designs for his Akari light sculptures 75 years ago, a milestone that's now being celebrated with a new exhibition, now on view at his namesake museum in New York. From then on, Noguchi relentlessly formed new iterations. Despite spawning a legion of copycats and dupes, Noguchi’s original Akari shows no signs of dimming in appeal. Here's what to know about the Akari lantern's history and influence. Isamu Noguchi photographed among Akari fixtures. (Image credit: Photo: Louise Dahl-Wolfe. © The Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum, New York / Artists Rights Society) When did Isamu Noguchi create the Akari lantern? Noguchi’s Akari light sculptures were born in 1951 during a visit to Gifu, Japan , where he encountered illuminated paper lanterns called chochin . The handcrafted lanterns made of mulberry bark paper were mostly used as decorations or advertisements, as Noguchi observed. Eventually, Noguchi was introduced to the city’s mayor, who requested that the artist revive Gifu’s lantern industry as it had become diluted by inferior replicas. Noguchi swiftly developed two ideas for lanterns with an eye toward the future:x he replaced the customary candle with an incandescent lightbulb. Early Akari lantern designs in the 1950s. (Image credit: Photo: Stephen Michael. © The Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum, New York / Artists Rights Society) What is an Akari lantern made of? Under the term Akari, a Japanese word meaning ‘light’ that’s also associated with weightlessness, Noguchi established paper lanterns as sculptures that blend traditional craftsmanship with modern living. He fashioned Akari from high-quality materials used in Gifu: strips of mulberry bark washi paper structured with bamboo ribbing. The washi paper’s durability with impressive plasticity allowed Noguchi to play with shapes while maintaining the practicality of their collapsible construction. With the ability to flatten and expand, the lanterns proved easy to ship and towed the line between material and immaterial. Isamu Noguchi’s studio in Kita Kamakura, Japan, 1952. (Image credit: © The Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum, New York / Artists Rights Society) A decades-long dedication to developing new designs In Noguchi’s lifetime, he created more than 200 Akari models. ‘Noguchi spoke of developing new designs as a way to ‘foil [his] many imitators, through innovation, to reach a point where they could no longer follow,’ ‘ says Kate Wiener, curator for The Noguchi Museum in New York , which has recently opened an exhibition dedicated to the influential lanterns. ‘Certainly, this was one motivation, but he also described his continued efforts as something more deeply felt: "[It] became like a cause with me—a new shape, merely, was not enough; it obviously had to be fitted into today's new ways and uses."' Noguchi working on a paper template for an Akari design. (Image credit: © The Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum, New York / Artists Rights Society) Noguchi fiercely believed in the modern relevance of Akari. ‘They embodied his lifelong vision of a hybrid, accessible form of sculpture that could transcend the boundaries between art and design and become an integral part of everyday experience,’ Wiener adds. ‘I think this is ultimately what kept him returning to Akari. He saw in them seemingly endless possibilities and was continually inspired to explore just how far he could take them.’ The earliest versions of Akari are a table lamp identified as 9A and floor lamp labeled 14A , says Evan Scott, the museum’s director of retail and merchandising. Set on three-legged metal frames, both styles feature wooden collars and evenly spaced bamboo ribbing. Other Akari models range from globe-shaped ceiling lights to column-shaped shades with minimal bamboo ribbing. While they predominantly come in an off-white hue, some models feature colourful screen-printed designs on the neutral background. Noguchi designing Akari with Japanese architect Kenzo Tange and Michio Noguchi in 1952. (Image credit: © The Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum, New York / Artists Rights Society) The enduring allure of Akari light sculptures Akari light sculptures still enthrall the contemporary era. ‘There is an obvious beauty to the way light suffuses and filters through the mulberry bark paper used for Akari that probably accounts for a good bit of their lasting appeal,’ says Matthew Kirsch, curator and director of research for The Noguchi Museum. ‘There is a warmth in the way light is transmitted through the paper of an Akari that is missing from its many imitators.’ Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. Akari lanterns also possess a fine handmade quality, partly apparent in the shades’ natural wrinkles. ‘The method of construction for most models, based on the chochin lantern's spiral bamboo ribbing, is relatively unchanged from how they were made when Noguchi began working with the Ozeki family in Gifu in the 1950s and, obviously, for many decades before that,’ Kirsch explains. Noguchi among colourful Akari light sculptures in 1954. (Image credit: © The Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum, New York / Artists Rights Society) How to buy an Akari lantern of your own Over the years, design lovers seeking ‘elegant people’s art,’ as Noguchi

items.title: Wallpaper* checks into The Webster hotel, a design-led gem for your next London stay
items.summary: Boasting cosy interiors with contemporary creativity, this new hotel feels like a countryside manor in the heart of London
items.text: (Image credit: Adam Firman) Jump to category: What's on your doorstep? Who is behind the design? The room to book Staying for drinks and dinner? Where to switch off The verdict Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter ‘Morning,’ said the businessman next to me as we waited for the lift to take us from the ninth floor to reception at The Webster Hotel in Covent Garden. There was something reassuringly un- London about his greeting. In the spirit of lift small talk, I asked if he was checking out and how he'd enjoyed his stay. His face lit up. ‘I’ve come down from Harrogate, and I always struggle to find a hotel in London that I actually like,’ he said, as he smoothed down his trench coat. ‘Here I feel like I’ve stepped into a countryside manor. I’ve been here for two weeks and eaten dinner at the restaurant almost every night and loved every minute. It's a hotel that feels inviting. It's been wonderful.’ To that, I agreed. It's a surprisingly hard balance to strike. The appeal of The Webster is its domestic scale. While many London hotels favour grand entrances and expansive public spaces, here the reception is intimate, the interiors inviting and the atmosphere closer to that of a country house than a conventional city hotel. There's a sense of British manor-house character, without the period flourishes. What's on your doorstep? (Image credit: Adam Firman) The Webster in Covent Garden is a new hotel brand, designed to reconnect guests with analogue pleasures. Though new, it is already thinking ahead with a second outpost set to open in Times Square, New York , in 2028. The Webster is a two-minute walk from Holborn station, ten minutes from Tottenham Court Road, and, of course, Covent Garden. The hotel sits opposite Lincoln's Inn Fields, which was also the moody backdrop for Charles Dickens’ novel Bleak House. Who is behind the design? (Image credit: Adam Firman) Behind the design is London-based architecture firm, Red Deer, which they describe as ‘magical realism’. ‘This felt like a natural expression of the playfulness we wanted for The Webster: something familiar and welcoming, with moments that gently interrupt your expectations,’ says Lucas Che Tizard, co-founder, lead architect and designer of the firm. ‘There’s a freedom to hotel design because people arrive ready to step outside their everyday lives. We wanted to encourage that curiosity.’ (Image credit: Adam Firman) They captured this through a dialogue of materials and colour: bespoke terrazzo, hand-painted murals and tactile fabrics. Says Che Tizard, ‘For me, the magic is in discovering something slightly unexpected within a space you already feel at home in.’ Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. (Image credit: Adam Firman) The hotel’s architecture itself feels cosy. Gone are the intimidating entryways and unused lounge areas. The check-in desk is bijou, evoking nostalgia for small boutique hotels of the 1970s. The architect explains: 'We approached The Webster through its own story and surroundings. The relationship with Lincoln’s Inn Fields, the energy of Holborn and the idea of a hotel as a creative meeting place all helped shape its character. That comes through at every scale, from the terrace connecting the hotel to the square to the mohair headboards in the guestrooms.' The room to book (Image credit: Adam Firman) Considering its quaint feel, there are 167 keys. There are three room options: the King Deluxe with a park view really showing off what the hotel has to offer. The room has beautiful bespoke joinery to hang and store clothes for longer stays. There is also a design-led mini bar offering Torres crisps, Form protein bars, ‘healthy’ sweets, and to enjoy with tea, coffee, or something stronger. The bathroom is generous, with contemporary tiling and Malin + Goetz products. Staying for drinks and dinner? (Image credit: Adam Firman) Carmelina's has all the character of a restaurant with a life of its own. Tucked down a set of hidden steps to the right of The Webster entrance, it feels more New York than London: a moody, intimate space of low ceilings, wood-clad walls and an open kitchen, with velvety green booths, a nostalgic black-and-white tiled floor and petal-shaped chandeliers. (Image credit: Adam Firman) Carmelina's avoids the familiar Italian restaurant shorthand. Its contemporary interiors provide a backdrop for a menu rooted in Italian cooking, overseen by head chef Simone Serafini and restaurant manager Francesco Patti. (Image credit: Adam Firman) Towards the back of the restaurant is a secret cloaked bar, Carla’s. Helmed by bar manager Peppe Corallo, the space has a 90s energy that encourages you to spark up a conversation with a stranger. The menu is something special. Peppe has expertly crafted each cocktail, each nodding to traditions found when dining with family, from the woody scents of the cabinet that holds special-occasion drinkware to the idea of having a remedy concoction to help ease a cold, or perhaps a bad day. But at the heart of his menu is La Conserva, a stunning take on a martini that feels fragrant and refreshing, with strong basil notes; it is an ode to a late-summer Italian ritual where families jar and preserve fresh tomatoes. It is worth visiting Carla’s just for that. Where to switch off (Image credit: Adam Firman) The lounge area just off the reception feels comfortable and sociable, as Che Tizard also notes, ‘with enough intimacy to make yourself a little corner of it.’ It is the character shift throughout that day which charms the designer, as he continues, ‘In the morning, there’s something quite studious about it – somewhere to read, work or simply sit with a coffee. items.title: Amansara: a revived royal guesthouse in Siem Reap
items.summary: Fresh from a thoughtful renovation, Amansara in Siem Reap revisits its 1960s royal heritage, pairing New Khmer architecture with Aman’s signature hospitality and easy access to the temples of Angkor
items.text: (Image credit: Courtesy of Aman) Jump to category: What’s on your doorstep? Who's behind the design? The room to book Staying for drinks and dinner? Where to switch off The Verdict Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter The former Villa Princière, a royal guesthouse commissioned by Cambodia’s King Norodom Sihanouk, lives largely behind a long white wall in Siem Reap. To most, Amansara flies subtly under the radar, unnoticed by almost anyone unaware of what lies beyond its discreet gate – and all the better for it. Siem Reap may beep and honk like most Southeast Asian cities, but this corner of Cambodia moves in a softer lane, in line with its ancient sites and therefore slower, more spiritual pace. The temples are a big reason guests come here; the other is the chance to retreat afterwards to the gentle hug of Aman’s beyond-exceptional service and fragrant cold towels. Fresh from a thoughtful renovation, the 24-suite hotel feels like stepping right back into the 1960s, where, if you squint hard enough, Jackie O might just be sunbathing beside the cool curving pool. What’s on your doorstep? Angkor Wat (Image credit: Courtesy of Aman) Amansara sits on the main road towards Angkor, a remarkable fact that a site as striking and transcendent as the UNESCO-listed temples is just ten minutes from the hotel, and perhaps part of the reason Amansara feels so relaxed is its proximity to all that ancient history. Villa Princière was built with privacy in mind, set along the French Quarter, among the royal parks and leafy streets around Charles de Gaulle Boulevard and the Siem Reap River. The obvious excitement is its nearness to Angkor Wat, but tying in a few other surrounding temples into a ‘petit circuit’ makes the most of an early rise: Bayon, with its big-block carvings of smiling faces, and Ta Prohm, where a web of enormous tree roots winds through mossy ruins. Amanbala boat trips (Image credit: Courtesy of Aman) Downtown Siem Reap is walkable or a speedy remorque ride away, with the bright lights of its night market stirring up street food and cold bottles of beer, while the Made in Cambodia Market and Kandal Village are good for daytime pottering – the latter has a run of smarter shops selling lacquered homeware, silk scarves, and silverware. While Aman’s knack for detail and serious service make it all too easy to stay put, its experiences take on something totally different. The Amanbala boats, for instance, head out to the floating village of Chong Kneas on Tonlé Sap, garnering an up-close look at life on the country’s largest freshwater lake. Who's behind the design? (Image credit: Amansara, courtesy of Aman) It’s worth remembering the many iterations of a residence like this, too. French architect Laurent Mondet was commissioned to design Villa Princière in 1962, one of two state guesthouses built for Prince Sihanouk. The single-storey white cement buildings feature stone accents, while two uniquely shaped pools sit at the centre of the grounds and a grand circular dining room occupies one corner of the property. It was a subtle, modern design for its time, with long columned corridors and areas that made the most of the Cambodian climate. (Image credit: Aman) After changing hands and names over the years, the property eventually fell into disrepair before Aman took it on in 2002. Kerry Hill Architects handled the latest round of work and took care not to disrupt the long-standing formula. The building’s minimalist shapes and time-worn charm are a near-perfect example of 1960s New Khmer architecture, a shift in Cambodian design that moved away from French colonial nostalgia in favour of expressive curvilinear forms, layered concrete, and plenty of open-air spaces. The bones have been left largely unchanged, with a few modern amendments: armchairs have given way to sweeping banquettes in the restaurant, and the palette remains an earthy mix of dusty browns, stark whites, and bold blacks. The room to book (Image credit: Amansara) All 24 suites follow a familiar monochrome scheme, with a hint of orange here and there, nodding to the saffron-coloured kasaya robes worn by Buddhist monks. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. (Image credit: Amansara, courtesy of Aman) The latest update has been artful: all suites have been spruced up, and five additional guest suites have been upgraded to include private swimming pools, expanding Amansara’s collection of Pool Suites. Two new categories have also been added: a Junior Pool Suite and a Two-Bedroom Family Pool Suite for young families who’d prefer to stick together. The look is pared back and modernly spiffed, with enough warmth (and natural light) to keep it from feeling too two-toned. Staying for drinks and dinner? Dining at Amansara (Image credit: Courtesy of Aman) The food is reliable, flavourful and intentionally familiar, mixing international dishes with local staples that are intriguing to try. Breakfast comes on an A3 printout of traditional Khmer dishes alongside the usual spreads, including avocado toast, colourful fruits, chia pudding and eggs any style. Try something traditional: Bor Bor Bangkear is a rice-style porridge with bean sprouts, spring onion, and stir-fried prawns. When the humidity drops, take over an outdoor table by the pool for a pre- or post-dinner drink – Cambodian gin comes with a tumbler of tonic for topping up. (Image credit: Amansara, courtesy of Aman) There's also a new bar, located in the room that originally served as a personal dining space for King Sihanouk and the royal family between 1962 and 1965, where you can have afternoon tea alongside retro photographs. At supper, the menu moves through Khmer salads – pomelo with prawns, or chicken with banana blossom – as well as Cambodian

items.title: Feast your eyes on the Wallpaper* Entertaining Issue – on sale now
items.summary: See out 2026 with decadent dining, homes made for hosting and a wonderful winter wardrobe, and embrace 2027 with your exclusive design horoscope; find December Wallpaper* on newsstands
items.text: With our newsstand cover (left), we go over to the dark side for a deliciously decadent dining story, while our limited-edition subscriber cover takes you out to new London restaurant Lunette (Image credit: Left, newsstand cover photography: Joss McKinley. Entertaining: Melina Keays. Interiors: Alfie di Trolio. Right, limited-edition cover photography: Phil Dunlop) Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter The Wallpaper* Entertaining Issue, on newsstands now in its December 2026 iteration, is a timely reminder that it's never too early – or too late – to dim the lights and dial up a favourite playlist or two, safe in the knowledge that we have left no stone unturned in our search for the best and brightest opportunities to celebrate in style. To this end, we deliver a veritable feast for the senses, inviting us all to consider how a degree of old-school decadence can transform a dining tableau. And, keeping conviviality at the heart of the matter, we take a trip to St Clement , the riverside London hotel co-developed by Mark Wadhwa and Nick Jones, atop which the capital's favourite chef, Florence Knight, has worked with interior design and furniture studio Eagle + Hodges to create Lunette , the city's most in-demand restaurant. Florence Knight's first solo fine-dining restaurant, Lunette is guided by produce, seasonality, and a distinctly painterly aesthetic (Image credit: Photo by Phil Dunlop) Elsewhere, we run around town with the impresarios re-erecting some of Paris ' legendary nightclubs; honour the timeless appeal of the Greek klismos chair, a classic style given a contemporary twist by contributing editor Nick Vinson; and profile the winner of the inaugural Fendi Design Prize. Could an indulgent new purchase be in the stars for you? Check your 2027 design horoscope in the December issue (and treat yourself to this Tory Burch ‘Bunny Knot Runway’ shoulder bag anyway) (Image credit: Photography: Neil Godwin. Art direction: Cindy Parthonnaud) Further afield, we tour a trio of private homes that put a warm welcome at their heart; discover the bountiful, and beautifully packaged, world of Japanese confectionery; reveal the ‘ Ferrari of football tables', as its designer, Jaime Hayon, describes this one-of-a-kind objet featuring ‘players' delightfully fashioned after Hayon's whimsical ‘Chicken'; and consult our resident astrologer on what we can look forward to (and what should join us) as we see in a new year. And if peering into the future fills you with dread, then fear not – for this month's End Paper, our design critic Hugo Macdonald explains why fortune favours those prepared to see what's written in their stars. Thank you for reading, and enjoy the issue. Bill Prince Editor-in-Chief Wallpaper’s December 2026 Entertaining Issue is available from 5 November, in print on newsstands, on the Wallpaper* app on Apple iOS, and to subscribers of Apple News +. In addition to editing, writing and brand curation, Bill is an acknowledged authority on travel, hospitality and men's style. He is the author of two books, Royal Oak: From Iconoclast To Icon – a tribute to the Audemars Piguet watch at 50 – and The Connaught , a history of the legendary Mayfair hotel, both published by Assouline

items.title: Ones to watch: Betyle Studio searches for a talisman in every project
items.summary: The Marseille-based studio investigates history and archives to inform its interior design work
items.text: Nicolas Cazenave de la Roche and Carla Romano, founders of Betyle Studio, at Arcane 17, a Paris restaurant where they designed the interiors (Image credit: Axel Aurejac) Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter A bétyle is a sacred stone, a votive that was revered in ancient Greece and Rome . It is also the name of a new Marseille interior design practice founded in 2025 by Carla Romano and Nicolas Cazenave de la Roche. ‘In antiquity, these raw stones were raised as dwelling places for the divine; some were meteorites fallen from the sky. This mysterious matter says everything about our approach,’ explains Cazenave de la Roche. For the pair, each project is an enigma, where they slowly discover how it unfolds and find the perfect balance of subtlety and bold design choices. In conversation with Betyle Studio The duo at Le Figuier, which transformed a 19th-century agricultural building into a home (Image credit: Axel Aurejac) Long before the duo met, their paths had a lot of similarities. Both have Vietnamese roots on their fathers’ sides. Romano grew up in Marseille, with summers spent in Saint-Florent, while Cazenave de la Roche was between Paris and Corsica; they shared this connection to the city's rushed rhythms and its contrast with time spent in nature. They both studied at L’École Beuve in Paris, where their paths crossed. ‘Right after our studies, we decided to work together. Marseille, my hometown, naturally became our starting point: a city in transformation with everything still to invent,’ Romano tells Wallpaper*. Le Figuier (Image credit: Axel Aurejac) Their first project together wasn't an interior, but instead, a podcast. ‘We recounted pivotal moments in the lives of Gio Ponti or Jean-Michel Frank,’ explains Cazenave de la Roche.’ We learned to dive into the material, to weave together story and research, and to create a dialogue between history and the contemporary.’ This provided the foundation for their practice. Le Figuier (Image credit: Axel Aurejac) The young studio begins each project with a close study of what is already there: a careful reading of the history of a building, its architectural details, and how light interacts with the space. ‘Every project begins with archives and historical research of the building itself, the trades that occupied it, and the neighbourhood,’ notes Romano. This is evident in the studio's Le Figuier project, the transformation of an 1820 agricultural outbuilding into a residence. The duo scoured through archival photographs to inform the choice of materials. Old feeding troughs became a metal washbasin, while farm hooks were transformed into flower holders. Le Figuier (Image credit: Axel Aurejac) This process is then bookended with references the studio returns to again and again: Pierre Chareau’s functionalism and the glass blocks of his Maison de Verre, the core furniture principle found in Mies Van Der Rohe ’s Farnsworth House, Gae Aulenti ’s Palazzo Pucci in Florence, or Frank Lloyd Wright ’s wood-clad interiors. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. ‘Furniture is never decorative. It is a fragment of architecture’ Nicolas Cazenave de la Roche Arcane 17 (Image credit: Axel Aurejac) Other recent works include Arcane 17 , a restaurant in Paris, named after the star card of the Tarot de Marseille, and a new series of stores for leather goods and accessories brand Léo et Violette. ‘Every place is unique, and every place has its talisman, which we search for,' says Romano. At Le Figuier, 'there was a great fig tree in the garden, which gave the farmhouse its name. The star of the tarot [became a signature for] Arcane 17, and for Léo et Violette, it is the tuning fork, the house’s emblem, born of [brand co-founder Violette Sanchez’s] first love for opera singing. Once we have found the symbol, the whole project tunes itself to it.’ Arcane 17 (Image credit: Axel Aurejac) Furniture is another core pillar in their work. ‘We are as much interior architects as we are curators,’ says Cazenave de la Roche. ‘Furniture, whether custom-designed or carefully selected, is never decorative. It is a fragment of architecture. At Le Figuier, a structure of okoume wood and glass organises the entire space. At Arcane 17, a stainless-steel tube bar rises like a prow and turns the open kitchen into an arena.’ Léo et Violette store interior (Image credit: Ludovic Balay) Since the studio’s conception, the duo have chosen to work with simple materials while exploring new ways to render them. As designers, they move away from a picture-perfect finish, and instead leave room for imperfection; the beautiful aftermath of artisanal craftsmanship. ‘We prefer character to perfection,’ they say. ‘Working with local artisans is not only an ecological and responsible commitment, but it is a way of reconnecting with traditional know-how’ Carla Romano and Nicolas Cazenave de la Roche Le Figuier (Image credit: Axel Aurejac) In a world where attention span is dwindling, and the desperate pursuit of uniqueness too often results in similitude, how does a new studio stay relevant? ‘By not chasing trends,’ say the duo. ‘Diving into the past of a building, a neighbourhood, or a craft is where our creative process begins. Working with local artisans is not only an ecological and responsible commitment, but a way of reconnecting with traditional know-how. We always start from function to define form. That is what makes things last.’ betylestudio.com TOPICS Tianna Williams Staff Writer Tianna Williams is Wallpaper’s staff writer.
