items.title: Winter nights just got interesting – step inside Amsterdam’s Gashouder and join the party
items.summary: Gashouder, a former ‘temple to techno’, matures into a dynamic city concert hall, retaining its 19th-century architecture and experimental character with an immersive interior by Inside Outside
items.text: Inside Gashouder, a former gasholder and occasional techno music venue that’s now transformed as a permanent cultural venue (Image credit: Gashouder) Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Culture has long claimed abandoned industrial structures, drawn to their atmospheric voids and the freedom found in their decay. In 1990s Amsterdam , one such structure, a 19th-century gas holder in Westerpark, was revered as a ‘temple to techno’. Now, after hosting one-off events for years, Gashouder (Dutch for 'gas holder') has opened as a permanent cultural venue for live and electronic music, performance and art with capacity for 3,500 revellers. (Image credit: Gashouder) (Image credit: Angelina Nikolayeva) Tour the reborn Gashouder Gashouder ’s new chapter balances its restoration as a heritage-listed ‘Rijksmonument’ with a subterranean extension that enables its functional, long-term operation. Arriving through historic red-brick arches, visitors now descend into the old gasholder’s futuristic new concrete ‘underworld’ that directly mirrors the perimeter of the concert hall above. Amsterdam-based interdisciplinary studio Inside Outside designed the architecture and interiors of this underworld as an experiential and flexible 21st-century system driven by the venue's 19th-century geometry. 'We love restoring historic industrial buildings, but we also want to lift them up with an extra layer that gives them new life,' says Aura Luz Melis, partner at Inside Outside . (Image credit: Peter Tijhuis) (Image credit: Peter Tijhuis) Radial strips of light echoing the former steel skeleton guide visitors towards a central gathering space lit with a glowing lamp by Lumus Instruments, inspired by the gasholder’s former flame. A series of curved sliding and demountable walls of aluminium and polycarbonate shift into five different event configurations, dividing the functions of the bar, toilets, backstage and merchandise kiosk. Glitches in this sci-fi scenography reveal the raw roughness of the steel sheet-pile retaining wall, almost at one with the texture of the earth. Meanwhile, sections of glossy, reflective PVC flooring contrast with ‘ghost’ sections of matte-black corrugated steel, energising the space, alongside lighting informed by the minimalist experimentalism of the 20th century’s avant-garde Zero art movement. (Image credit: Angelina Nikolayeva) Founded by Dutch designer Petra Blaisse in 1991, Inside Outside has pioneered shifting interior atmospheres through textile design, landscape, light and perspectives. Rather than being superfluous or aesthetic, those ‘layers’ are in fact 'functional, flexible and demountable', explains Melis, and over the past ten years she’s seen their work become even more relevant as cultural institutions seek to be less extractive and more resourceful. A staircase twists up to the expansive concert hall, which has a soaring 14.5m ceiling height. The exposed architecture dates back to 1881 and was technically restored by architect André van Stigt of Buro van Stigt. Inside Outside printed new acoustic panels with a grainy, to-scale photograph of the building’s brick walls, camouflaging them abstractly into the historic atmosphere. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. (Image credit: Angelina Nikolayeva) (Image credit: Peter Tijhuis) For Lennart Rottier, founder of Universe Building and co-owner of Gashouder and the wider Cultuurpark Westergas (together with Duncan Stutterheim), the roof and the bricks are essential to the performances, forging a moment of connection between time, creativity and place. The venue’s programming plugs a gap in Amsterdam’s music scene for mid-career artists, and has an alternative edge inspired by its rave history, yet you’ll also find the National Ballet and Royal Orchestra on the agenda. Rottier hopes the industrial architecture will challenge these more traditional art forms, while attracting younger audiences to them. 'The monument determines our direction, the heritage determines our values,' he explains, proud of the place-making vision that’s been forged under an owner-developer-operator model in collaboration with the municipality. (Image credit: Angelina Nikolayeva) (Image credit: Peter Tijhuis) This means that the cultural experience of the Gashouder starts at the entrance to the 23-hectare Westerpark, and in the village of 19th-century red-brick ‘Hollandsche Neorenaissance’ buildings hosting bars, restaurants, clubs and galleries. Inside Outside’s collaboration extends across the park with a scheme of lighting, wayfinding and bike parking (80 per cent of Gashouder visitors arrive by bike) set to unfold in 2028. Amidst the trees, the authentic silhouette of Gashouder sculpturally looms, preserving its original power, before revealing its futuristic underworld that equips it for the next century. (Image credit: Angelina Nikolayeva) Gashouder , Klönneplein 1, 1014 DD Amsterdam, gashouder.nl insideoutside.nl universebuilding.com TOPICS Harriet Thorpe Harriet Thorpe is a writer, journalist and editor covering architecture, design and culture, with particular interest in sustainability, 20th-century architecture and community. After studying History of Art at the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS) and Journalism at City University in London, she developed her interest in architecture working at Wallpaper* magazine and today contributes to Wallpaper*, The World of Interiors and Icon magazine, amongst other titles. She is author of The Sustainable City (2022, Hoxton Mini Press), a book about sustainable architecture in London, and the Modern Cambridge Map (2023, Blue Crow Media), a map of 20th-century architecture in Cambridge, the city where she grew up.
designers: architect André van Stigt of Buro van Stigt

items.title: At Lunette, Florence Knight brings an artist’s eye to the table
items.summary: Florence Knight’s first solo project, Lunette at London’s St Clement hotel, serves up beautifully framed riverside views and picture-perfect dishes
items.text: (Image credit: Photo by Phil Dunlop) Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter A bright but overcast afternoon in late September. Eleven floors up at the St Clement hotel – a new build near the river, looming over Temple Gardens at 180 The Thames – Florence Knight is holding court at her new 30-seat restaurant, Lunette. Flooded with early autumn light, its off-white palette, swathes of pale wood, steel tabletops, artist monographs artfully arranged on a coffee table and an abundance of Jean Prouvé’s modernist ‘INSA’ panels lining the walls make it resemble a curated loft apartment as much as a dining room. Lunette is a deeply personal project for Knight and, though the space was a concrete shell when she first saw it, the potential was clear. ‘I could see it instantly; the kitchen here, the bar there. The light, the movement and the water, it feels like it's almost holding you,’ she says. Lunette at St Clement Lunette, helmed by chef Florence Knight, is located on the top floor of Nick Jones’ new London hotel St. Clement, which forms part of the wider 180 Quarter development project (Image credit: Photo by Phil Dunlop) Knight is a quietly totemic figure in London 's food scene; first leading the pass at Polpetto (a standalone spin-off of Russell Norman's game-changing Soho bacaro Polpo), and then at Clerkenwell’s Sessions Arts Club, the beautifully weathered palazzo of a restaurant she co-founded with artist Jonny Gent in 2021. In 2024, she departed Sessions with the intention of opening her first solo venture. Where Sessions was ‘a roaring beast’, Knight says, ‘I realised that I wanted a sense of intimacy, something smaller.’ Nearly three years on, Lunette – developed with 180 Quarter’s Mark Wadhwa, St Clement mastermind (and Soho House founder) Nick Jones, and interiors studio Eagle + Hodges – is the result. Given Knight’s epicurean bona fides, it may seem disjointed to talk design before dishes. But Lunette – named after the arched windows of the nearby disused Aldwych underground station, and a word that ‘writes beautifully’ – is a full-service undertaking, and irrefutably dreamy to look at. Knight studied fashion before segueing into kitchens, and she has the vibe of an artist who just happens to be a dynamite chef, too. (Image credit: Photo by Phil Dunlop) All of Lunette’s sofas, dining surfaces, chairs and lighting (save a midcentury Pierre Chapo teardrop table, and a wooden service station fashioned by Southampton’s shipyard fabricators Calshot) are of Eagle + Hodges’ own design – as is the chic utilitarian staff garb, created by co-founder Alex Eagle’s fashion label. But Knight commissioned nearly everything else: from the steely open kitchen to ceramics by Tetsuya Otani and Michel François, sinuous blown glassware by Danish designer Alexander Kirkeby, and even the finely layered and weighted paper menus, the embossed double ‘t’ in Lunette resembling a Lilliputian table. The room’s speaker system was created by artist and audio engineer Devon Turnbull, a neat callback to his immersive listening room up the block at 180 Studios, while the Prouvés were drawn from the personal collection of real-life couple Wadhwa and Eagle. ‘Florence has got amazing taste,’ says Eagle, a longtime friend of Knight’s. ‘She cares about texture, about light, about feeling and space – which is what makes me and Sophie [Hodges] tick. The collaboration is people coming together and being inspired, rather than trying to elevate or change her.’ Image 1 of 2 French guinea fowl with a hazelnut and celeriac sauce, beetroot purée, and a jus split with hazelnut and tarragon oils (Image credit: Photo by Phil Dunlop) (Image credit: Photo by Phil Dunlop) Image 1 of 2 View Original Image 2 of 2 View Original Fundamentally, Eagle says, the room functions as a ‘very chic blank canvas’ for Knight’s food – which is, naturally, the main draw at Lunette. Even then, says Knight, ‘it’s completely transmissible’ to the surroundings. The balancing of layers and textures, of hard and soft (not least in the curtains, which she insisted were translucent, ‘like a thin onion skin’), is integral to her identity as a chef. ‘I’m always seeing things from a visual perspective,’ she says. ‘I just think that food is my material.’ Knight’s cooking is precise, seasonal, ‘reasonably gentle in flavour’, and inspired by nature and art. It has developed over the years, but there are through-lines for those who’ve been following. Take the fêted Sessions dish of layered confit potato and eel cake – at Lunette, it’s reconfigured into a pomme soufflé with smoked eel, roe and nasturtium flowers. These things, she says, ‘just matured with my technical ability, and with where I am as a person’. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. Image 1 of 2 Rice cooked in crab stock, with a sauce of long peppers and tomato juice, egg-yolk jam and cock crab in crab-shell butter (Image credit: Photo by Phil Dunlop) (Image credit: Photo by Phil Dunlop) Image 1 of 2 View Original Image 2 of 2 View Original There’s a painterly assemblage of raw, late-summer runner and yellow French beans with slow-cooked squid, dressed with tomato water; a sunny dish of rice cooked in crab stock, with a sauce of long peppers and tomato juice, egg-yolk jam and cock crab in crab-shell butter; a more autumnal plate of French guinea fowl with a hazelnut and celeriac sauce, beetroot purée, and a jus split with hazelnut and tarragon oils; and an edgeless chocolate tart, its super-short pastry crisp with rice flour and depth afforded by tea-soaked raisins. The full dinner menu will feature eight courses, plus sundries. Even on a restaurant scene as punctilious as London’s, the presentation is impressive, but ‘the precision is not to intimidate people’, Knight says
designers: Hoxton Mini Press later this year

items.title: Connaught House is a north London landmark reborn as five boutique homes
items.summary: In St John's Wood, Connaught House and its long history live on, brought into the 21st century by architects Darling Associates and interiors studio Gunter and Co for owner Marcus Cooper Group and developers Valouran
items.text: (Image credit: Studio Rochowski) Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter The site of Connaught House is a storied one. Its corner of north London on St John's Wood Terrace is a stone's throw from Abbey Road Studios , Lord's Cricket Ground and Regent's Park. The building itself was initially a chapel, but then evolved into a squash club for a while, and the studio where Queen filmed Radio Ga Ga. Now, the Grade II-listed structure is entering a new chapter in life, as owner Marcus Cooper Group and developer Valouran reveal a new, boutique family of homes within, featuring architecture by Darling Associates and interiors by Gunter and Co. (Image credit: Studio Rochowski) Explore Connaught House in London Connaught House was originally built in 1841, a handsome neoclassical religious structure, featuring intricate Corinthian columns and crisp white stucco. Designed by architect John Tarring, it's been a local landmark and popular community spot for decades. The redesign project has been a painstakingly detailed one, transforming the interior into just five contemporary homes. The original chapel's striking crowning cupola, which was lost for almost 100 years due to past alterations, was beautifully restored. Meanwhile, handcrafted windows and refined rooflines help bring the building into the 21st century. (Image credit: Studio Rochowski) (Image credit: Studio Rochowski) The resulting five apartments are all unique, designed using a common language of green and neutral tones, and timber and stone surfaces to create a coherent whole. Gunter and Co's Irene Gunter says: 'Our approach to the interiors was shaped by a pursuit centred on bringing back the chapel's original character- celebrating the arches, the period detailing, and the quality of daylight, and restoring features lost to a series of unsympathetic alterations over the years. We were careful, though, not to simply wind the clock back. It was just as important that the five homes felt luxurious, refined and considered for modern-day living, not a museum piece. (Image credit: Studio Rochowski) (Image credit: Studio Rochowski) 'The overarching approach was to let the architecture dictate the language, room by room, rather than applying one flat design across all five homes. The apartments with the arched windows at the front of the building lean into a more classical style, in keeping with the chapel's original proportions and detailing. To the rear, where the building is more contemporary, the interiors shift into a more modern design language,' she continues. 'What ties the apartments together is a shared material palette - sympathetic wood tones, neutral paint colours, and consistent ironmongery and tapware carried through both the classical and contemporary spaces. That common thread is what gives the collection cohesion, even as each apartment's character shifts depending on where it sits in the building.' Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. (Image credit: Studio Rochowski) (Image credit: Studio Rochowski) Soft furnishings, curated artwork and the building sense of space and generosity – through tall ceilings and large windows that open up to the surrounding green spaces – complement perfectly the design studio's craft-led approach. Says Gunter: 'Every supplier and maker was chosen through the same lens as everything else on this project – quality, craft and longevity. We leaned heavily on a team of suppliers we've tested and trusted over years of projects, with a strong focus on UK makers. Around 80 per cent of what you'll find across the homes is UK-made. This is a proudly British project, and investing in that craftsmanship felt like the right way to honour it. We also wanted this to be a chance to shine a light on new artisans we've discovered along the way. In each of the apartments, you'll find beautiful bespoke pieces created by makers we've met at craft fairs, and others discovered along the way and beyond.' (Image credit: Studio Rochowski) gunterandco.com valouran.com connaught-house.com TOPICS Ellie Stathaki Ellie Stathaki is the Architecture & Environment Director at Wallpaper*. She trained as an architect at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in Greece and studied architectural history at the Bartlett in London. Now an established journalist, she has been a member of the Wallpaper* team since 2006, visiting buildings across the globe and interviewing leading architects such as Tadao Ando and Rem Koolhaas. Ellie has also taken part in judging panels, moderated events, curated shows and contributed in books, such as The Contemporary House (Thames & Hudson, 2018), Glenn Sestig Architecture Diary (2020) and House London (2022).
designers: Darling Associates and interiors by Gunter and Co

items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Bar carts are not just for someone who likes to host a cocktail soirée. In fact, the predecessor of the bar cart was once a Victorian-era tea trolley. Only when the Prohibition hit did these side tables on wheels find their true calling. Many, many iterations later—think: Alvar Aalto’s iconic tea trolley, which has inspired many picks on this list, and USM ’s blessedly minimalist spin on the genre—the beauty of this booze trolley remains that it can completely transform a room or give a useless nook some purpose. Though they’ve fallen out of favor in many modern homes, these rolling wonders make an elegant—and functional—home base for all your mixology essentials, from stemware and decanters to liquor bottles and mixers. They also don’t have to be used to haul booze at all, instead doubling as portable storage for crafts, books, beauty or bathroom supplies, and houseplants. Employed outside, a stylish bar cart can give a dinner party some polish or emulate a poolside butler. Load it up with a pitcher of lemonade and a basket of sunscreen on top, and extra towels on the bottom and you’ll never have to leave your lounge. items.title: In This Midcentury Nashville Home a Mosaic Rainbow-Hued Window Brings Color to the Earthy Interiors
items.summary: Founders of Eneby Home combined one-of-a-kind pieces with a natural palette to create their memorable family home
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Here’s one you may not have heard before: What do Serge Mouille sconces, a Louis Poulsen artichoke pendant, and Borge Mogensen dining chairs have in common? Hint, hint: They all live in the Nashville home of Doug and Carina Jenkins, the founders of antiques and vintage furniture store Eneby Home . One might reasonably presume the home of antiques purveyors to be chock-full of one-of-a-kind finds from far-flung locales, and while that is certainly the case here, the husband-and-wife duo’s house otherwise expertly subverts expectations. Built in 1970, the uber-quiet four-acre property sits at the top of a hill overlooking seemingly endless rolling valleys. It’s surrounded by native honeysuckle bushes and Tennessee Fieldstone, and the sun sets on the front side of the home at 6:37 p.m., says Doug, who dreamed of building what he describes as an “art gallery” for their furniture. The Jenkinses kept the wall of original Tennessee Fieldstone—and the original copper fireplace—but added their own flair with vintage furnishings, like a La Mura sofa, Gianfranco Frattini for Cassina leather lounge chairs, a Charles Dudouyt credenza, and a 1960s marble fossil coffee table from Italy. “It’s super unique,” says Doug. “It doesn’t have a name behind it.” Save to wishlist Save to wishlist CB2 Leather Square Brown Pouf $229 CB2 Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Slow Roads Tabac & Noir Hand Towel $45 Shop $45 Slow Roads Doug and Carina Jenkins, the founders of Eneby Home, with their daughters. They kept the original Tennessee Fieldstone on the wall and paired it with an antique marble dining table that’s “huge and heavy,” says Doug. “The guys hated bringing stuff to our house.” Even though the Louis Poulsen artichoke pendant is often seen in copper, the Jenkins were able to source one with a green finish, seen here. The chairs are Borge Mogensen; the 1960s geometric painting is from France. The couple bought the house as-is—black toilets, mustard-hued siding, and early 2000s kitchen included—and embarked on a “bigger than expected” renovation, says Doug, that translated to moving walls, updating floor plans, a new roof and flooring, and overall furnishings, of course. With the resulting minimalist white walls and clean lines, how does one amass the amount of character evident here? “When you build in materials that have inherent imperfection, that naturally bakes in a lot of warmth,” says Dutton. Think locally sourced, character-grade white oak flooring throughout; imported reclaimed European bluestone that’s well over 100 years old in the primary bath; and an original copper fireplace in the living room. “The mosaic supposedly came from a building in Bologna,” says Doug. “The morning sun comes up on this side” and ignites a fire of filtered light within the home. “The island has a commercial look to it,” says Doug of the Vipp system. “It hit every box. It’s sick.” Dutton helped reconfigure the space’s floor plan to open the room to the dining area. The oven is by Miele. A Guillerme et Chambron cabinet, sourced from Eneby Home, houses curiosities. The 1960s pendant light is Stilnovo. The guest bathroom originally had a black toilet and smoked glass. Now it features vintage Serge Mouille sconces, of which Doug has “never seen another pair,” a 250-year-old antique Italian mirror from the 1800s, and a Josef Hoffman bench. “Flaws make the house feel better, not worse,” says Dutton. “But creating something that looks effortless actually takes a lot of coordination. We wanted it to feel like it had just happened that way, and installing materials that feel like they’ve been there forever automatically gives the house permanence and ensures it’ll age gracefully over time.” The push-and-pull between old and new, simple and full of character, clean and distressed is one the Jenkins family is familiar with. The balancing act makes the house interesting, says Doug, and the same inclination to lean on historic materials translates just as well to furnishings. “Some of this stuff we’d been saving in hopes we’d one day be able to use it for our own house,” says Doug. One such example is a 1940s or ’50s-era, rainbow-hued mosaic window the couple bought five years ago and stored in a crate ever since. “We asked Greg to change the layout of the wall to make it work,” says Doug. The stone sculpture on display in front of the window is another; it’s 2,000 years old, from Rome. An earthy palette in the primary bedroom lets the landscape through the windows do the talking. The sconces are by Biny; the oversized 1880 landscape painting is from France; the chairs are Borge Mogensen; the side table is Charles Dudouyt, and the floor lamp is La Borne. “The fireplace is original, and we ran with it,” says Doug. “It’s New Mexico style and is super cool.” It’s paired with an abstract geometric art piece and a collection of vases from Denmark. items.title: Everybody Wants to Do Shabbat Dinner at Erin Foster and Simon Tikhman’s Cozy, Playful LA Home
items.summary: The creator of Netflix’s Nobody Wants This and music executive worked with JDP Interiors to bring in color, pattern, and an AI assistant to their historic home
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story The recently dropped third season of the hit Netflix rom-com Nobody Wants This begins with a picture of domestic bliss: Kristen Bell and Adam Brody’s characters cheerfully lugging boxes and eating pizza sans dishes—living together at last. The fictional romance between the witty podcaster and “hot rabbi” is inspired by that of series creator Erin Foster and her husband Simon Tikhman, albeit loosely. Like Bell’s Joanne, Foster converted to Judaism before their wedding in 2019; unlike Brody’s Noah, Tikhman is a music executive, not a rabbi—but art is still intermingling with life. As their onscreen alter egos feather their nest, Foster, Tikhman, and their two-year-old daughter Noa are starring in a new season of their own, moving into a 1920s Los Angeles home that mixes undefinable colors and bold pattern play with the “European flavor” of an old-world estate, per Tikhman. Researching the house’s roots, Foster found Spanish, Mediterranean revival, and English influences, and the couple felt free to embrace all three. “I don’t tend to like following a set of rules,” Foster says, “whether it be in fashion or in television writing or in design.” To create more of a grand entrance, the entry foyer was opened up on the second floor and “guests often mistake the entry tile as original,” Pickens Dinwiddy says. The stair runner is by Stark and the vintage mirror is from Nickey Kehoe . The walls are painted in Benjamin Moore’s Soft Chamois . Tikhman, Foster, and Noa seated on the custom living room sofas upholstered in a Schumacher fabric. “I had girls over for drinks and we sat in the room together,” Foster says. “It’s kind of like the gossip room.” The sofas flank a custom coffee table in the living room. The vintage chair is from 1stDibs , the ottoman is upholstered in a fabric by Scalamandré, and the vintage floor lamp is from PRB Collection. The sconces are from Aqua Gallery and the curtain fabric is by Rose Tarlow Melrose House . The chandelier is by Cox London. “They handmake each metal leaf,” Pickens Dinwiddy says. The artwork is by Danielle Orchard from Perrotin Gallery. The multihyphenate cohost of The World’s First Podcast and cofounder of cool-girl fashion line Favorite Daughter acknowledges that she runs in a “circle of really fashion-forward women who have been featured in AD and have elevated taste in art and in design, and it’s very intimidating,” including when it came to selecting a designer. “There starts to be this culture of, ‘Well, you have to use this person,’” Foster says. Instead, she discovered her own on Instagram. Foster cold-messaged Joyce Pickens Dinwiddy, founder of LA’s JDP Interiors (and later the brains behind Favorite Daughter’s Beverly Hills boutique) about masterminding the new-old home’s four-year renovation and redesign. “They’re a cool couple and they don’t want this stuffy, old-school, fully British-feeling home,” Pickens Dinwiddy says, but Foster and Tikhman still craved classicism their way—something “cozy, young, and playful but sophisticated at the same time.” “I’ve realized I’m obsessed with the color green,” Foster says. “The color feels a little shocking sometimes to people, but it’s also inviting and it’s also kind of earthy and cozy.” The kitchen is painted in Denali Green from Dunn-Edwards and the cabinets are backed in a Rose Tarlow Melrose House fabric. Tikhman requested and received a dedicated drinks fridge in the kitchen, filled with clean sodas and seltzers. “Simon was like, ‘I want a Kardashian fridge,’” Foster says. The kitchen backsplash includes custom hand-painted tiles by Lascaux Tile and the hood is copper. The range is by Lacanche, the fridge is Sub-Zero , and the sink fittings are by Waterstone . The pendants are custom. The result is a warm, hip house where Pickens Dinwiddy, who’s married to a Brit, introduced charming flourishes familiar to UK country homes . She softened cabinetry in the not-quite olive green kitchen with floral chintz fabric by Rose Tarlow Melrose House and added a skirt beneath the sink in the scullery, a hybrid mud room/potting room traditionally used to water herb pots from the garden. The glass-ceilinged breakfast nook—an “architectural feat,” according to Pickens Dinwiddy, that was lowered into the home via crane and which Foster says “probably added a year to the project”—has been crowned the solarium. With sun drenching its slate blue walls and sculpted medallion details, “it’s a really special place for us to have early dinner with our daughter,” Foster says, and also where she pops open her laptop, morning coffee in hand. “Erin likes to wake up, have her coffee, pull up her computer, and sit in a room,” Tikhman says. “And her dream was that’s what the solarium was going to be.” The custom banquette is upholstered in a fabric from Perennials Fabrics and topped with pillows covered in Robert Kime fabric . The chairs by Casamidy are upholstered in a Perennials by Rose Tarlow fabric . The pendant is by Vaughan . “I wanted to do wall-to-wall paneling somewhere,” Pickens Dinwiddy says. “This felt like the place for it so that there wasn’t a wall treatment competing with this beautiful tile floor.” The floor tile is by Ann Sacks. The mudroom bench is upholstered in a fabric by Décors Barbares. The custom dining room table is surrounded by custom chairs covered in a Jasper fabric . The 1950s chandelier is from Fargo Design and the vintage Swedish sconces are from 1stDibs . The 1970s Danish sideboard is from Chairish and the mirror is custom. I revel in the regal room names, but the couple is decidedly unfussy about their solarium and scullery—“words that Erin and I never used before building this house,” Tikhman says. “We actually only speak with English accents when we’re at home,” she cracks. In fact, Foster applauds Tikhman for gently voicing concerns when, in the throes of the project, her old-world sensibilities started to feel a bit too old. Or as Tikhm

items.title: Meghan Trainor. Zedd. Joe Jonas and Sophie Turner. This $18 Million Manse Is Collecting Celeb Owners. Who’s Next?
items.summary: Maybe it’s the pub, maybe it’s the recording studio, but there’s certainly something about the home—which just returned to the market—that LA elites find enchanting
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Meghan Trainor has listed her Encino, California, home for just under $18 million. If the songstress and her actor husband, Daryl Sabara, pass the torch to another notable name , it would continue the estate’s ongoing chain of celebrity stewards. Trainor bought the house from DJ Zedd in 2024 for about $17 million; Zedd had paid $15.2 million in 2021 when he bought it from Joe Jonas and Sophie Turner, who were the first to move into the six-bedroom, 12-bathroom manse when it was completed in 2019. They scooped it up for $14.1 million . To put it simply: The property has never been owned by someone without a Wikipedia page. As its listing description reads: “This compound is for the most discerning Buyer.” Unsurprisingly, the home hosts a swath of amenities that are as elite as its residents. Tucked behind tall gates and hedges, the contemporary-style build, designed by Jae Omar, spans nearly 15,000 square feet. The dwelling’s main floor hosts a great room with two fireplaces, wall-to-wall pocket doors that open to the backyard, and a library nook . The eat-in kitchen is complete with a built-in bar and a sprawling center island with a live-edge wooden breakfast bar seating seven. An additional catering kitchen, an office, and an impressive playroom outfitted with a climbing wall, a slide, and a foam pit round out the main level, along with a fitness and wellness center and “perhaps the best-sounding studio in the world,” according to Zedd , who added that amenity during his ownership. Five ensuite bedrooms are situated upstairs, as well as another fireplace-warmed living area. The primary suite boasts yet another fireplace, a wet bar, a bathroom, two spacious dressing rooms, and walls that slide open to a sizable balcony. Outdoor amenities include a pool and spa, a kitchen, a putting green, a projection screen, and a fire pit. A guesthouse with a billiards pub and a movie theater round out the compound. Watch this space to see if some lucky celeb buyer keeps the home’s hot streak alive.

items.title: The Kitchen Trends Designers Expect to See Everywhere in 2027
items.summary: The National Kitchen & Bath Association’s 2027 forecast has arrived.
items.text: 2 min read Above: the kitchen of an Athens home designed by Nashmita Rajiah. Partial walls, hidden appliances, and pantries with room for prep are among the kitchen features expected to gain ground next year, according to the National Kitchen & Bath Association’s 2027 Kitchen Trends Report . Based on a survey of 830 kitchen-industry professionals—including designers, manufacturers, remodelers, and architects—the report looks at the layouts, materials, lighting, and technology they expect to be popular over the next three years. Here are the main takeaways. Defined Layouts Gieves Anderson In a David Netto-designed apartment , linen curtains with Samuel & Sons trim divide the space between the kitchen and dining area. NKBA reports growing interest in partial walls, movable partitions, and separate kitchen zones—a shift from last year’s forecast, when open layouts were still gaining ground. Dedicated prep spaces and back kitchens are also emerging features, cited by nearly half of designers. Kitchens are still expected to get bigger, with 52 percent of designers anticipating growth. The kitchen’s surrounding rooms are growing, too. NKBA reports that mudrooms and laundry spaces are increasingly being integrated into kitchen plans. The vast majority of designers expect attached mudrooms to be popular over the next three years, with 45 percent anticipating mudrooms getting larger and 43 percent expecting laundry spaces to grow. Hidden Appliances and Enclosed Storage Appliances are increasingly being incorporated into cabinetry rather than left on display. Eighty-five percent of designers agree cabinets are being designed to hide appliances and other functional elements, and roughly two-thirds say open shelving is on its way out in favor of enclosed storage. Pantries are taking on more work, too. Nearly 90 percent agree they are becoming multifunctional extensions of the kitchen, and three-quarters expect dedicated small-appliance stations to be popular. Separate beverage areas continue to gain support, with 90 percent anticipating their popularity, up from 85 percent in the 2026 report. Martin Morrell An English Victorian manor designed by Linda Boronkay features an enclosed pantry with bespoke oak joinery. Wood Cabinets and Neutral Colors Neutrals remain the leading color of choice, followed by greens and blues. For cabinetry, light and medium tones draw equal interest, and white oak is the preferred wood for roughly half of designers. Islands don’t necessarily have to match: a little more than half expect them to feature a different color from the surrounding cabinets. Quartzite and quartz lead countertop preferences, with nearly half of designers favoring honed or matte finishes. Layers of Lighting The lighting forecast includes under-cabinet lights, illuminated cabinet interiors, nighttime path lighting, sconces, and pendants. Eighty-four percent of designers agree kitchens will incorporate multiple layers of light, and 78 percent say lighting is increasingly being used as a design feature rather than just a functional necessity. Under-cabinet lighting leads the forecast at 87 percent, followed by interior-cabinet lighting at 76 percent. Ventilation, Water Filtration, and Leak Protection NKBA identifies ventilation, water filtration, touchless faucets, and sound-absorbing materials among the report’s wellness features. Designers are also discussing ways to make kitchens more resilient: 65 percent cite leak-detection systems and automatic shut-off valves, 62 percent cite backup power, and a little over half point to ventilation and air filtration. Julia Cancilla Social Media & News Editor Julia Cancilla is the social media & news editor at ELLE Decor, where she oversees the brand's socials and covers design, pop culture, and emerging trends. She also authors the monthly ELLE Decoroscope column. Her work has appeared in Inked magazine, House Beautiful, Marie Claire, and more. items.title: 7 Gilded Age Homes Where You Can Live Like the Astors
items.summary: In honor of   The Gilded Age  ’s fourth season, here are the period mansions-turned-hotels you can stay in right now.
items.text: Erin McGinn Above, Castle Hill Inn in Newport, Rhode Island. Gilded Age barons of industry constructed extravagant homes—year-round mansions and summer “cottages”—that were more palaces to their wealth than practical residences. Notable families like the Vanderbilts, Carnegies, and Astors once had houses dotted across New York City and throughout fashionable summer retreats like Newport, Rhode Island. Many of these elaborate structures have since fallen to the ravages of time, with the staggering costs of upkeep rendering their use as private residences all but obsolete. Yet, though some of these private homes have disappeared, our curiosity about them has only increased. Since HBO’s hit show The Gilded Age debuted, interest in visiting the era’s architectural marvels has surged, and in Newport, which is home to one of the country’s largest concentrations of Gilded Age mansions, there’s been a steady rise in visitors touring the town’s mansions specifically because of the show. Visiting the opulent, and often wildly impractical, mansions that inspired the fictional lives of The Gilded Age ’s characters has its charms, but rather than just taking a tour, why not spend the night? Up and down the East Coast, a handful of Gilded Age mansions are preserved not as museums, but as hotels—inviting curious travelers to do more than just visit and admire the history, but to sleep within the jewel boxes of their walls. Courtesy of Castle Hill Inn Castle Hill Inn Newport, Rhode Island Castle Hill Inn is a different kind of Gilded Age mansion, one that turns to timber and antiquities over marble and gilding. The home’s original owner, Alexander Agassiz, was a Harvard professor of natural sciences who made his fortune in copper mining. With his newfound wealth, Agassiz built his summer home—Castle Hill—on a relatively isolated parcel of forty acres, a fifteen minute drive away from the pomp and pageantry of the Vanderbilt’s side of town. He used the home as a summer research lab, hosting students in its many rooms and running the lab in what is today the parlor, while also entertaining a who’s who of literary luminaries, including Edith Wharton and Mark Twain. Today, Castle Hill Inn is one of the most famous places to stay in Newport, not only for its luxurious rooms, afternoon tea, and award-winning restaurant, but also for its sweeping ocean-front lawn and seaside views. Thorton Wilder lived in the turret suite—Agassiz’s former observatory and today the hotel’s most beautiful room—while writing his last book, and Grace Kelly lived in one of the beach cottages during the 1955 filming of “High Society.” Stopping by Castle Hill Inn for a drink and taking a short walk to its still in-use lighthouse remains a summer essential in Newport, but there is nothing quite like staying the night. Courtesy The Chanler at Cliff Walk Hotel Chanler Newport, Rhode Island Hotel Chanler is, unlike Castle Hill, right in the thick of Newport’s Gilded Age neighborhood, and it’s clear from its location that it was built (to use a period expression) to keep up with the Joneses. The opulent mansion was constructed in 1873 as the summer “cottage” of New York Congressman John Winthrop Chanler and his wife Margaret Astor Ward. Chanler hosted an elaborate range of guests at his summer home, including President Theodore Roosevelt and poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow. The home, which Chanler called “Cliff Lawn,” was the very first mansion to be built on the Cliff Walk, now a public walkway with views of these historic homes. Over the years, the mansion went from being a private residence to a museum and later a girl’s school. It wasn’t until 2003 that it opened as the twenty-room Chanler Hotel. Today, it’s ornately decorated in various period-specific styles such as Regency, Louis XVI, Renaissance, and English Tudor. Last spring, The Chanler opened a more pared down restaurant, Remy’s Loose. Remy’s feels fit for Mr. Chanler and his guests, who we can imagine sprawling out across the chenille, fringed edged slipper chairs, and enjoying the just fussy-enough French menu. Advertisement - Continue Reading Below Courtesy of The Fifth Avenue Hotel The Fifth Avenue Hotel New York, New York The Fifth Avenue Hotel, which opened its doors in late 2023, has a multi-layered history rooted in the Gilded Age. In 1856, legendary hostess and doyenne of New York society, Charlotte Goodridge, commissioned the construction of a lavish private home and carriage house at the coveted corner of Fifth Avenue and 28th Street. Goodridge filled her mansion with treasures from around the globe and entertained lavishly. But following her death, Goodridge’s home met the same fate as much of the neighborhood and was torn down. However, rather than being replaced by a skyscraper like much of the surrounding area, Goodridge’s mansion was reborn in 1907 as a striking five story neo-Renaissance palazzo design by McKim, Mead & White, the architects behind many of the New York’s most famous early 20th century buildings including The Morgan Library and Museum, the Bowery Savings Bank, and the Metropolitan Club. More recently, a decades-long renovation overseen by Flâneur Hospitality, Martin Brudnizki Design Studio, and architect Perkins Eastman transformed the building into a 153-room hotel, with a restored limestone and brick façade, an added-in glass tower, a ballroom fit for a Goodridge party, and a European inspired restaurant, Café Carmellini. The hotel now has a Gilded Age-inspired look, complete with polished marble floors, grand arched windows, rich color palettes, and art and curiosities from around the world. Michael Worthington Hotel Bardo Savannah, Georgia Hotel Bardo may have opened in 2024, but its history extends much further back. It was built in 1888 as a private home for Lewis Kayton, a businessman from Baltimore who settled in Savannah. Kayton tapped architects Alfred Eichberg and Hyman Witcover to create his brick and terracotta mansion right on the

items.title: Next-Gen Mineral Surfaces for Your Kitchen, Bath, and More
items.summary: Éclos by Cosentino merges natural beauty and breakthrough technology.
items.text: Courtesy of House Beautiful 3 min read As a homeowner, the two things you tend to expect most from your ideal kitchen countertop are all too often in conflict: You want it to be truly beautiful, to evoke elemental, one-of-a-kind natural stone. But you also want all the resilience, innovation, and eco-friendliness that 21st-century technology can provide. Renowned sustainable-surfaces brand Cosentino has made its reputation bridging those desires, and its Éclos line is both good-looking and good for the planet, simultaneously timeless in appeal and tech-forward in performance. That’s exactly what made it a surface of choice for many of the rooms in the House Beautiful Whole Home in Charleston, South Carolina, an effort of our sister publication. Here’s what makes Éclos the next generation of surfaces: Technology Courtesy of House Beautiful The Whole Home kitchen (also shown at top) is clad in Éclos Legnd. Unlike traditional stone that is cut from a quarry and installed in discrete slabs, Éclos is manufactured from a combination of minerals fused together with a proprietary technology the company calls Inlayr—the name of which gives rise to this new category of high-tech materials: inlayered mineral surfaces. Advanced robotics allow the surfaces to be imbued with sophisticated, three-dimensional veins and patterns that echo those of precious materials pulled from the earth. The result is the unique appearance of prized stone like marble or granite, with a strength that natural stone could never achieve on its own. Durability Courtesy of House Beautiful The powder room countertop was fabricated with Éclos Wonder. So what does that mean once you actually install Éclos in your kitchen or bathroom? For one thing, far less maintenance than might be required of natural materials. Éclos is nonporous, so it never needs to be sealed, much less resealed every six months to a year as, say, you might need to do with a marble counter. And it’s as solid as a rock—wait, more solid than rock: In the kitchen, it can withstand temperatures up to 428°F without showing signs of damage such as stains or cracks. In the bathroom, a knocked-over bottle of nail polish remover is no big deal. Dings, scratches, stains... things of the past. Sustainability Courtesy of House Beautiful A guest bathroom’s double-sink countertop features Éclos Landr. One of Cosentino’s core values as a company is sustainability—the brand devotes a large portion of its research and development resources to discovering new and better ways to employ recycled materials and reduce its overall carbon footprint. In the case of Éclos, Cosentino says the development of the surface involved nearly 30,000 hours of research and testing. The result is its most advanced product yet; Éclos uses zero crystalline silica and a minimum of 50 percent recycled materials (in some products in the new line, that goes up to almost 90 percent). That’s welcome news for designers and homeowners who are committed to incorporating sustainable, socially and environmentally responsible materials and practices into their renovations and new builds. Aesthetics Courtesy of House Beautiful Éclos Wondr gracefully tops a counter in another Whole Home bathroom. Of course, when it comes to creating a space you love and will be happy living with for years, state-of-the-artness only goes so far—style and sophistication are the other half of the equation. It’s a principle Cosentino, which also created designer-beloved modern surfaces like Silestone and Dekton , has doubled down on. The Éclos line is characterized by a carefully curated selection of quietly luxurious colors and textures, each crafted to mirror the richness and tactile appeal of quarry-cut stone. The surfaces have a visual depth and luster that almost make you forget how hardworking they are. For kitchens and bathrooms—anywhere you can envision the sophistication of stone— Éclos can be key to crafting a space that is high-end but never high-maintenance. It's the future of surfaces, delivered right now. Advertisement - Continue Reading Below

items.text: Following its acquisition of Casa Collective, Domes Resorts has announced three new hotel openings in Greece for 2027. The expansion will see Casa Cook debut in Halkidiki and Santorini, alongside a new Cook’s Club property in Kassandra, marking the next phase of development for the lifestyle hospitality brands. Casa Cook Athos will open in northern Greece in Summer 2027, reviving a 1959 Modernist landmark overlooking a sheltered bay on the lesser-known peninsula near the gateway to Mount Athos. Originally designed by one of Greece’s leading architects, Periklis Sakellarios, and now reimagined by Berlin-based studio Vision Alphabet, the 60-key hotel’s architectural character has been preserved through a sensitive restoration with Casa Cook’s distinctive, understated design, and will open a further 45 rooms its second stage. The hotel will comprise guestrooms, suites and a villa, two restaurants with local dishes and wines that reflect paréa, direct beach access and a spa with Yoga, breathwork, meditation and sound rituals amongst its wellness programming. The launch of Cook’s Club Kassandra marks the next evolution of the brand, introducing its first property on the Greek mainland, alongside a new creative direction. Scheduled to open in Summer 2027 among the pine-covered hills of Kriopigi on Halkidiki’s western peninsula, the adults-only property resembles a relaxed, private summer house centred around the main pool and pool bar area. The Boathouse, an open kitchen and restaurant, offers locally sourced dishes, the spa and outdoor gym are accompanied by yoga platform and the landscaped gardens provide social areas for extended relaxation. Art plays a heightened role with contemporary pieces and large murals displayed throughout the hotel, and a collaboration with Brazilian artist Luciano Cian marks the beginning of a wider series of creative partnerships, from original works and live murals to occasional artist residencies. Casa Cook Santorini will be the third property to open in 2027 in the village of Firostefani with just six traditional cave-style residences. Rooted in the island’s traditional whitewashed cave houses with striking Caldera views, the adults-only boutique hotel brings the brand’s design philosophy to a more personal scale, through tailored experiences, privacy and the flexibility to discover the island at one’s own pace. “The acquisition of Casa Collective represents an important step in our growth strategy, allowing us to expand our lifestyle ecosystem while building on the distinct identities of Casa Cook and Cook’s Club,” saidsaysDr. George P. Spanos, CEO of Domes Resorts and Chairman of Casa Collective. “These three openings in hotels we own showcase how much we believe in the soul and the character of these brands.” Remo Masala, Founder of Casa Collective and Vision Alphabet, adds: “As Casa Collective grows, we’re building on our deeper understanding of our guests to create meaningful reasons to return, with experiences that respect the individual character of each brand and destination.” casa collective Casa Cook Domes Resorts europe expansion Greece Related Posts 24 January 2025 Casa Cook to launch first mountain retreat 29 March 2023 Domes announces further Greek expansion 6 December 2021 Domes Resorts to expand internationally

items.title: Q&A: Magnovent explores bioclimatic design in hospitality settings
items.summary:
As rising temperatures and energy costs place greater pressure on hospitality operators, Magnovent CEO Jonathan Jover explores how intelligent airflow […] 
 The post  Q&A: Magnovent explores bioclimatic design in hospitality settings  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Q&A: Magnovent explores bioclimatic design in hospitality settings 5 November 2026 | In Products | By Hannah Wintle As rising temperatures and energy costs place greater pressure on hospitality operators, Magnovent CEO Jonathan Jover explores how intelligent airflow and bioclimatic design can improve guest comfort while reducing energy consumption. How are changing guest expectations reshaping environmental comfort in hospitality? Rising temperatures and increasingly demanding guest expectations are making thermal comfort a strategic priority for hospitality operators. At the same time, rising energy costs are putting pressure on operating margins. The challenge is to create consistently comfortable environments without allowing energy consumption to escalate. This requires a more intelligent approach to managing temperature, airflow and insulation. What is bioclimatic architecture, and why is it so important for hotels and residences? Bioclimatic architecture considers the relationship between a building, its local climate and the people who use it. In hospitality, this means combining effective insulation, natural or mechanical ventilation and efficient heating and cooling systems to reduce reliance on air conditioning. By designing for climate from the outset, hotels can improve thermal comfort, reduce energy demand and create spaces that feel naturally comfortable while preserving their architectural identity. How can climate and airflow enhance the guest experience? Comfort is not determined by air temperature alone. Air movement influences how the body perceives heat, allowing guests to feel comfortable at higher thermostat settings. By combining air conditioning with well-designed ventilation, hotels can create a more balanced and pleasant indoor climate, while reducing energy consumption. The result is an environment that feels better, operates more efficiently and supports a more enjoyable guest experience. How do your solutions help hotels reduce energy use without compromising comfort? The key is to move beyond the assumption that lower temperatures automatically mean greater comfort. Setting air conditioning to 20°C, for example, can significantly increase energy consumption without necessarily delivering a better guest experience. By combining efficient ceiling fans with air conditioning, hotels can maintain comfort at higher thermostat settings and reduce cooling energy consumption. Based on results reported by our clients, this approach can deliver energy savings of 30–45%, depending on the building, climate and operating conditions. Our objective is to make comfort measurable, efficient and easier to manage. Can you share a hospitality project that demonstrates the impact of your approach? One Ibiza Suites is a good example of how a considered combination of building performance and airflow can transform the guest experience. By improving roof insulation and introducing ceiling fans in the lobby and restaurant, the hotel enhanced thermal comfort in key shared spaces. The combined intervention achieved a reduction in perceived temperature of approximately 4°C, demonstrating that comfort can be improved without relying exclusively on more intensive air conditioning. What’s next for Magnovent? Our next step is to help hospitality operators reduce their reliance on air conditioning, in both summer and winter, with a target of reducing energy consumption by an average of 30%. Through increasingly sophisticated control systems, we aim to manage airflow, heating and cooling as an integrated solution, helping operators maintain their desired level of perceived comfort while optimising energy use. Ultimately, we want to move the industry towards a more intelligent understanding of temperature: one in which buildings are designed and operated around how people actually experience comfort, rather than simply the number displayed on a thermostat. www.magnovent.eu air conditioning bioclimatic design climate change guest comfort magnovent Related Posts 19 September 2023 Inside FOH’s luxury hospitality solutions 22 June 2023 Madera talks timber, bespoke design and hospitality interiors 5 December 2019 Cameron Design House’s Inari chandelier designed for hospitality settings

items.title: Thompson Hotels lands in Rome
items.summary:
Hyatt has announced the opening of Thompson Rome, a 69-room hotel owned and operated by AG Group and Rossifin Group, […] 
 The post  Thompson Hotels lands in Rome  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Hyatt has announced the opening of Thompson Rome, a 69-room hotel owned and operated by AG Group and Rossifin Group, marking the brand’s debut in Italy . Set within a reimagined iconic landmark on Via delle Botteghe Oscure, Thompson Rome draws on the architectural character of its 1940s home and the layered history of Via delle Botteghe Oscure, one of Rome’s most significant streets and a landmark in post-war Italian political history. Original elements, including a sweeping marble staircase, have been carefully restored, while a sculptural wall and inlaid floor by celebrated Italian artist Gio Pomodoro, rediscovered during the renovation after decades hidden from view – have been preserved and given new prominence within the hotel. Bespoke furnishings, refined detailing and layered natural materials bring a contemporary expression to the building’s history. Thompson Rome’s 69 guestrooms and suites take cues from the character of a contemporary Roman residence, pairing warm natural materials with custom furnishings and understated details. With 19 suites, nearly one-third of the hotel’s accommodation offering, guests can choose from Junior Suites, Suites with patios or terraces, and the 104-square-metre Thompson Suite with 80-square-metre private terrace. Designed as a counterpoint to the energy of the city outside, the rooms feel residential and refined, with select accommodations offering views across Rome’s historic rooftops and landmarks. Several rooms feature balconies overlooking Via delle Botteghe Oscure, while select rooms offer private patios facing Rome’s historic buildings. Thompson Rome’s art programme, creates a dialogue between the history of the site and contemporary art. The collection brings together works by artists associated with the Scuola Romana and the Scuola di Piazza del Popolo, alongside contemporary artists whose practices reflect Rome’s longstanding cultural openness and international influences including Francesco Del Drago, Giangaetano Patanè, and Guido Strazza. Presented throughout the hotel’s public spaces and guestrooms, the artworks are an integral part of the guest experience, connecting the memory of the site with the creativity of Rome today. A rotating artist-in-residence programme will further extend Thompson Rome’s connection to the city’s creative community through exhibitions, conversations and other cultural programming. Three distinct food and beverage venues carry Thompson Rome from morning espresso and leisurely lunches through aperitivo, dinner and drinks above the city. At Lyve Restaurant, Executive Chef Fabio Fioravanti brings a contemporary Mediterranean approach to ingredients and traditions from the Italian coast and across the region. Seafood is central to the menu, with Mediterranean fish and shellfish alongside dishes that draw on bouillabaisse, rockfish broths, wild coastal herbs and rouille, reworked with a lighter touch while preserving the depth and character of the originals. The same attention extends to the pastry kitchen, where precise technique and contrasting flavours and textures shape the dessert menu. A native of Ostia, Fioravanti brings more than two decades of international experience, including time with the Alain Ducasse group and at the three-Michelin-starred Le Louis XV – Alain Ducasse at the Hôtel de Paris Monte-Carlo. At Lyve, that technical precision carries through a dining experience that is refined yet relaxed, with the quality of the ingredients and clarity of the cooking taking centre stage. Above the hotel, Lyve Rooftop pairs views across Rome with cocktails, Italian aperitivi and a menu designed for sharing. The Lobby Lounge offers the hotel’s most casual gathering place throughout the day, from coffee and light fare to aperitivo and cocktails. The hotel will extend the guest experience through a year-round programme shaped by Rome’s culinary, artistic and creative communities. Experiences will range from culinary workshops and guided tastings to Empire of Light, a photography-led experience from the hotel’s seventh floor that invites guests to discover Rome from above. “Rome has such a strong identity, so we wanted Thompson Rome to start with the city itself,” says Amar Lalvani, Chief Creative Officer, Hyatt Corporation and President & Creative Director, The Lifestyle Group, Hyatt . “The building, the neighbourhood, the food, the people and the way Romans live all shaped the hotel. The goal was to create a Thompson hotel that feels at home in Rome, a hotel travellers want to discover and Romans want to come back to.” architecture europe hotel design hyatt interior design italy rome thompson hotels Related Posts 14 June 2023 Thompson Hotels heading to Rome 21 February 2022 Design Hotels welcomes four new members 9 August 2021 Thompson Hotels arrives in Savannah

 The post  Capella to open at Dubai Peninsula in 2030  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Capella Hotel Group has announced Capella Dubai, set to open in 2030 on the Dubai Peninsula in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. The 115-key hotel will include a collection of suites with private pools, culminating in a 600m 2 Capella Suite conceived as a residential-style retreat. Set along one of Jumeirah’s most desired shorelines, Capella Dubai will open within the 210-acre waterfront destination by H&H. Conceived as a first-of-its-kind, design-driven destination, the Dubai Peninsula brings together hotel brands and private residences, complemented by dining, retail, a superyacht marina, a kilometre of private beach and over two million square feet of botanical gardens. Developed by H&H and designed by Denniston , the hotel will feature five social venues from the lobby lounge and The Living Room to the signature restaurant. Above it all, the rooftop will be home to a specialty restaurant and destination bar, inviting guests to dine against the Dubai skyline. Stretching nearly 70m across the rooftop, the pool will offer a tranquil retreat above the city, alongside single and double cabanas. A family pool will also feature at beach level. Capella Wellness will offer a holistic approach to wellbeing, encompassing the Auriga Spa, a Fitness Centre and Mind Body Studio, as well as an outdoor fitness area. Inspired by the restorative rhythms of the moon, Auriga Spa will feature male and female treatment rooms, a co-ed suite and VIP suite, alongside a hammam, hydrotherapy circuit pool, two biohacking facilities and grooming services. Dedicated relaxation lounges will offer quiet spaces to pause before and after treatments. For celebrations and gatherings, Capella Dubai will offer a spacious ballroom with a pre-function lounge, complemented by two meeting rooms, a VIP Majlis and an outdoor event lawn. “As Capella grows beyond Asia Pacific into the Middle East and Europe, we are entering an important new chapter for the brand,” says Roland Fasel, President, Capella Hotel Group. “The Middle East shares our appreciation for craftsmanship, culture and exceptional service, making it a natural home for Capella. Capella has always been deliberately selective about where it goes, choosing destinations where we believe we can create something meaningful and distinctive. “At Dubai Peninsula, our partnership with H&H is the foundation for all that we are building. They share our vision for the intimate, highly personalised experience Capella is known for, one that connects guests more deeply with Dubai, its culture and its people. With the opening of Capella Dubai in 2030, we will further establish our presence in one of the region’s most compelling cities, while remaining true to the hospitality that defines Capella.” Shahab Lutfi, Chairman, H&H adds: “Dubai Peninsula is conceived as a destination with a distinct identity, bringing together some of the world’s most renowned hospitality brands, exceptional residences and a unique waterfront setting. Capella brings a different dimension to this vision through its intimate, highly personalised approach to hospitality. We see a strong alignment between Capella’s emphasis on individual experiences and sense of place and our ambition to create a destination that offers more than exceptional design and location. Capella Dubai will introduce a more intimate, service-led hospitality experience to the city’s resort landscape, adding depth and character to the overall offering. “Working alongside Denniston, we are bringing hospitality, architecture and landscape together from the outset, ensuring that each responds to the setting and contributes to a coherent vision. For us, the strength of Dubai Peninsula lies in the way its different elements come together, from its shoreline and central park to its collection of hospitality and residential offerings. Capella’s distinctive character will be an important part of that mix, shaping a destination that feels considered, cohesive and different.” capella capella dubai Denniston dubai dubai peninsula H&H Jumeirah Related Posts 27 August 2025 Mandarin Oriental to open second Dubai outpost 11 October 2024 Ennismore’s Delano lands in Dubai 9 December 2009 Dusit Princess debuts in Dubai

items.title: Spagnulo & Partners redesigns Milan Marriott Hotel
items.summary:
The historic Milan Marriott Hotel has entered a new chapter following an extensive interior renovation by Spagnulo & Partners, the […] 
 The post  Spagnulo & Partners redesigns Milan Marriott Hotel  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: The historic Milan Marriott Hotel has entered a new chapter following an extensive interior renovation by Spagnulo & Partners, the Milan-based architecture and interior design studio led by Federico Spagnulo, Alessandra Carbone and Andrea Spagnulo. Encompassing the hotel’s 317 guest rooms, public areas and event spaces, the project establishes a contemporary architectural language that draws on the property’s history and its longstanding relationship with the city. The project is guided by a principle of architectural continuity, expressed through a system of geometries, proportions and materials that evolves across the interiors according to their scale and function. The grid emerges as a recurring design element, first appearing in the full-height shelving that structures the public areas before becoming a graphic motif reinterpreted in handwoven rugs and textiles. As it shifts in scale and material, its precise geometry takes on a softer, more tactile expression. In the communal areas, the design creates a sequence of spaces with different degrees of openness and intimacy. Bespoke furnishings define the various areas while maintaining visual continuity, whereas the use of wood introduces a warm, tactile element that balances the rigour of the geometry. The predominantly neutral colour palette is punctuated by carefully chosen colour accents, provided by upholstered furniture and rugs, which help to characterise the spaces and create different atmospheres. The same attention to proportion and the guest experience informs the renovation of the 317 guest rooms, where clean lines, natural finishes and contemporary furnishings create interiors conceived around comfort and functionality. The design responds to the requirements of international hospitality, balancing practical considerations with material quality and a distinctive visual identity. From the organisation of the spaces to the design of the furnishings and the lighting scheme, the project embodies Spagnulo & Partners’ bespoke approach, rooted in the relationship between architecture, materials and the quality of living. The result is a hotel that reinvents its character through a restrained design language, capable of interpreting the demands of contemporary hospitality whilst maintaining a connection with its history. hotel renovation italy Marriott milan renovation Spagnulo & Partners Related Posts 27 September 2023 Marriott International launches new midscale brand 9 May 2023 W Hotels to debut in Milan 27 July 2015 First-ever Marriott Hotel in Makkah

items.text: Hilton has announced the opening of Casa Verbena Madrid, Outset Collection by Hilton, an intimate 45-room hotel on Calle de Preciados in the heart of the capital. Marking the first Outset Collection hotel in Europe, the hotel features interiors by Madrid-born designer Lorenzo Castillo, complemented by views across the city’s rooftops. Casa Verbena Madrid takes its name from the traditional Spanish verbena: a lively neighbourhood celebration that brings people together through food, music and shared traditions. The hotel also draws on costumbrismo, the Spanish artistic tradition of depicting local customs, characters and daily rituals, looking beyond the capital’s landmarks to the cafés, streets and squares that shape life for Madrileños. The hotel’s interiors reflect a distinctly local perspective on the city. Costumbrismo-inspired artwork, warm materials, fluted glass, brass finishes and layered textures reference Madrid’s architectural and cultural heritage in a contemporary way. Many guestrooms look onto Preciados street and its typical Madrid façades, while Preciados Rooms open onto terraces with views across the city’s rooftops and towards the Royal Palace. “Casa Verbena Madrid offers a fresh perspective on the capital, whether guests are discovering it for the first time or returning to experience it differently,” says Álvaro Mazaheri, Managing Director, Arte Hoteles. “From a breakfast inspired by local favourites to recommendations we would share with friends, we want each stay to reveal more of the Madrid that lies beyond its best-known sights.” Elizabeth Scruggs, Brand Leader, Outset Collection by Hilton, also comments: “Casa Verbena Madrid represents the essence of Outset Collection, offering guests a stay that feels deeply connected to the destination. As our first hotel in Europe, it sets the tone for how we envision the collection growing around the world: through independent hotels with compelling stories, strong local identities and a genuine sense of discovery. With more than 100 hotels under development globally, we are building a collection of individual hotels that invite travellers to experience a destination through a more personal lens, all with the benefits of Hilton.” David Kelly, senior vice president, Continental Europe, Hilton, concludes: “Madrid is a special destination for Hilton, and in recent years we’ve broadened our presence in the city with distinctive brands and properties designed to meet different traveller needs. Casa Verbena Madrid builds on that story as the European debut of Outset Collection by Hilton. Full of character and with a strong sense of place, the hotel reflects the creativity and energy of Madrid. We’re delighted to welcome the hotel to our growing portfolio of collection properties across Europe.” europe hilton lorenzo castillo madrid outset collection spain Related Posts 24 June 2024 Curio Collection by Hilton debuts in Croatia 17 May 2024 NH Collection debuts in Finland 11 May 2021 Hilton debuts Tapestry Collection in mainland China

items.title: First Look: Andaz Turks & Caicos
items.summary:
Andaz has unveiled a first look at the interiors for Andaz Turks & Caicos. Set to open in Spring 2027, […] 
 The post  First Look: Andaz Turks & Caicos  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Andaz has unveiled a first look at the interiors for Andaz Turks & Caicos. Set to open in Spring 2027, the property will mark the first Hyatt hotel in Turks & Caicos and the first Caribbean island resort for the Andaz brand. The 132-key resort is designed by architecture by RAD Architecture with interiors by Modus Operandi in collaboration with Hyatt. Gently curving with the coastline, the west-facing property will offer a sunset perspective at every touchpoint. Set directly on the white sands of Grace Bay and steps from Bight Reef within Princess Alexandra National Park, Andaz Turks & Caicos will comprise 59 hotel rooms and 73 branded residences, also available for stays, with 10 penthouses featuring their very own rooftop plunge pools. The resort will feature three swimming pools, the 7,000ft 2 Runa Spa & Wellness, four dining concepts, a dedicated Kids Club, tennis and pickleball courts, in addition to ample weddings and event space. The structural narrative of Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay will unfold around an arrival sequence that takes cues from the island’s early history, when visitors arrived exclusively by boat. The entrance will recreate this experience, translating the pier into a long, immersive progression toward Grace Bay. Guests will move along a wood-lined corridor whose framing references the skeleton of an overturned boat. Set 15ft above the sea, the vantage point will immediately give the feeling of floating over the water as panoramic ocean views open up. That connection will continue throughout the interiors, where local stone and rich, natural materials add warmth while shifting hues of blues draw the surrounding waters indoors. The guestrooms’ expansive views and indoor-outdoor living will be balanced by a sense of privacy. Teak and hardwoods, richly textured fabrics and streams of natural light filtering into the bathrooms will create a tactile warmth, while artwork by Caribbean artists and pops of colour will bring the island’s character indoors. A traditional Turks & Caicos dress, distinguished by its colourful stripes representing the individual islands, will serve as a cultural touchpoint for the interiors. The striped pattern is reinterpreted in the wooden headboards, translating a recognisable element of local dress into a subtle design detail. In addition to 59 standard guestrooms, the 73 branded residences include studios as well as one-, two-, three- and four-bedroom layouts, with the largest four-bedroom residences spanning up to 8,336ft 2 of indoor and outdoor space. Each residence will offer a balcony or terrace, indoor-outdoor living spaces and a Bosch-equipped kitchen. Natural woods, textured fabrics and contemporary furnishings are paired with handcrafted pieces and Caribbean-inspired graphics, creating a warm, layered interior palette. Ten penthouses will feature private rooftop plunge pools, while select residences offer private pools. Anchoring the resort’s social scene, the lobby bar is inspired by the colourful homes found throughout the Caribbean. Saturated hues, natural materials and an open-air setting will create a relaxed, residential feel, while the bar’s expansive setting will make the landscape part of the backdrop. As one of Grace Bay’s only indoor-outdoor oceanfront restaurants, Tamarà’s interiors will feature deep bottle-green tile to evoke the lushness of a tropical forest, balanced by limestone tiling and natural materials. A fishnet-inspired canopy will shade the expansive outdoor terrace, where a central tree will be framed by cascading lights that echo the movement of leaves overhead. Baie will unfold across two levels beside the pool, with the upper level offering a lounge-like perch above the water. The laidback sanctuary will serve as a casual pool bar by day, shifting into a more refined setting with sunset rituals in the evening. Adjacent to the lobby, Palmette will blur the line between neighbourhood café and marketplace, pairing daytime fare with a considered edit of locally made goods including baskets, clothing, tableware, candles and other provisions. The coastline also informs Runa Spa & Wellness, where the calm of Grace Bay’s reef-protected shallows finds expression across natural woods, neutral tones and sculptural forms punctuated by pops of colour that reflect the bay’s shifting hues of blue. The resort’s fitness centre will complement the spa with Life Fitness equipment throughout.
