items.text: L’Occitane en Provence presents hotel amenities offer 22 October 2026 | In Products | By Hannah Wintle Rooted in 50 years of Haute-Provence savoir-faire, L’Occitane en Provence craft a world of refined hospitality and sensorial excellence with proven results, designed for the guest who seeks the extraordinary in authenticity. For nearly three decades, the beauty brand has crafted hotel amenities for some of the most prestigious hotels worldwide. From the very beginning, its products have been manufactured with the same expertise and in the same facilities as its retail collections, ensuring uncompromising quality and authenticity. Today, L’Occitane en Provence also partners with high-end restaurants, airlines and wellness centres, carefully selected for their excellence and exceptional guest experience. The wide range of products available to hoteliers includes refillable amenities, which have been available since 1999 and are crafted with the expertise and care of its Haute-Provence manufacture, showcasing an authentic French craftsmanship. All made in France, the brand’s dispenser solutions feature recycled and recyclable packaging and are formulated without animal testing, reflecting its commitment to responsible beauty. L’Occitane en Provence also offer a complete expert skincare and turndown offering ​with retail formulas made in France,​ from body care to face care and ​fragrances, as well as a soap collection comprising solid soaps that combine high-quality formulas with a responsible approach to elevate the guest experience. Completing the amenities offer is a refined accessory collection, fragrance diffusers, and hotel giftsets wrapped in pouches and boxes. www.hospitality.loccitane.com amenities bathroom amenities hotel amenities L'Occitane L'Occitane en Provence Related Posts 6 October 2023 Groupe GM announces collaboration with Trussardi 5 January 2016 Demista equips refurbished Ritz Hotel 21 October 2014 Luxury boutique hotel features Grohe Spa products

items.title: Rodolphe Parente envisions Experimental Roma
items.summary:
Experimental has announced the opening of its new Roman address, a vibrant and cinematic hotel designed to embody a contemporary […] 
 The post  Rodolphe Parente envisions Experimental Roma  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Experimental has announced the opening of its new Roman address, a vibrant and cinematic hotel designed to embody a contemporary Dolce Vita. Located on the Via Veneto in a building that formerly housed a bank, the hotel features 82 rooms, a rooftop, a suspended swimming pool, and an interior scheme by Rodolphe Parente. “For Experimental Roma, I did not want to recreate or imitate a nostalgic vision of Rome,” says Parente. “Instead, I wanted to create a living tribute, a free interpretation expressed through materials and space. A place charged with the same tensions that define Rome itself: sacred and profane, splendour and decadence.” In the lobby, the designer has curated an intimate interior that blends heritage and reinvention. Italian opulence is revisited through a French lens and the legacies of great Italian masters – such as Gio Ponti, Carlo Scarpa and Luigi Caccia Dominioni – are referenced through subtle nods to the 1970s: chrome tubing, disco-inspired accents, lurex carpets, a sculptural staircase and rich and textured materials. Throughout the restaurant and public spaces, enveloping banquettes, quilted drapery and exposed beams pay homage to Italian cinema, while the rooftop features an expansive bar overlooking the Eternal City, a swimming pool and a terrace. The hotel’s 82 rooms are divided into two principal categories. The first evokes the theatrical Roman bedroom, bathed in light filtered through interior shutters. Large blocks of colour, dramatic headboards inspired by antique drapery and a sense of romantic intimacy reminiscent of Villa Medici define these spaces. Colourful basins, vibrant details and a richer, more expressive design language create a dialogue between ancient Roman baroque influences and the hedonism of the 1970s. The second category embraces a more refined, almost futuristic aesthetic. Mineral patinas, two-tone lacquered ceilings and ribbed stainless-steel headboards resembling contemporary sculptures create a contemplative atmosphere. Artworks throughout the rooms evoke the worlds of Cy Twombly, Christo, Ugo Ferranti and the Yvon Lambert Gallery. The bathrooms are conceived as contrasting boxes, balancing warm wood with cool stone, raw materials with bespoke graphic details. “Experimental Roma is a hotel of inverted perspectives,” Parente concludes. “A French interpretation of Italy; an Italy reinvented through materials, textures and light. Noble materials interact with reimagined industrial elements. Marble converses with folded stainless steel, while terracotta tones vibrate against polished metal surfaces. Rome is reflected – quite literally – as if in a mirror. It is a city of shadows and reflections, a city that never exhausts itself, that continues to inspire dreams, desire and thought. This is the Rome we invite our guests to inhabit.” experimental experimental roma italy rome rudolphe Parente Related Posts 1 November 2023 Experimental Group shares first look at three new European hotels 22 September 2023 Inside Cowley Manor Experimental 20 March 2023 Experimental Group unveils Ibiza redesign

items.title: concrete pairs with brushed metal for hybrid automotive gallery café in hong kong
items.summary:
studio ruei designs macchina gallery café showcasing rotating automobiles against raw industrial interiors. 
 The post  concrete pairs with brushed metal for hybrid automotive gallery café in hong kong  appeared first on  designboom | architecture & design magazine .
items.text: [FEATURED] STUDIO RUEI designs hybrid AUTOMOTIVE GALLERY and CAFÉ IN WAN CHAI Designed by Yuisze Wong of Studio Ruei, Macchina is a hybrid gallery café in Hong Kong’s Wan Chai district that integrates automotive exhibition spaces with hospitality programming. Framing vehicles as cultural and industrial artifacts rather than commercial commodities, the interior provides a social venue where automotive design, mechanical engineering, and specialty coffee converge. all images ©matte is the new black CONCRETE, BRUSHED METAL, AND TIMBER FORM INDUSTRIAL INTERIOR Behind a restrained street-facing envelope, expansive glazed apertures create direct sightlines into the main display bay, framing a single vehicle as the focal sculpture, inaugurated by the Aston Martin Valkyrie. Studio Ruei organizes the internal layout and circulation through calibrated visual corridors, connecting the central vehicular plinth to surrounding lounge seating, curated display cases, and the primary espresso bar. Rotating vehicular displays introduce distinct engineering narratives over time without requiring physical alterations to the surrounding architecture. Macchina is a hybrid automotive gallery and café designed by Studio Ruei in Wan Chai, Hong Kong ADAPTABLE CEILING lights AND ACOUSTIC PANELs BALANCE AMBIANCE Drawing from Brutalist precedents, the spatial enclosure utilizes a tactile palette of textured concrete, brushed metal, and natural timber, pairing industrial finishes with precise architectural reveals that reflect automotive manufacturing tolerances. Overhead, an integrated ceiling grid pairs diffused wash lighting with directional spotlighting to delineate vehicle surfaces and contours under studio-grade illumination. Recessed acoustic panels across the walls and ceiling temper reverberation, balancing acoustic comfort across the café with the focused atmosphere of an exhibition gallery. the exhibition space displays an Aston Martin Valkyrie as a central sculptural centerpiece the minimalist service counter utilizes clean horizontal planes to minimize distraction from the exhibits custom shelving units display curated literature, automotive models, and design objects low lounge seating arrangements allow visitors to observe vehicle profiles from varied eye levels the interior design avoids conventional showroom aesthetics in favor of a gallery and café environment minimalist specialty coffee service counter features sleek metal finishes and espresso equipment a lounge area with timber elements balances the cool tones of concrete and exposed metalwork 1/10 project info: name: Macchina designer: Studio Ruei | @studio_ruei location: Gloucester Road, Wan Chai, Hong Kong area: 2150 sqft photographer: matte is the new black | @matteisthenewblack designboom has received this project from our DIY submissions feature, where we welcome our readers to submit their own work for publication. items.summary: The innovative project 'ZIN in No(o)rd' aims to reuse the emblematic WTC I and II towers located in the heart of the Northern Quarter in Brussels. Instead of a simple restoration of the existing building, it is a question here of adding an unprecedented dimension to the project by connecting the towers with a new volume of 14 double-height floors, creating a new condition for the development of a hybrid building mixing a new way of working on housing, a hotel, sports and leisure spaces, shops and lots of vegetation.

Studio Gang, the international architecture and urban design firm led by Jeanne Gang, has completed Populus, a 265-room hotel poised to become a new social center for downtown Denver . Marking Studio Gang's first completed project in Colorado and the American Southwest region, Populus's design draws from the growth processes of the state's native Aspen trees (Populus tremuloides) to establish a new architectural icon for Denver. "Denver strikes a unique balance between being a vibrant city and a gateway to some of the country's most awe-inspiring natural landscapes. Our goal was to draw from this distinct urban character and rich ecology to create a building that would help define the skyline of this thriving city," says Jeanne Gang, Founding Partner of Studio Gang.

items.text: Art Houston Center for Contemporary Craft Celebrates 25 Years with Steinbeisser Each month, TJ Girard explores the intersection of food and design, from what we eat to how it’s made, presented, and experienced, in her Taste column. 11.06.26 | By TJ Girard Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email View Slideshow Steinbeisser's Experimental Gastronomy dinner at Houston Center for Contemporary Craft brought together artist-made tableware and plant-based cuisine to celebrate the institution's 25th anniversary. Photography by Kerrisa Treanor; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. I’ve covered Steinbeisser in this column before, and the Amsterdam studio’s approach to rethinking objects and how we use them continues to hold my interest. Its latest chapter took place on Oct. 23 at the Houston Center for Contemporary Craft (HCCC) , where 50 guests sat together at a single long table in the main gallery, surrounded by the exhibition A Material Inheritance , to celebrate the institution’s 25th anniversary. Houston Center for Contemporary Craft’s 25th-anniversary experimental dinner in collaboration with Steinbeisser. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. Founded in 2009 by Jouw Wijnsma and Martin Kullik, Steinbeisser launched its Experimental Gastronomy initiative in 2012, pairing chefs and artists for one-of-a-kind dinners worldwide. This was its first in Texas and one of the few held in the U.S. The menu was entirely plant-based and seasonal, with produce from regional farms that use organic and biodynamic growing practices. The cooking came from two Michelin-starred restaurants: Tatemó in Houston and Nicosi in San Antonio. The evening opened with Bohyun Yoon’s Singing Buoys , an interactive work in which guests used handheld remotes to steer blown-glass vessels carrying small bites across a water table. When the vessels collided, they rang like bells. Guests interact with ‘Singing Buoys,’ an interactive sonic installation by artist Bohyun Yoon, created for the amuse-bouche at the Steinbeisser dinner. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. The dinner itself kept the focus on the objects. Tatemó’s first course of nixtamalized squash, rice, kosho, and carrot came on Jaydan Moore’s Sustenance #1, a platter assembled from salvaged antique silver-plated serving pieces. The first course featured nixtamalized squash, Koshihikari rice, kosho, and carrot, served on Sustenance #1 by Jaydan Moore, a sculptural platter assembled from reclaimed antique silver-plated servingware. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. Nicosi’s Kudzumochi Tamal, with pumpkin juice, mushroom, masa foam, hoja santa, and gold leaf, was prepared by chefs Jorge Luis Hernández and Ben Hjelm. Chefs Jorge Luis Hernández and Ben Hjelm of Nicosi plate the second course. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. items.title: A Modern Seattle Floating Home Takes Coastal Living to New Heights
items.summary: This Lake Union residence combines Nantucket-inspired interiors with the engineering required to live directly on the water
items.text: Architecture A Modern Seattle Floating Home Takes Coastal Living to New Heights 11.04.26 | By Murrye Bernard Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email View Slideshow Photography by Andrew Giammarco A Modern Seattle Floating Home Takes Coastal Living to New Heights Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email 1/14 Photos Photography by Andrew Giammarco 2/14 Photos Photography by Andrew Giammarco 3/14 Photos Photography by Andrew Giammarco 4/14 Photos Photography by Andrew Giammarco 5/14 Photos Photography by Andrew Giammarco 6/14 Photos Photography by Andrew Giammarco 7/14 Photos Photography by Andrew Giammarco 8/14 Photos Photography by Andrew Giammarco 9/14 Photos Photography by Andrew Giammarco 10/14 Photos Photography by Andrew Giammarco 11/14 Photos Photography by Andrew Giammarco 12/14 Photos Photography by Andrew Giammarco 13/14 Photos Photography by Andrew Giammarco 14/14 Photos "c"JSJ Before arriving at its permanent home in Seattle’s Eastlake floating-home community, this two-story residence took a journey of its own. Built entirely on a concrete float at Dyna Builders ‘ Ballard docks, the house was towed across the lake and installed in its Eastlake slip. Now, with expansive glass walls opening directly onto the water, Modern Beach House feels firmly connected to its surroundings, even as it floats above them. Photography by Andrew Giammarco Designed by Hoshide Wanzer Architects + Interiors and constructed by Dyna Builders, the 2,123-square-foot residence combines the relaxed character of a Nantucket beach house with the clean lines and material richness of Pacific Northwest architecture. Its three bedrooms and open living spaces accommodate an active family whose daily routines revolve around swimming, boating, and entertaining. Photography by Andrew Giammarco “The homeowners were drawn to the relaxed, coastal aesthetic of Nantucket, and that influence really helped shape the character of the home,” says Ren Chandler, president and founder of Dyna Builders. Rather than relying on overt nautical motifs, the design incorporates weathered wood, tactile finishes, and a palette of blues, greens, and warm neutrals. Photography by Andrew Giammarco Constructing a house on water requires a different approach from building on solid ground. The new concrete float provides a stable foundation for the home while accommodating utilities and simplifying long-term maintenance. Building at Dyna’s Ballard docks gave the team easier access to trades and equipment while minimizing disruption to neighboring floating homes. “Weight, balance, and structural integrity are all critical considerations, and everything needs to be carefully coordinated from the beginning,” Chandler explains. Unlike a conventional foundation, the floating structure requires precise weight distribution, influencing decisions about everything from the structural system to interior finishes. Photography by Andrew Giammarco On the main level, the kitchen, dining area, and living room share an open plan oriented toward Lake Union. Large Fleetwood glass doors slide into pockets within the fireplace massing, allowing the living spaces to extend seamlessly onto the waterfront deck. The chimney continues through both floors, functioning as an architectural spine that organizes the interior. Photography by Andrew Giammarco A deep blue sectional anchors the living room, complemented by sculptural lounge chairs and a softly textured fireplace surround. Nearby, a built-in dining banquette wrapped in patterned upholstery offers generous seating beneath a chandelier of colorful glass globes. The kitchen pairs warm wood cabinetry with white upper cabinets and dramatically veined countertops. Photography by Andrew Giammarco Durability is central to the design. Weathered yakisugi siding extends from the exterior into the stairwell, while cork-rubber flooring, stain-resistant cabinetry fronts, and resilient tile accommodate wet gear, pets, and frequent gatherings. A dedicated mudroom with interior and exterior showers provides a practical transition between the lake and the living spaces. Photography by Andrew Giammarco “Living directly on the water introduces some unique considerations, particularly when it comes to moisture, durability, and long-term maintenance,” Chandler notes. Careful detailing around exterior openings, decks, and exposed surfaces helps the home withstand the Pacific Northwest’s damp climate. Photography by Andrew Giammarco Upstairs, the primary suite opens directly onto a private deck overlooking Lake Union. Glass railings preserve the view, while a corner fireplace, upholstered headboard, and warm wood millwork create a more intimate atmosphere. Photography by Andrew Giammarco An adjacent dressing area features a particularly striking detail: a sculptural wood partition composed of vertically arranged slats with carved, undulating profiles. Integrated storage turns the partition into both a functional element and a tactile architectural feature. Photography by Andrew Giammarco The two additional bedrooms maximize their compact footprints with custom built-in bunks featuring internal steel framing fabricated in Dyna’s metal shop. One features illustrated maritime imagery, while the other incorporates botanical motifs. Photography by Andrew Giammarco The stairwell offers another example of the project’s custom craftsmanship. Illuminated resin panels form a translucent screen alongside the steel-and-wood stairs, offering a subtle nautical reference while casting a soft glow across the circulation space. Carefully positioned ribbon windows and layered window treatments address privacy within the closely spaced floating-home community without sacrificing natural light. items.title: A Sofreh Alum Showcases Persian Wraps in Brooklyn
items.summary: An alum of notable New York City Persian restaurants like Sofreh and Eyval is opening up his own fast-casual restaurant dedicated to Persian wraps. Chef Soroosh Golbabae is opening Āzar in Williamsburg at 740 Driggs Avenue, at South Second Street, on Saturday, November 7.  Golbabae is focusing on the idea of loghmeh, a Persian word […]
items.text: NYC Restaurant News A Sofreh Alum Showcases Persian Wraps in Brooklyn ﻿Chef Soroosh Golbabae debuts Āzar in Williamsburg this weekend by Nadia Chaudhury Nov 6, 2026, 6:35 PM UTC Facebook Link Noah Fecks Nadia Chaudhury is a born-and-raised New Yorker who is the deputy editor for Eater’s Northeast region and Eater New York, was the former Eater Austin editor for 10 years, and often writes about food and pop culture. An alum of notable New York City Persian restaurants like Sofreh and Eyval is opening up his own fast-casual restaurant dedicated to Persian wraps. Chef Soroosh Golbabae is opening Āzar in Williamsburg at 740 Driggs Avenue, at South Second Street, on Saturday, November 7. Golbabae is focusing on the idea of loghmeh, a Persian word that means “morsel” or “perfect bite.” He explains, “Loghmeh is a super-easy homey concept that never made it out of the home,” and he’s doing something about that. To that end, Āzar is serving lavash flatbread wraps with Persian fillings that aren’t overly huge. His version of the Iranian home dining staple ghormeh sabzi ($12) is made with beef cheeks instead of the typical lamb. “Beef cheeks are a favorite cut, and it’s really hot right now, so let’s try it,” he says. It’s cooked in a herby stew with kidney beans and black limes, “until the herbs are really incorporated with all that meat flavor,” he adds, and is garnished with fresh white onions. The food spread at Āzar. Noah Fecks Soroosh Golbabae at Āzar. Noah Fecks Then there’s the koobideh ($12), with a mixture of grilled ground lamb and beef made with saffron butter, plus sumac onions, grilled tomatoes, and fresh basil. The chicken fesenjoon ($9) will be on the menu through the spring; it’s a bright filling with a pomegranate-walnut sauce, grilled chicken thighs, and pickled red cabbage. The vegetarian option is the kashk bademjoon ($9) — a “super-comforting eggplant dish,” he says. “To me, it’s the umami of Persian cuisine.” It’s made with a slow-cooked eggplant, kashk (Persian whey) , and crispy onions. He made his own lavash recipe with some whole wheat flour to add structure, as well as butter “to make it more delicious, more aromatic, and, when it reheats or holds the food, it adds a little more strength.” It’s baked in the on-site pita oven. Golbabae had been working on the idea for some time; “ Āzar is on the back burner, cooking for a long time,” he tells Eater. He knew the name from the beginning, after his mother. He grew up in Tehran, watching his mother shop and cook. “I had that education growing up without even understanding it in the beginning,” he says. The zereshk tanchin at Āzar. Noah Fecks The doogh drink at Āzar. Noah Fecks Look for sides like the tahchin ($8), a smaller take on the iconic Persian rice dish. He shares that he’s generally particular about tahchin. For this one, he went for a “softer, jasmine-like rice; we overcook it intentionally to get a little mushy,” he says. It gets seasoned with yogurt, egg yolks, saffron, and salt “so it becomes really nice and moist and fatty — kind of sticky.” While it’s typically stuffed with meat, vegetables, or barberries, he opted to serve it with the zereshk sauce (made with barberries and prunes) and pistachios for that cold-hot temperature combination. “Two things I really like to play with when I’m coming up with dishes are temperature and texture,” he says. “If you can get a few things in one bite, it’s just amazing; it’s a unique experience.” Drinks include saffron sharbat ($5), made with basil seeds and lime (“super-refreshing, he describes); and doogh ($5), the yogurt drink with dry mint and rose that gets steeped overnight. Growing up in Tehran, Golbabae frequented local street carts, kebab shops, and restaurants, and eventually worked at a few places. He worked there for a bit, and then moved to New York City to attend the Culinary Institute of America, but he wanted to go back to learning more about Persian cuisine. “I started digging [into all the old Persian recipes, thinking about how we can do that, how we can dress it in a different way that New York likes and also not lose the authenticity of it,” he says. That’s when he ended up on the opening team of Prospect Heights restaurant Sofreh (which opened in 2018) and Bushwick’s Eyval ; and then he was the opening chef and chef de cuisine of Park Slope Lebanese restaurant Sawa . He also ran Persian pop-ups and worked as a private chef. All the while, he knew that the Persian community was looking for restaurants that were more accessible and affordable. “In a lot of restaurants nowadays, in many different cuisines, they are inspired by street food, but by the time the food goes on the table, to me, it’s not anymore because they played with it too much — I’m guilty myself — but I was like, maybe this is the time to take a little risk and come out of that comfort zone,” he explains. He met Fardad Zabetian, who founded Kudo , a live-translation program, during a pop-up, and they teamed up to open Āzar. Āzar’s dining room. Noah Fecks Āzar’s exterior. Noah Fecks The 350-square-foot counter-service space is small, with only 10 seats. It’s designed by architecture firm Roudiani.Harelson . Golbabae talks about how the firm’s co-founder, Bahar Roudiani, immediately understood his Iranian architectural references because she lived in Iran. He’d ask her about old houses in Iran and stainless steel details in the Albanian sandwich shops, and she knew them all. For Āzar, that means a stainless steel counter and amber glass blocks. The walls feature artwork by fellow Iranians and Iranian Americans. Sina Choopani, who runs Tehran-based silk-screen print studio Garage.co , has some silk prints up. Zeynab Izadyar, the founder of Vvork Vvork Vvork , has patched-together quilts. Tierney Plumb is an editor of Eater’s Northeast region, covering D.C., Boston, Philly, and New York. November 6 Spotlight Dumbo : After three years, Bark Barbecue will close its first-ever permanent outpost inside Brooklyn’s Time Out Market on Saturday, November 7. “All good things must come to an end,” its cowboy hat-wearing pitmaster Ruben Santana tells followers in a video message near his walk-up food hall stall. But luckily, fans of his Central Texan barbecue with Dominican touches don’t have to go far to find white oak-smoked brisket, ribs, pulled pork, and plenty of sides. Bark’s huge Bushwick location, complete with 1,000-gallon smokers, opened this summer to much excitement. Bark originally got its start as a pop-up in Queens in 2020 and grew a fan base from there. 55 Water Street, near Dock Street And the rest… East Village : La Linea , the longstanding bar and lounge known for its rotating DJ nights, watch parties for everything from the World Cup to the Knicks playoffs, and happy hour rum punches, shut down right after Halloween after a 32-year run. However, the space will get a new tenant soon. Per EV Grieve , there’s a recently approved application for a to-be-named tavern to slide in and take over. The new owners have affiliations with now-closed McKenna’s Pub and the Mayfly. 15 First Avenue, between First Street and Second Street Midtown : That was quick: Osaka, Japan-based omurice-slinging restaurant Dearbros already closed its nine-day-old pop-up at Japanese cafe BentOn on Thursday, October 29, because they were overwhelmed with guests. items.text: NYC Restaurant News ICYMI: A Portuguese Bakery Spins Off a New Soft Serve Shop And more New York City restaurant intel to know this week by Nadia Chaudhury Nov 6, 2026, 3:02 PM UTC Facebook Link Soft serve at Lisbonata. Lisbonata Nadia Chaudhury is a born-and-raised New Yorker who is the deputy editor for Eater’s Northeast region and Eater New York, was the former Eater Austin editor for 10 years, and often writes about food and pop culture. We’ve been covering various NYC restaurants, food, drinks, bars, etc. news intel over on our daily newsletter ( please sign up if you haven’t already! ), but we’re also making it easier for everyone to catch up by rounding ‘em up here every week (check out October , September , August , July , and June’s ). November 6 Soft serve > fro-yo (!?!) Looks like Crown Heights Portuguese bakery Lisbonata is opening a spinoff location focused on its soft serve , Sofi , in the West Village, at 31 Carmine Street, between Bedford and Bleecker streets. Eater has reached out for more information. Why a chef left a hyped art museum restaurant The New Museum’s new restaurant Oberon opened in July on the Lower East Side, by the Oberon Group (which runs places like Rhodora , June , and Rucola ) with co-executive chefs artist Julia Sherman and Ali Ghriskey. But then, less than a month later, Sherman left the operation. In her Substack newsletter, Salad for President , on Friday, October 30, she explained what happened behind the paywall, calling it an “ultimate failure to launch.” She recounts how the owner told her, “food doesn’t matter,” and that she wasn’t supposed to talk about the restaurant in the press. An omurice pop-up shutter That was quick: Osaka, Japan-based omurice-slinging restaurant Dearbros already closed its nine-day-old pop-up at Japanese cafe BentOn on Thursday, October 29, because they were overwhelmed with guests. They’re turning their attention to opening a permanent New York City restaurant. Eater has reached out for more information. A ramen restaurant returns One of Brooklyn’s earlier ramen slingers, Chuko Ramen , closed its 15-year-old Prospect Heights location over the summer. But it turns out the team is reopening the restaurant on the border of Clinton Hill and Bed-Stuy at 395 Classon Avenue, at Greene Avenue, in January 2027. New NYC food and drink book alerts First, Ayesha Nurdjaja , the chef and partner behind NYC restaurants Shuka and Shukette , published her first cookbook, Mediterranean All the Way . And then, drinks-focused writer Robert Simonson ’s latest, Bourbon & Rye Cocktails . “Music for a pizza restaurant” Harry Styles ended his record-breaking 30-show residency at Madison Square Garden at the end of October, and he celebrated with food, of course. For his final show on Halloween, aka Harryween, he dressed up as a full-on pizza rat, a reference to his first-night banter about how much he loves grabbing a late-night slice when he’s in NYC, and switched to the rat ears and a white shirt declaring “I am a rat.” That’s when he and his band ate pizza from Williamsburg Pizza on stage, per Yes Williamsburg . Continuing the theme, his girlfriend, Zoë Kravitz, dressed up as a plastic takeout bag . “I just wanna taste it” Earlier during the residency, Styles celebrated the birthday of one of his fans at the show with a cake from East Village bakery From Lucie . Political dining out NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani spent his Halloween touring the final night of the Queens Night Market with New York City Governor Kathy Hochul, who had been up for reelection that week and won. Learn about an acclaimed winemaker There’s a new documentary about renowned California winemaker Randall Grahm from director Jeffrey Reiner and producer Darin Bresnitz coming out this fall called The Terroirist . They’re hosting a preview screening on Monday, November 9, at the Loft at City Winery in Chelsea starting at 7 p.m., with a discussion between Grahm, Reiner, and moderator/winemaker/sommelier André Hueston Mack, plus wines from Grahm’s vineyard, for $36. The documentary premieres on streaming services such as Apple TV and Amazon Prime on Friday, November 13. items.text: Dining Reports This Revived Brooklyn Restaurant Serves the Best Spaghetti and Meatballs Sam’s might have a new owner, but it remains a classic﻿ by Nadia Chaudhury Nov 4, 2026, 6:37 PM UTC Facebook Link The spaghetti and meatballs at Sam’s. Nadia Chaudhury Nadia Chaudhury is a born-and-raised New Yorker who is the deputy editor for Eater’s Northeast region and Eater New York, was the former Eater Austin editor for 10 years, and often writes about food and pop culture. In our Dining Reports, we share a firsthand perspective of a recent restaurant visit, covering everything from the vibe to must-get dishes. See more in the Eater app. Download the app Sam’s isn’t a new restaurant for New York City. The neighborhood institution has been around since 1930 and has been passed down through the same family for generations. That is, until recently, when the then-owner, Louis Migliaccio, handed his legacy restaurant over to a regular, Georgia Fulton, a longtime server at the neighboring Long Island Bar . Fulton reopened Sam’s this past September, keeping its original ethos alive but in a slightly zhuzhed-up way. There’s now a much shorter food and drinks menu, still full of familiar hits. Looks-wise, the facade is unchanged, with the American and Italian flags; neon signage declaring there’s Italian cuisine, lunch, and dinner; and a couple of steps down to the front door. Inside, it’s mostly the same, but now there’s more dining room, and the front bar has actual stools. But still, familiar favorites remain, like the pizza on the menu, those same plates and glasses , and the cozy, family-friendly vibes. What to order Shrimp cocktails had been on my mind, and the one at Sam’s ($18) is a classic one with an ever-so-slightly spicy sauce with four shrimp. I had heard a lot about Sam’s baked clams ($23), and I liked them. The bivalves were chewy but tricky to pull off the shell; a little fork would’ve been nice. I adored the buttery sauce and wished I ordered bread to sop it up. The spaghetti and meatballs ($26) were some of the best I’ve ever had. It’s the ideal format, doused in Parmesan, paired with a nice zesty tomato, soft-strong meatballs, and chewy pasta. I ended with the tiramisu ($12), a classic square cut out of what is probably a huge slab of the Italian dessert with a double-ladyfinger layer. The facade of Sam’s. Nadia Chaudhury The drinks Given Fulton’s background, the drinks are quite classic and good at Sam’s. I adored my very-dirty gin martini with three olives. For dessert, my server recommended the Amaro Montenegro, which was perfectly not sweet and paired well with the tiramisu. Best seat in the house The booths are cozy and good for groups up to four. The back room is pretty, with stained glass windows and a mural of a lush garden with spouting fountains. Sit back there at the larger table for bigger groups. Hole up at one of the bar stools for solo dining and good eavesdropping. Fulton added a drink rail separating the bar from the rest of the front dining room, much like Long Island Bar . Know before you go The upstairs bathrooms offer powdered hand soap only. Insider tip Head upstairs for relics of Sam’s past, including the nonfunctional phone booth, an amazing doll lamp, and an official Brooklyn proclamation issued in 1996 recognizing the restaurant and the Migliaccio family for their mom-and-pop business efforts. items.text: NYC Restaurant News Jean-Georges Vongerichten Is Opening Two New Restaurants in Hudson Yards A dressed-up lobby restaurant, a takeout place, and a 46th-floor event space are headed to a new office tower in the neighborhood by Melissa McCart Nov 2, 2026, 11:39 PM UTC Facebook Link Some dishes at ABC Kitchens. Jutharat Pinyodoonyachet/Eater NY Melissa McCart is the lead editor of the Northeast region with more than 20 years of experience as a reporter, critic, editor, and cookbook author. Prolific chef and restaurateur Jean-Georges Vongerichten is bringing two restaurants, along with catering and an events space, to 70 Hudson Yards, the 50-plus-story office tower under construction at Hudson Boulevard East and West 35th Street, the New York Post first reported. The centerpiece is a 50-seat, 2,000-square-foot restaurant in the lobby. Vongerichten tells Eater it will feel like the polished power-dining restaurant Four Twenty Five or iconic French-leaning Nougatine ; he didn’t come forth with a name yet. The larger of the two will be the 3,000-square-foot ABC to Go, a grab-and-go take on Vongerichten’s ABC restaurants, which include a farm-to-table sustainable kitchen, a Mexican-inspired restaurant, and a vegetarian staple with locations in Manhattan and Dumbo. A view of Hudson Yards. Getty Images Jean-Georges Management will also oversee more than 5,000 square feet of event space on an upper floor and will provide catering for office tenants. The three projects cover roughly 10,000 square feet. Related Companies and Oxford Properties Group are developing the tower, with a 2028 opening in sight, the Post reports. Vongerichten’s company runs more than 60 restaurants in 14 locations worldwide. In New York, that includes the flagship Jean-Georges and Nougatine, Four Twenty Five, as well as the ABC spots. The hugely ambitious and short-lived Tin Building closed after three years. Hudson Yards and its surrounding blocks have steadily added restaurants. Mercado Little Spain from José Andrés, Gabriel Kreuther’s Saverne , and Dan Kluger’s Greywind are all nearby, and Tao Group’s Peak sits on the 101st floor of 30 Hudson Yards. There’s neighborhood favorite Danny Meyer’s Ci Siamo , along with the newest location of Locanda Verde . Peruvian restaurant Papa San and British import Queensyard round out the dining options. See our ethics statement. Mezzaluna was known for its pies. Mezzaluna This is Eater’s guide to all the New York City restaurants, bars, and cafes that closed in October 2026. This list will be updated weekly (see: September , August , July , June , May , April , March , February , January ), serving as a round-up of the dining and drinking places that have shuttered around the city. If a restaurant or bar has closed in your neighborhood, let us know at ny@eater.com . October 30 Spotlight Upper East Side : After months of speculation and a neighborhood petition to get the trattoria to stay, Italian institution Mezzaluna will finally throw in the towel on Sunday, November 1, after 42 years of service. “The lines have been down the block with locals waiting hours to enjoy just one more delicious Mezzaluna meal,” a rep tells Eater. Lined with terracotta floors and framed Italian art, Mezzaluna was known for its wood-fired pizza prepared out of a small kitchen. It is also among the first restaurants in the city to import olive oils and pasta from now-86-year-old founder Aldo Bozzi’s native Italy. The idea of resigning a new 10-year lease and committing to extensive renovations was ultimately a big factor in deciding not to stay in the current space. A newly formed GoFundMe page created by Jennifer Miller Jewelry supports its now-unemployed staff, which has already raised $17,000 of its $25,000 goal. 1295 3rd Avenue, near E. 74th Street And the rest… East Village : Tokyo Taiyaki , the cute kiosk for the fish-shaped Japanese dessert served with a variety of fillings and matcha soft serve, closed after a six-year run. 9 St Marks Place, at Third Avenue East Village : Mexican restaurant 345 Cantina closed after a four-year run. A handwritten sign outside reads, “It was an honor to serve you, and we hope to meet again,” and a closing message to its social media followers on Friday, October 16, hints at hope of resurfacing again. EV Grieve notes that the landlord has taken legal possession of the space, however, citing a city marshal’s notice listing October 13 as the eviction date. 345 E. Sixth Street, near First Avenue East Village: Hunan Slurp Shop , a nearly decade-old destination for Hunan-style rice noodles and other dishes synonymous with chef-owner Chao Wang’s native Hengyang, China, closed in late September . In a farewell message on Instagram , which doesn’t list a cause for the closure, the Hunan Slurp team points customers to its sibling slurp shop (Sofun Noodle Bar) in Summit, New Jersey. 112 First Avenue, near Seventh Street East Village : Taiwanese pastry chain Bake Culture , known for its Asian and European mix of cakes, tarts, and savory buns, closed after a little over four years, flags EV Grieve this week. Two other NYC locations remain. 22 St. Marks Place between Second and Third Avenues. Greenpoint : Family-owned Mexican mainstay Vamos al Tequila called it quits this week after 16 years, per a handwritten sign on the door flagged by Greenpointers . Vamos was one of the more budget-friendly options in Greenpoint when it came to generously sized orders of tacos, nachos, tortas, and enchiladas; it scored extra points for sidewalk seating on Franklin Street. 162 Franklin Street, at Kent Street, Brooklyn Greenpoint : Japanese American fusion spot Lingo closed on Sunday, October 25. But owner Misako Hsu tells Greenpointers the plan is to “start a new chapter” in the same space along Greenpoint’s so-called “restaurant row” in April: “Since I first moved to New York, I’ve had a dream of creating a Japanese-inspired all-day cafe and food counter, and after many years, I finally feel that the timing is right to bring that vision to life.” 27 Greenpoint Avenue, at West Street, Brooklyn October 23 Spotlight Flatbush : Compact-sized Errol’s Caribbean Delights , the Brooklyn favorite for fruit cakes, coco bread, oxtail, jerk chicken, and sorrel mixed with ginger beer, will close on Saturday, October 24, after a 25-year run next to Prospect Park. Turns out the owners, who are in their 80s, want to retire and spend more time with their grandkids (as one should), its workers tell News 12 Brooklyn . 661 Flatbush Avenue, near Hawthorne Street And the rest… Chinatown : After 16 years on Chrystie Street, NY’s OG boba bar chain Yaya Tea opted to not renew its lease at this particular address. A final farewell is set for Friday, October 23, from 1 p.m. to 7 p.m. There’s still a bunch of locations left, nine in all, including the closest one in Little Italy, as well as Gramercy, Brooklyn, Queens, and New Jersey. Along with bubble teas served in fun flavors, Yaya is known for its onigiri rice balls. 51 Chrystie Street, at Canal Street Clinton Hill: After four years in Clinton Hill, homegrown java shop Sweetbee has closed its location and shifted its Brooklyn attention to Prospect Heights instead. The arrivals of Smør and Coffee Land likely created competition in the area, a tipster pointed out to Eater. 1039a Fulton St reet, at Downing Street Greenpoint : After three and a half years, modern Japanese kitchen Lingo is set to close on Sunday, October 25. But the owners flag plans to reinvent the space into something else: “We’re excited to share that we’ll be returning to the same location with a brand-new concept.” 27 Greenpoint Avenue, at West Street Greenpoint : After a 13-year run, the Brew Inn — a sports bar that sided with the currently-undefeated San Francisco 49ers — closed on Sunday, October 18, following a hairy rent dispute with its landlord that ultimately ended in eviction proceedings, reports Greenpointers . The popular dive was known for its wings and a “killer” burger, so said Infatuation . 924 M

And if you need some ideas on where to drink, here’s our list of the hottest places to get cocktails in town. For a generous, soulful platter: Anjahles by Jazzy in West Adams Anjahles by Jazzy. Mona Holmes When the clocks fell backwards last weekend, I woke up in need of something savory and hopped in the car to find it. I remembered seeing an Instagram post by chef Jazzy Harvey , in which she bakes cornbread in a circular foil takeout container, cuts a hole in the center, then fills it with stewy oxtails, candied yams laced with rum, smoky collard greens, and a pile of creamy mac and cheese. The end of daylight saving time provided me an extra hour to chat with Harvey and watch a steady stream of folks arrive to try out her platter at her business Anjahles by Jazzy. Harvey has been operating her soulful Jamaican-LA pop-up since 2020 and has pretty much perfected her game. Pre-orders come with extras (free drink, priority pick up). Place an order through the Anjahles by Jazzy website , and pick up in West Adams on Sunday between noon and 3 p.m. 4976 West Adams Boulevard, West Adams, CA 90016. — Mona Holmes, editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest For one last visit to a legendary spot: Everson Royce Bar in the Arts District Nachos from Everson Royce Bar. Kat Thompson If I were to build a perfect bar in my head, it might end up a lot like Everson Royce Bar in the Arts District. You enter a dim, elegant interior, but you can also continue out back to a shady patio with enough space to host a large rehearsal dinner (literally mine). Cocktails are thoughtful but unpretentious, the list of spirits is contained in a mysterious book, beer and wine are carefully curated, and there are micheladas in both red and green varieties. The food menu is short but has no skips; the biscuits and burgers are the best in town. ERB recalls a more optimistic time in the Arts District and in LA generally, characterized by casual extravagance and a sunny disposition: a Peak TV-era mindset. But that time is over, and ERB is leaving with it — the bar is closing on December 19 . That means we’ve only got a few too-short weeks to celebrate this local icon, sampling rare whiskeys and crushing smoky potato taquitos under the tree in the middle of the patio like it’s 2016 again. 1936 E. 7th Street, Los Angeles, CA 90021 . — Ben Mesirow, editor, Eater Travel For a feast of Taiwanese flavors: Sinbala in Arcadia Kat Thompson I’ve written about the magic of legendary Taiwanese restaurant Sinbala before . It’s been serving up plates of snappy Taiwanese sausage, hearty beef noodle soup, and comforting tomato egg for more than 20 years. The menu of this strip mall cafe is expansive, ranging from snackier bites like popcorn chicken and chewy fried fish cakes to more traditional Taiwanese fare like fried pork chop rice and stewed pork belly with preserved mustard greens. Whatever you end up ordering, save room for refreshing shaved ice that comes with a slew of topping options — including but not limited to bouncy rice cakes, custardy flan, and sweet canned lychee — and a glaze of burnt brown sugar syrup. 651 W. Duarte Road Suite F, Arcadia, CA 91007. — Kat Thompson, audience editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest For a mini English breakfast near LAX: Tomat in Westchester Tomat. Matthew Kang There was a never a good answer for where to eat near LAX before a mid-day flight, until Tomat opened in nearby Westchester. The handy all-day restaurant provides a peaceful morning or mid-day meal with some interesting modern British dishes that won’t weigh you down before boarding a long flight to Asia (which I did recently). The full English breakfast, usually a bit of a gutbuster, comes in a three-quarter-size portion at Tomat, featuring farmers market potatoes, house-made pudding, comforting stewed beans (not the canned variety), and half-crispy bacon. The egg is poached instead of pan-fried, and the toast is hearty sourdough. You’ll want another dish — in our case, the pastrami hash topped with a fried egg, laden with crispy chopped potatoes and plenty of fresh herbs — to feel completely full. The fermented hot sauce adds a vibrant punch and a simmering heat that will linger. Note: Breakfast is served only Wednesday to Sunday. 6261 W. 87th Street, Los Angeles, CA, 90045. — Matthew Kang, correspondent, Eater Related The 38 Best Restaurants in Los Angeles See More : Dining Out in LA Dining Out

items.text: Dining Reports Mariscos El Muelle 8 Delivers a Sensational Taste of Culiacán in Downey The new restaurant has an expanded menu, a full liquor license, and a bright, boisterous energy by Bill Esparza Nov 6, 2026, 4:40 PM UTC Facebook Link Ceviche Muelle 8 at Mariscos El Muelle 8 Bill Esparza Bill Esparza is a James Beard award-winning food journalist, author of LA Mexicano, and onscreen food television personality covering food in United States and Latin America. In our Dining Reports, we share a firsthand perspective of a recent restaurant visit, covering everything from the vibe to must-get dishes. See more in the Eater app. Download the app Culiacán-based Mariscos El Muelle 8 has closed its East LA food truck and upgraded to a brick-and-mortar restaurant in Downey that opened on Friday, October 30. The owner of Mariscos El Muelle 8 USA , Jay Orozco, had launched the food truck in Garden Grove in 2025 after closing a previous brick-and-mortar location of Mariscos El Muelle 8 in Downey. His new 95-seat restaurant has a full liquor license and big-screen TVs for sports events. Founded in Culiacán in 2020 by Orozco’s cousin, the late Abel Martínez, Mariscos El Muelle 8 launches its new Downey restaurant with an extensive menu of barra fría (cold bar) dishes such as ceviches, aguachiles, and seafood cocktails, as well as barra caliente (hot bar) items like seafood tacos and soups. The bright cantina is ideal for sipping margaritas, micheladas, and carajillos while catching a variety of sports events (especially a Canelo fight). Mariscos El Muelle 8 delivers a unique Sinaloan seafood experience as the only Mexico-based mariscos franchise in Los Angeles. What to order Tostada lovers are in for a treat. The tostada chavita — a very Sinaloan take on the popular tuna tostada — piles cubes of sweet and sour marinated tuna on a fried wonton, with a scattering of black sesame and a crown of crispy fried onions on top. It’s a little inspiration from the sushi bar that Sinaloan chefs learned in culinary school and working at sushi bars stateside. The tostada chavita is compact and leaves plenty of room for other dishes. The shrewdest scheme to get a taste of pricey callos de hacha (pen shell clams) is in an order of Ceviche Muelle 8 , a mix of cooked shrimp, raw shrimp, cooked octopus, and those prized callos de hacha in a medium spicy salsa roja. One of the hallmarks of any barra fría is a number of variations on aguachile, a dish consisting of raw, high-quality shrimp, cured à la minute in a spicy lime juice blended with chile serrano or chile jalapeño. Ordering an aguachile negro made with the restaurant’s umami-rich salsa negra is the move; pair it with a michelada. The best seafood taco selection in town announces itself with the Taco Gaxiola , a seared strip of tuna rubbed in adobo, topped with guacamole and pico de gallo, and dressed with a chipotle-mayo. Everything zarandeado is en vogue north of the border, and camarones zarandeados are a noteworthy plate on any barra caliente. Here, large shrimp are grilled in a spicy marinade and served with undressed salad and coleslaw. The vibe The roar of crowds and booming sportscaster voices transmitted on flat-screen televisions displaying rival matches reverberate off the walls and tavern-style ceiling. The nautical-themed dining room, white with navy blue trim, features a mural depicting a day at the beach in Sinaloa. Diners are casually dressed — snapbacks are a sharp accessory for young sinaloenses — and it’s best to come with friends or family to enjoy sharable ceviches, aguachiles, and botanas (snacks). Insider tip If you want spicier, just ask when you order dishes from the barra fría. And check out the shellfish behind the bar on your right as you walk in for the day’s selection, which can include pata de mula, reina, and chocolata clams as well as Pacific oysters. Tostada chavita at Mariscos El Muelle 8. items.summary: In late October, Downtown’s Everson Royce Bar announced it would close permanently at the end of 2026. In the 11 years it was open, Everson Royce Bar appealed to casual and knowledgeable drinkers alike, serving as a watering hole […]
items.text: LA Restaurant Closings With LA’s Bar Scene in Crisis, Everson Royce Bar Announces Last Call Co-owner Randy Clement says tourism is down, costs are up, and the entertainment workforce is staying home﻿ by Mona Holmes Nov 4, 2026, 11:51 PM UTC Facebook Link Everson Royce Bar in Arts District. Wonho Frank Lee Mona Holmes is an editor at Eater Southern California/Southwest, a regular contributor at KCRW radio, and a 2022 James Beard Award nominee. In late October, Downtown’s Everson Royce Bar announced it would close permanently at the end of 2026. Hundreds of comments on its Instagram page lamented the loss of another fundamental Los Angeles bar. In the 11 years it was open, Everson Royce Bar appealed to casual and knowledgeable drinkers alike, serving as a watering hole for the hospitality industry. Cocktail culture writer Esther Tseng recalls the bar’s impact on the region. “It’s a bar that always had seriously good (but not serious) cocktails,” says Tseng. “It was probably one of the first places I knew Downtown that could accommodate small parties in an intimate bar setting, or larger, casual parties on the patio out back. It had great food, too.” Partners Joe Capella, Randy Clement, April Langford, and chef Matt Molina debuted Everson Royce Bar in 2015 with an uncomplicated approach to cocktails, a selection of rare whiskeys, Molina’s notable cheeseburger and food menu , plus that welcoming outdoor area. The team brought plenty of experience from restaurants and bars across Southern California. Capella and Molina are longtime operators of Hippo and South Pasadena’s Cannonball , which opened in 2025. Wife-and-husband team Langford and Clement are the minds behind Good Neighbor Bar as well as West Altadena Wine, which the couple closed in October. Eater spoke to Clement about the reasoning behind his decision to shutter Everson Royce Bar and West Altadena Wine. Clement cited the same challenges other operators have in Los Angeles’s current business and consumer climate : a significant drop in tourism, rising operational costs, changing drinking trends, plus the long-term effects of the pandemic and entertainment industry strikes. This year has been one of the hardest for Southern California bars and nightlife. Clement sees businesses losing their customer base as the many film and television workers who have long fueled Los Angeles restaurants and bars — hospitality workers pursuing entertainment dreams with side gigs as well as higher-paid industry professionals — can no longer afford to go out to eat and drink regularly. “Closing Everson Royce was the perfect storm of everything going wrong at the same time,” says Clement. “But unless there is this other unnamed industry waiting in the wings to replace the industry that’s driven our town for the last decades upon decades, I’m concerned that there’s no looking back.” The foursome saw the numbers and had acknowledged the inevitable for some time. They extended the closure announcement to keep their workers employed, with a persistent optimism that conditions would improve. As for West Altadena Wine, which is attached to Good Neighbor Bar’s patio, Clement says he was unwilling to continue the lengthy conflict with a residential neighbor who allegedly targeted the business by complaining to government agencies like Los Angeles County’s Department of Public Works, Building and Safety, LA County Planning, and the Department of Public Health. Clement also says that the complainant called law enforcement before Langford and Clement finally closed West Altadena Wine in late October. Eater reached out to the complainant but did not hear back. Clement and Langford moved from Albuquerque, New Mexico, to Los Angeles in 1996. The couple currently resides in Altadena and, along with other Los Angeles operators, worries about business sustainability and the city’s culture. “Here in LA, anything is possible, and now it doesn’t feel like that,” says Clement. The year 2026 is proving challenging for Los Angeles nightlife. West Hollywood’s the Belmont shuttered in August, and the neighborhood’s renowned Employees Only closed in late September. On November 2, Augustine Wine Bar announced it will close on December 19, the same day as Everson Royce Bar. SF Gate reports that cocktail (and wings) favorite Ye Rustic Inn might lose its outdoor seating and cites lease concerns with the landlord. Owner Susan Wood hosted an event to bolster support for the almost 30-year-old bar, where Los Angeles mayoral candidate and councilmember Nithya Raman showed up to offer support for independent businesses. (As of this writing, one day after Election Day, Raman holds a small lead over incumbent Mayor Karen Bass.) Clement sees an emergency unfolding and hopes solutions can come from elected officials for all independent businesses. “If you’re the group formulating legislation for economic incentives or tax credits, the fact that this hasn’t happened yet, maybe it’s all too late,” says Clement. “I don’t know. What Everson Royce Bar is going through is what the florist, yoga studio, and bookstore are going through.” Everson Royce Bar Everson Royce Bar 1936 E 7th St, Los Angeles, CA, 90021, US Booking Book a table Phone (213) 335-6166 Link http://www.erbla.com/ See More : LA Restaurant Closings LA Restaurant News Cocktail Bars Most Popular The Best Restaurants in Palm Springs, According to Eater Editors The Best Los Angeles Restaurants for Thanksgiving Dinner The 21 Best Indian and South Asian Restaurants in Los Angeles The Best Brunch Destinations in Los Angeles The 18 Best Santa Monica Restaurants Advertiser Content From This is the title for the native ad

items.summary: What began 12 years ago as a single Buena Park pho shop has evolved into Kei Concepts, one of Orange County’s most dominant restaurant groups. Co-founded by James Beard-nominated chef Viet Nguyen, the group’s portfolio now spans nine unique brands — ranging from Italian-Japanese fusion to contemporary Chinese — across 14 locations and 1,200 employees.  […]
items.text: Coming Attractions Orange County Dining Juggernaut Kei Concepts Is Finally Expanding Into LA ﻿The restaurant group behind Vox Kitchen and Rol will anchor a massive new $24 million development in Culver City by Cathy Chaplin Nov 3, 2026, 11:05 PM UTC Facebook Link Wonho Frank Lee Cathy Chaplin is a former senior editor at Eater LA, a James Beard Award–nominated journalist, and the author of Food Lovers’ Guide to Los Angeles. What began 12 years ago as a single Buena Park pho shop has evolved into Kei Concepts , one of Orange County’s most dominant restaurant groups. Co-founded by James Beard-nominated chef Viet Nguyen, the group’s portfolio now spans nine unique brands — ranging from Italian-Japanese fusion to contemporary Chinese — across 14 locations and 1,200 employees. Next fall, Kei Concepts will make its move into Los Angeles, anchoring Culver Commons — a $24 million Regency Centers development at the intersection of Washington Boulevard and Centinela Avenue — with outposts of its Peruvian-Chinese staple Vox Kitchen and Japanese handroll counter Rol . (Kei Concepts operated Súp Noodle Bar in Cerritos from 2017 to 2020.) At Culver Commons, the two OC imports will join a stacked tenant lineup that includes Wanderlust Creamery, Smog City Brewing, and El Moro Churrería. While the partners behind Kei Concepts considered expanding beyond its Orange County “bubble” for years, Nguyen says, the group didn’t take the leap until Regency Centers approached them about the opportunity in Culver City. Previously, the two companies partnered at Heritage Plaza, an Irvine shopping complex owned by Regency Centers, where Kei Concepts operates three restaurants: Nếp Cafe, Súp Noodle Bar, and Rol Hand Roll Bar. “Culver City is the perfect location for our introduction of Kei Concepts to LA residents,” says Nguyen. He notes that the city’s demographics and income levels closely mirror those of the group’s most successful Orange County markets like Irvine, though with a smaller Asian population. Bringing Vox Kitchen to Los Angeles marks a full-circle moment for Nguyen. “When I was working all over LA, the number-one restaurant I always went to every single week was Mario’s Seafood,” he says. The long-standing Hollywood Peruvian restaurant’s signature ceviches and lomo saltado inspired Vox Kitchen. Vox Kitchen Culver City will seat 200 diners across a 5,000-square-foot dining room and a 1,000-square-foot patio, making it significantly larger than existing locations in Fountain Valley and South Coast Plaza. To further differentiate the restaurant from its predecessors, the Culver City menu is adding what Nguyen calls a “Nikkei flair” to its Chifa standards, introducing a raw bar and a dynamic slate of cocktails. Madrid-based architecture and experience firm Livit designed the restaurant’s sleek interiors. Three doors down, Rol, which currently operates in Fountain Valley, Irvine, and La Habra, will span 2,000 square feet, with counter-only seating. Its core menu of handrolls and donburi bowls will expand to feature a new lineup of traditional and innovative onigiri, including Korean-inspired variations like bulgogi and kimchi. Nguyen views the dual Culver City openings as a litmus test for the brand’s viability outside its home turf. “Culver City will be the defining moment,” Nguyen says. “If we open it and nobody shows up and they hate us, then we still have a lot of work to do. But if it succeeds and people love it, we’ll be in 50 states.” While it is too soon to say how the Orange County powerhouse will fare in a hyper-competitive market like Los Angeles’s, Nguyen’s underlying mission to foster connection within the Vietnamese diaspora through shared meals remains steadfast. “When you sit around the dinner table, everything becomes softer; you find it easier to forget. I feel like my job is to bring people together at the dinner table,” he says. “Everything I’m doing is for Little Saigon. Everything I’m doing is for Vietnamese people to come together to share stories.” Vox Culver City. Livit Vox Culver City. Spacca Tutto Chef Nancy Silverton debuted her modern Italian steakhouse Spacca Tutto on October 15 in Rick Caruso’s recently reopened Palisades Village . The restaurant takes cues from Chi Spacca with a menu of steaks cooked over live fire, plus salads, branzino, lamb chops, and lunchtime paninis, along with robust cocktails, served in an ornate dining room and expansive patio. Also find the same escarole Caesar served at Chi Spacca, along with chopped steak tartare, and grilled prawns dressed simply with lemon and olive oil. Loved it Want to try Location 15225 Palisades Village Lane, Pacific Palisades, California 90272, United States External Link Phone (310) 459-3210 Link Visit Website Anne Fishbein See more The Best New Restaurants in Los Angeles, November 2026 Nov 5 The Best New Restaurants in Los Angeles, November 2026 Gott’s Roadside Santa Monica Napa Valley’s cult-favorite roadside burger stand, Gott’s Roadside , has opened its second Southern California location in Santa Monica following its Los Angeles debut at the Original Farmers Market in Beverly Grove. Set in downtown Santa Monica, a few blocks up from the shore, the restaurant serves all the Gott’s hallmarks, including green chile cheeseburgers, ahi poke crispy tacos, chile cheese dogs, and chicken tenders. The Santa Monica location also features a dedicated soft serve counter for vanilla or Dutch chocolate cones. Loved it Want to try Location 401 Wilshire Boulevard, Santa Monica, California 90401, United States External Link Phone (424) 900-6188 Link Visit Website Brianna Marie Bar Fortuna Santa Monica’s Bar Fortuna made its Main Street debut on October 21. Chef and owner Brian Bornemann’s charming, almost 40-seat restaurant is barely a three-minute walk from his noted seafood restaurant, Crudo e Nudo . Elcielo Elcielo received a Michelin Star for its 18-course tasting menu by chef Juan Manuel Barrientos. The modern Colombian menu varies, but expect experiential moments like the restaurant’s “Tree of Life,” bread service entangled on a small tree; and the “Chocotherapy” which invites you to literally wash your hands in liquid cocoa. The tasting menu ranges from $245 to $289 per person (excluding beverages, tax, and a 20 percent added gratuity). Elcielo will accommodate people with allergies and offer a vegetarian menu upon request. There’s also a $98 bar experience where guests will experience a selection of cocktails, each paired with snacks. items.summary: As a gateway between the U.S., the Caribbean, and Latin America, Miami has long been a champion of diverse flavors — rum and agave spirits mingling with notes of citrus and exotic fruits. Recently, vermouth and sherry-based drinks, along with classic Spanish cocktails and Italian spritzes, are popping up in the local scene, further shaping […]
items.text: Tin Tin Dining Out in Miami The Best New Bars in Miami Where to grab a drink right now in the Magic City by Allison Ramirez Updated Jul 15, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC Facebook Link Allison Ramirez is a freelance journalist with over 15 years of experience covering food and drink, travel, art, culture, and more. As a gateway between the U.S., the Caribbean, and Latin America, Miami has long been a champion of diverse flavors — rum and agave spirits mingling with notes of citrus and exotic fruits. Recently, vermouth and sherry-based drinks, along with classic Spanish cocktails and Italian spritzes, are popping up in the local scene, further shaping the city’s evolving cocktail landscape. Miami’s drinking culture really reflects its melting pot history, and this year, some iconic bars and restaurants have reopened with a refreshed look and feel, bringing back old-school favorites alongside international, travel-inspired drinks. From tiki recipes and passion fruit infusions to sparkling concoctions of all sorts, our latest cocktail map highlights the best drinks and the hottest new spots to try them, from Coral Gables to Miami Beach and everywhere in between. As a gateway between the U.S., the Caribbean, and Latin America, Miami has long been a champion of diverse flavors — rum and agave spirits mingling with notes of citrus and exotic fruits. Recently, vermouth and sherry-based drinks, along with classic Spanish cocktails and Italian spritzes, are popping up in the local scene, further shaping the city’s evolving cocktail landscape. Miami’s drinking culture really reflects its melting pot history, and this year, some iconic bars and restaurants have reopened with a refreshed look and feel, bringing back old-school favorites alongside international, travel-inspired drinks. From tiki recipes and passion fruit infusions to sparkling concoctions of all sorts, our latest cocktail map highlights the best drinks and the hottest new spots to try them, from Coral Gables to Miami Beach and everywhere in between. Sunny’s Steakhouse Sunny’s Steakhouse in Miami’s Little River has been the talk of the town (many towns, actually) since opening in October 2024. The massive space and the dishes are worth the hype, but the unspoken star is the bar, featuring cocktails like the refreshing Green Ghoul (tequila, mezcal, poblano, cucumber, lime) and the Monchito, a coconut-washed agricole rhum drink with sherry that evolved from a piña colada to a ti punch of sorts. The menu includes house cocktails, martinis, and “fine & fancy” options — the fino martini service, which comes with a sidecar, is a must. Made with gin, clarified passionfruit, and fino sherry, it’s a steal at $18 per person. items.summary: A new Mexican seafood restaurant, Mi Vecino, is opening in Circle C, courtesy of chef Amir Hajimaleki and his brother Ali Hajimaleki of Roya Hospitality Group. items.text: Austin Restaurant News Fire-Grilled Mexican Seafood Is Coming to South Austin The team behind Roya and Oasthouse will open Mi Vecino, a coastal restaurant focused on raw and fire-kissed dishes by Erin Russell Oct 28, 2026, 6:47 PM UTC Facebook Link Chef Amir Hajimaleki will oversee the menu, managed by Mi Vecino’s executive chef Jose Alajandro Sanchez. Sarah Natsumi Moore/Eater Erin Russell is a journalist and an Austin native, who has been writing about food for eight years. A new Mexican seafood restaurant, Mi Vecino, is opening in Circle C, courtesy of chef Amir Hajimaleki and his brother Ali Hajimaleki of Roya Hospitality Group. It’s slated to open between now and early 2027, per a release. The restaurant, Mi Vecino, will open at 5701 West Slaughter Lane, replacing another of the group’s restaurants, Keeper’s Coastal Kitchen , which closed Saturday, October 24. Mi Vecino, which means my neighbor in Spanish, will focus on Mexican seafood dishes, both raw and fire-grilled. That means offerings like shrimp enchiladas with white mole, ceviche, oysters, and fajitas served with fresh tortillas. Drinks-wise, there will be a full bar with margaritas, ranch waters, palomas, and other cocktails. Chef Hajimaleki will oversee the menu, which will be executed by chef Jose Alajandro Sanchez. The Hajimalekis’ restaurants are mostly clustered on Slaughter Lane in South Austin. Gastropub Oasthouse Kitchen + Bar , cocktail bar Daisy Lounge , and forthcoming Mi Vecino all share a building, and the group’s first restaurant , American spot District Kitchen + Cocktails , is just down the street. Mi Vecino replaces Keeper’s Coastal Kitchen, a different Roya Hospitality Group restaurant that closed in October. Jasmin Porter Photography This is not the first time Roya Hospitality Group has reimagined one of their restaurants. Roya , Hajimalekis’ highly personal Persian restaurant in North Shoal Creek, opened this year in a space that was previously Shortie’s, the group’s foray into New England Greek-style pizza. Roya is the group’s only North Austin restaurant, and sits above a former second District Kitchen, which closed and became an event space. Given the group’s penchant for reinvention, only time will tell whether it stays an event space. items.text: Fonda San Miguel Dining Out in Austin The Best Restaurants in Austin for Private Dining, Events, and Parties Everywhere to book for all of your small weddings, celebratory dinners, bridal showers, and more by Darcie Duttweiler Updated Oct 22, 2026, 2:00 PM UTC Facebook Link Darcie Duttweiler is an Austin-based freelance writer, who covers food, beverages, travel, and lifestyle. Whether you’re planning a milestone birthday, hosting a corporate dinner, or gathering friends for an engagement celebration, Austin has a private dining room to suit your needs. Some are swanky and tucked into Downtown dining landmarks. Others are cozy, or perched on patios with sweeping views. All of them make an outing feel like an event, while also taking the stress out of group dining — meaning, there’s no awkward table shuffling, no shouting over the crowd, and no fighting for the check. The city’s best private dining spaces are more than just a curtain and a prix fixe menu. Many spots go beyond dinner, offering perks like custom cocktails, floral design, built-in audio and video setups, and after-hours buyouts. From iconic institutions like Fonda San Miguel, Matties, and Jeffrey’s to sleek hotspots like Eberly, La Condessa, and Bar Toti, these venues combine atmosphere with standout service and memorable menus. Here are the city’s most impressive private and semi-private dining options — spaces that strike the right balance between style and function. items.title: Cotoletta’s Only Entree Honors Italian Traditions and Age-Old Techniques
items.summary:
At Cotoletta in Coconut Grove, there are no decisions to make. The Miami restaurant serves only one entree: Cotoletta alla… 
 The post  Cotoletta’s Only Entree Honors Italian Traditions and Age-Old Techniques  appeared first on  Resy | Right This Way .
items.text: Cotoletta’s Only Entree Honors Italian Traditions and Age-Old Techniques — Resy | Right This Way Cotoletta 4.7 · Italian · $ Miami Book Now Published: Nov. 9, 2026 At Cotoletta in Coconut Grove, there are no decisions to make. The Miami restaurant serves only one entree: Cotoletta alla Milanese. No substitutions. No alternatives. Just a golden, pan-fried veal cutlet — and a bet that it’s all you’ll need. Until recently, making a reservation required a phone call, which only deepened the sense that this place operates on its own terms. (The good news: You can now reserve a table on Resy.) The concept debuted in Coconut Grove in the fall of 2024 and comes from 84 Magic Hospitality, a restaurant group known for a growing collection of Miami restaurants with minimalist menus ( San Lorenzo , San Marco , and the lasagna speakeasy, Si Papa 3190 , are the others). Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Still, the story behind the concept stretches back further than its Miami address might suggest. Cotoletta is the creation of partners Ignacio Lopez Mancisidor and Mattia Cicognani, and former co-founder Andrea Fraquelli — who share a background in hospitality and a frustration with how transactional the industry had become. From the start, their goal at Cotoletta has been to make things simple for guests and allow them to focus on what really matters: great food and genuine connection. “Across the globe, many of the best restaurants do one item and they do it to absolute perfection,” co-founder Mattia Cicognani says. “We drew inspiration from the Italian essence of committing to one hero dish and prioritizing ingredients of the highest quality.” “Only serving one dish was a risk,” Cicognani acknowledges, “but the popularity and love for the concept has proven that it really works. Our customers learned that they love what we do and that is why they continue to come back.” Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Head chef Davide Rosselli shared the process that delivers a consistent, classic cotoletta every time. Premium veal is hand-trimmed, gently pounded to its thin-yet-tender texture, coated in fresh egg and breadcrumbs, and fried in clarified butter until it emerges with a crisp, even, golden crust. Each cutlet weighs in at roughly 20 ounces, made to be shared between two people. The result is a traditional veal Milanese that is a signature of Northern Italian craftsmanship. Everything else on the table exists to support that centerpiece. “While the process sounds simple, it’s backed by decades of Italian tradition and time-honored techniques passed down by chefs across generations,” Rosselli says. For $90, two diners share the full prix-fixe experience: two antipasti courses of bruschetta and truffle arancino to start, followed by the veal cutlet, and two sides (the only real choice you have to make here). Dessert (tiramisu or a flourless chocolate cake) can be added on for $14. “Each appetizer sets the tone for a true Italian experience, while the sides are thoughtfully chosen to complement the veal without overpowering it.” Rosselli says. “Lighter elements like crisp salads and simple pasta dishes help balance the richness of the veal, creating a well-rounded meal.” Those side options include pasta al pomodoro, zucchine fritte, insalata di rucola, or patatine fritte. Rosselli’s personal picks: the pasta in just the right portion to leave you wanting more of the main event, and the zucchine fritte offering a warm, light bite that balances out the richness of the veal. (Wondering what happens if you bring a third wheel or want to dine solo? Odd-numbered parties can add on an individual portion of bruschetta, arancino, a smaller veal cutlet, and one side for $55.) Guests return because the menu never changes, and neither does the reason to go back. “They know exactly what they are getting every single time,” Cicognani says. Cotoletta is open weekdays from 5:30 to 10 p.m. and until 10:30 p.m. on Friday. On weekends, it opens at 12:30 p.m. until 10:30 p.m. on Saturday and 9 p.m. on Sunday. Lyssa Goldberg is a Miami-based freelance writer and content strategist. She loves telling stories about food, wellness and travel, and you can find her byline in Parade, American Way, Mashable, Miami New Times, Time Out and more. Follow her on Instagram and Twitter . Follow Resy , too.
