items.title: The Resy Guide to Where — and What — to Drink This Fall in New York
items.summary:
Autumn is crackling with excitement this year: a flurry of new bars and restaurants have arrived, while existing venues are… 
 The post  The Resy Guide to Where — and What — to Drink This Fall in New York  appeared first on  Resy | Right This Way .
items.text: The Best Cocktails for Fall in NYC — Resy | Right This Way Published: Nov. 9, 2026 Autumn is crackling with excitement this year: a flurry of new bars and restaurants have arrived, while existing venues are rolling out fresh fall drink menus spotlighting the bounty of all those gorgeous gourds and apples showing up at local farmers markets. And if that’s not enough, this year, permanent outdoor seating has staged a return at many places, allowing extra time to enjoy al fresco drinks during these crisp months full of foliage and upcoming holiday cheer. For your next outing, here are the drinks to enjoy in cozy bars and outdoor patio spaces, spotlighting darker spirits, autumnal spice, and the first of the mitten-warming hot drinks, all season long. Must be 21 years of age or older to consume alcoholic beverages. Please drink responsibly. More From Resy Guides 27 New York Spots with Excellent Zero-Proof Cocktails By Kyle Beechey and Ellie Plass Resy Features The Martini Is Back, and It’s Not Going Anywhere By Kara Newman Guides The Resy Guide to New York’s Exceptional Rooftop Bars and Restaurants By Ellie Plass Guides The Resy Guide to Late-Night Dining in New York By Ellie Plass Guides The Resy Guide to 18 Classic Cocktails and the New York Bars That Do Them Best By Kara Newman Wine Hit List The NYC Wine Hit List, Spring 2026 Edition: Stars, Il Buco, Liar Liar, and More By Vicki Denig and Jon Bonné Guides The Resy Guide to Great Bar Food in New York By Kara Newman , Ellie Plass and Deanna Ting Interviews Stars Is Here to Prove Wine Bars Are Having Their Best Moment Yet By Jon Bonné Highball Ltd. Midtown Photo by Eric Medsker, courtesy of High Ball Ltd. Royal Scotsman Located just blocks from Grand Central, this bar nods to the golden age of luxury train travel, from the velvet upholstery to squared-off windows that suggest Pullman rail cars and perfectly frame nearby Midtown views. Drink names also nod to railway lines across the world; the Royal Scotsman is named for the opulent Royal Belmond lines that run through Scotland. This rich sipper features Scotch whisky (of course), alongside oloroso sherry, hazelnut liqueur, lemon, and honey. It’s just right for a nightcap. Book Now Photo by Eric Medsker, courtesy of High Ball Ltd. Titán Dumbo Photo courtesy of Titán Tepporocho While we’re still mourning the loss of Leyenda, the arrival of Titán is more than getting us through. This Mexican restaurant and bar is helmed by chef Alan Delgado and bar pro Ivy Mix, intended to explore the diversity of regional Mexican cuisine. The fall menu just dropped, and we can already see the toddy-like Tepporocho is going to be a cooler-weather favorite, made with reposado tequila, mezcal, ginger and cardamom, served hot. But we wouldn’t’ say no to the Fall Sangrita (golden beet, passion fruit) or carajillo-adjacent Bananajillo (coffee, Oaxacan aged rum, coffee, banana, salted crema) either. Read more about Titán here . Book Now Photo courtesy of Titán Raines Law Room Chelsea Legends of Gotham After a five-month closure due to a fire in the building, the original Raines Law Room has finally re-opened. It’s been given a well-deserved spruce, with new velvet settees, but the romantic charm remains, including the option to pull a cord to discreetly ring for drinks. Residing on the Reserve Cocktails menu, the Legends of Gotham is a luxe insider’s take on the classic Manhattan: it spotlights an Empire State heirloom rye (from Brooklyn’s Jaywalk distillery) and Degroff Amaro, a label from bartending legend Dale DeGroff, plus touches of Barolo chinato and torino vermouth. Book Now Confidant Brooklyn Heights Photo by Heather Willensky, courtesy of Confidant M&M Negroni Following a brief run in Industry City, this comfort food-driven spot has rebooted in Brooklyn Heights. Expect exposed brick, intimate tables, a focus on dry-aged meats and fish, and clever cocktails like the M&M Negroni. No, it’s not about the candy; it’s an insider-y mash-up of a mezcal Negroni and the M&M, a “bartender’s handshake” drink that mixes mezcal and Montenegro amaro. Now you’re in the know, too. Read more about Confidant here . Book Now Photo by Heather Willensky, courtesy of Confidant Velvet Cowboy Upper West Side Photo courtesy of Velvet Cowboy Good Negotiation Upper West Siders, rejoice: if you already love the barbecue-tastic Jacob’s Pickles and tropical Tiki Chick down the block, you’ll want to add Velvet Cowboy to the rotation. At this ode to the American Southwest, order a Frito Pie or perhaps the beer-battered onion rings, and chase it with the Good Negotiation, a mellow white Negroni riff fleshed out with fig leaf, Rockey’s liqueur, Suze, and coconut. The roadside-motel-Americana style décor just adds to the vibe. Book Now Photo courtesy of Velvet Cowboy Monkey Thief Hell's Kitchen Long Kiss Goodnight Bookmark this spot for your next Broadway theater outing; this pan-Asian spot re-opened in August, and it’s better than ever, with three individual spaces — and drink menus — to try. The Train Car, with a nod to classic rail travel, is a fun vibe, but if you can only book one space, lock in on The Den, a dark and date-worthy room with excellent drinks. We loved the Long Kiss Goodnight, a quirky sipper made with rum, Japanese whisky, black sesame, and cacao. The bartender will instruct: To enjoy the oceanic exhale that transforms the drink, take a bite of the strip of nori balanced on the glass rim, then a sip of the drink. Book Now Mūje Chelsea Midnight in Samui. Photo by Alexander Stein, courtesy of Mūje Midnight in Samui From chef Jungsik Yim, the name of this relative newcomer near Penn Station translates from Korean as “untitled.” Influences deliberately pull from across the Asian continent, and that extends to the drink menu, too. In addition to the thoughtful wine list, look to Asian-inspired cocktails like the Seoul Mule (soju, ginseng, ginger beer), or the Midnight in Samui (pictured here), a butterfly pea-infused rum drink

items.summary:
Miami offers plenty of chances to spend big bucks on dinner, but the harder question is where to make it… 
 The post  The Ultimate Resy Guide to Splurge-Worthy Dining in Miami  appeared first on  Resy | Right This Way .
items.text: The Ultimate Resy Guide to Splurge-Worthy Dining in Miami — Resy | Right This Way Published: Nov. 5, 2026 Miami offers plenty of chances to spend big bucks on dinner, but the harder question is where to make it count. Sometimes it’s at a five-seat sushi counter where the chef prepares every bite in front of you. Other nights call for a martini, a steak for two, and an outfit you’ve been waiting way too long to wear. This guide leaves room for both, from intimate omakase dinners and French tasting menus to waterfront Italian restaurants and dining rooms where you’ll want to stay for another round (or two). Expect to spend $125 or more per person for a full dinner at these spots, though what that buys varies. Some make the evening all about the cooking, while others give you the food, the crowd, and a place to keep the night going. Please note prices and menus are subject to change. items.text: The Ultimate Resy Guide to Splurge-Worthy Dining in D.C. — Resy | Right This Way Updated: Nov. 5, 2026 Sometimes, life calls for a big-time celebration. And when you want to feel like a big spender, D.C. has plenty of splurge-worthy places to choose from. Whether it’s elegant French cuisine in Georgetown, a refined omakase counter in Dupont, a Michelin-starred tasting menu in Shaw, or an unforgettable farm-to-table dinner outside of the city, we’ve put together the ultimate guide for opulent dining in the DMV with a projected budget of spending north of $125 per person. Translating to “my heart” in Arabic and inspired by his Palestinian heritage, Albi is where chef-owner Rafidi excels at bringing forth exemplary dishes from the restaurant’s wood-burning hearth, including lamb pies and potato pitas filled with blue crab, sweet corn, and green-garlic tatbili. The optimal way to enjoy a meal here is to fully indulge in the nightly Sofra, an ever-changing tasting menu, with a prime view of the hearth and open kitchen. Photo courtesy of Albi Cost: $165 per person for the five-course Sofra. Book Now ANJU map Dupont Circle Translating to the Korean word for dishes best served alongside alcohol, Anju fits the bill with its colorful, funky atmosphere and playful menus. The menu by chef-owner Danny Lee (who co-opened regional chain ChiKo in 2017) and executive chef Angelo Barreto includes the signature masterfully pan-fried pork mandu, brisket fried rice, the favorite ssam board to make wraps, and a section of hearty dishes dedicated to Lee’s mom. The traditional banchan is available in a set of three for everything from cubed kimchi radish and pickled cucumbers to sweet lotus root. End your visit with the stunning, amber-hued panna cotta made with sparkling Korean rice wine. Cost: While it’s possible to dine here on a budget à la carte, a meal for two, including drinks, will likely cost more than $125 per person. Mains range in price from $26 to $42 each, banchan and starters are $6 to $25 each, and cocktails are priced from $13 to $18. Book Now Annabelle map DuPont Circle Opened by D.C. restaurateur Ashok Bajaj ( Rasika Penn Quarter , Bombay Club ), Annabelle offers produce-forward, modern American cuisine in a vibrant setting of fucshia and emerald green. The seasonally rotating, succinct menu from chef Michael Fusano exhibits classic French techniques for its beef tartare, branzino drizzled with saffron beurre blanc, and Rohan duck breast with huckleberry mostarda. Pastry chef Bella Paul turns out works of art, like a swirl of chocolate mousse dotted in candied kumquats with pink peppercorn crumbs and topped with a tuile. Cost: A meal for two, including drinks, will likely cost more than $125 per person. Starters range in price from $17 to $24, mains are $35 to $45, and desserts are $15 with a $24 cheese cart option. Book Now Barbouzard map Downtown Walk into Barbouzard’s glitzy dining room and the first thing you’ll notice are stunning, hand-blown glass chandeliers that resemble a cluster of fish eggs. It’s a sign of things to come from French American chef Cedric Maupillier’s exquisite menu, which leans happily toward Mediterranean seafood. Order from the raw bar, indulge in caviar service, or go diving for scallops swimming in a peppery lobster bisque. The housemade pasta, fish entrees, and expert wine list are all an ode to the French Riviera. Photo courtesy of Barbouzard Cost: A meal for two, including drinks, will likely cost more than $125 per person. Entrees range in price from $27 to $66. Book Now Brasero Atlantico map Georgetown Transport yourself to Argentina while overlooking the C&O Canal at Brasero Atlántico, which opened its American location last year in a converted Georgetown firehouse. Ironically, flames are always on display from the open kitchen as wood-fired chorizo, tenderloin, and rib eye arrive charred and juicy from the grill. The nautical-themed menu also includes empanada varieties such as king crab and ossobucco, and a host of pasta and Argentinian staples to choose from. Keep the merriment going with a visit to its companion basement lounge Florería Atlántico for maritime-themed cocktails and DJ sets. Cost: A meal for two, including drinks, will likely cost more than $125 per person. Starters and pasta range in price from $18 to $58 each, with a special squid ink seafood linguini for two for $85, entrees are $31 to $79 each, and grilled meats such as Argentinian angus and prime cuts from the U.S. and Japan range from $71 to $330. Book Now Burnt Hill Farm map Clarksburg, MD Escape to a beautiful Montgomery County farm, vineyard, and restaurant from the team behind Old Westminster Winery . items.title: 7 Best Hotels in Antigua, the Caribbean Island With a Beach for Every Day of the Year
items.summary: From ultra-luxe five-star resorts to boutique beach hideaways, these are the properties worth booking in Antigua.
items.text: Central America and the Caribbean Chevron Antigua Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story With endless white-sand beaches , acres of rugged rainforest, and plenty of untouched tangle just waiting to be explored, the best hotels in Antigua celebrate its landscape, which remains largely true to how nature intended. Most of the properties on this glorious Caribbean island are a stone’s throw from the crystal-clear waters that lap its powder-soft shores. It’s a beach-lover’s dream, and anyone visiting would be hard-pressed to see every stretch of golden sand—as the saying goes, there’s “a beach for every day of the year” here (yes, an even 365). Visit between June and October , and you might just be lucky enough to watch baby turtles emerging blurry-eyed from their shells before scuttling to the sea. There are optimal times for surfing here, too, but the year-round promise is that the vibe on this island is chill. Days stretch lazily from sunrise swims to rum-fueled sundowners, with the opportunity for a poolside snooze in between. It’s easy to sink into vacation mode here, especially when you’re checking into one of the best hotels in Antigua. We've rounded up the most luxurious options on the island below, from high-end resorts with all the frills to boutique hideaways so good you’ll be booking your return before you’ve even left for home. items.title: 8 Dreamy Hotels Our NYC Editors Are Booking This Winter
items.summary: Because sometimes all you need is a quick change of scenery to tackle the winter blues.
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story If there’s one thing the editors at Condé Nast Traveler love, it’s weekendmaxxing . We’re all about scouting the very best hotels upstate , or catching a quick flight to Miami, all before returning back to our New York City office by Monday. The art of the weekend trip becomes especially important in the wintertime, when the city closes its blinds and hibernates until spring. This is when an off-season jaunt to the Rockaways, or a hideaway in a Berkshires lodge, becomes all the more appealing. Essentially, we love a trip where you can get cozy somewhere else—because sometimes all you need is a simple change of scenery to tackle the winter blues. From wellness sanctuaries nestled in the Catskills to country retreats in New England , these are the hotels our editors are eyeing for when the weather turns brisk, all within a few hours of NYC or a short flight away. I visited Mayflower Inn back in spring 2024 with one of my best friends while she was pregnant with her second baby, and I’ve been dying to go back ever since. I don’t know if I’ve ever felt more relaxed than I did while there—we spent hours in the spa, chatted by the firepits, stuffed ourselves with farm-fresh meals, and feasted our eyes on some incredible interior design. What are you eating? I won’t be leaving the hotel for food, that’s for sure. I’m always impressed by the F&B at Auberge properties, and the Mayflower Inn was no exception. The Garden Room offers creative but approachable seasonal cuisine from breakfast through dinner (don’t skip the burger), and the Tap Room is where you’ll find a tavern-style food menu plus a mixologist slinging delicious cocktails and mocktails. What do you hope to get up to in the area? The Mayflower Inn is located in Washington, Connecticut, a small town in Litchfield County , a region beloved by many of my colleagues. I’m imagining myself curled up with a good book by the lounge’s fireplace, draped in a Pendleton blanket, then dipping into the aforementioned copper clawfoot bathtubs. At just about two-and-a-half hours north of Manhattan, it’s a not-too-far excursion I’m saving for when I really need a break from winter in the city. What are you eating? Besides a pit stop at Phoenicia Diner, I imagine the furthest I’ll trek is over to the sauna and bowling alley. items.title: Where to Eat Gluten-Free in Montreal
items.summary: Travel and food writer Luke Pyenson shares where to find the city’s best gluten-free bites, sips, and dining experiences.
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Recently I’ve noticed more and more food people going to Montreal —and who can blame them? This laid-back bilingual gem on the St. Lawrence River is one of North America’s very best food cities. Personally I’ve loved it since my first visit almost 20 years ago. Montreal’s wonderful food scene draws me back year after year, sometimes multiple times,and by now the six-hour drive from my home in New York City feels like a breeze. It helps to know that my top meals of the year are waiting just across the border. But for the past two years, following my wife’s celiac diagnosis, I have been navigating the city a little differently. When I was younger, trips to Montreal meant poutine, bagels, smoked-meat sandwiches, and a plethora of other canonical Québécois favorites that happen to be full of gluten. These days we prioritize other local favorites and have developed a dependable roster of businesses we trust—and that don’t feel like a compromise. Luckily there are a ton of them; we’ve been thrilled to discover that Montreal is a paradise for gluten-free eating. Boulangerie Le Marquis Dedicated bakery scene In my opinion the only gluten-free Montreal-style bagels worth sampling are located in Burlington, Vermont. But Montreal is a city that takes its baked goods seriously, and it’s home to a handful of excellent dedicated gluten-free bakeries. You will not miss the bagels. Instead how about a croissant? Any gluten-free eater knows croissants are one of the hardest pastries to get right without gluten. As a rule my wife and I don’t really bother—unless we’re in Montreal. At Boulangerie Le Marquis , near Jean-Talon Market, and sister business Le Marquis Signature Santé , in Old Montreal, magnificent pains au chocolat and gluten-free croissants—available in plain, almond, and chocolate-almond varieties—arrive hot out of the oven all morning long. Flaky laminated pastry is a near-impossible feat in the gluten-free world, but Le Marquis has perfected it. We favor the pains au chocolat and almond croissants, but it’s tough to go wrong. Even more unique is the gluten-free manouché at La Bolo à Lolo , a GF market and takeaway in the Plateau. Chef and owner Gordy Moufarrej emigrated from Lebanon to Montreal as a boy and uses his mother’s homemade za’atar in these addictive flatbreads. Made from Moufarrej’s proprietary GF flour blend, they are topped with a paste of olive oil and za’atar, plus cheese if you want (you do). A number of sandwiches made with the same base are available, but we’ve never gotten past the manouché—on our last visit to Montreal, we went three days in a row. A sweet galette from Crêperie du Marché Luke Pyenson Perhaps unsurprisingly for a French-speaking city, crepes are another great option, and Montreal boasts an amazing spot for 100% buckwheat Breton-style galettes. At Crêperie du Marché , a bustling stall at Jean-Talon Market, cooks turn out a dedicated gluten-free menu of lacy galettes with both savory and sweet fillings. It’s a personal choice, but we like the cheeky selections that mix both: ham, cheese, eggs, potatoes, and a drizzle of maple syrup. Why not? Nearby is cheery, quirky Cantine Panella , a dedicated gluten-free bakery and café run by the Peruvian chef Alessandra Perona. Her South American sensibility means breads are made with flours like quinoa, cassava, and sweet potato, which gives them a delightful chewiness. We like to stock up on a few of these to bring home, though they sometimes don’t last the drive. Chicken Of all Montreal’s classic foods, rotisserie chicken might be my favorite. At Québécois-style rotisseries it’s slow-roasted on a spit and accompanied by gravy; at Portuguese spots it’s often spatchcocked and grilled over charcoal, then served with piri-piri sauce. In both cases gluten sometimes spoils the fun: Traditional establishments like the legendary Chalet Bar-B-Q and Portuguese eatery Ma Poule Mouillée both use wheat flour in their sauces. No matter—these are far from your only options. Piri-Piri Chicken at Rôtisserie Coco Rico Luke Pyenson At Rôtisserie Coco Rico , a Plateau institution open since 1970, the chicken is spit-roasted and served with GF piri-piri in a mélange of the two dominant local styles. On the side fries from a dedicated GF fryer are among the city’s best (and this is a city with great french fries), but don’t sleep on the roasted potatoes, full of savory chicken flavor. More refined, and representing the French Canadian tradition, is Little Italy’s Rôtisserie La Lune , from the team behind überpopular restaurant and wine bar Mon Lapin. Gorgeous, plump birds are served with rich gluten-free gravy and excellent fries that come from a blessedly dedicated fryer. The same fryer is also responsible for the unbelievable Croqu’Ailes Farcies XL, which are deboned chicken wings stuffed with more chicken and deep-fried. Every meal here should start with these. But the kitchen has an equally deft hand with seasonal salads and veggie-focused sides—almost always gluten-free and an essential counterweight on the table. Courtesy Mon Lapin Wine bars and neo-bistros Down the street from La Lune, Mon Lapin is equally adept at catering to gluten-free diners: On two recent visits most of the menu was in play. Dishes change with the seasons, but friendly servers will guide your choices (and help you navigate the impressive wine list). Make sure to save room for the restaurant’s signature buckwheat layer cake, accented with buckwheat honey caramel, fromage blanc, and crisp shards of buckwheat tuile. I’m not sure there’s a better gluten-free dessert on the continent. Mon Lapin’s co-owners, chefs Jessica Noël and Marc-Olivier Frappier, and wine director Vanya Filipovic, are all alums of the trendsetting Little Burgundy eatery and wine bar Vin Papillon , whose chef and owner happens to be celiac. Best known as half of the duo that opened Montreal icon Joe Beef , Fred Morin now presides over thos

items.title: These Bangkok Hotels Offer In-House Experiences, Beautiful Views, and Excellent Bang for Your Buck
items.summary: Whether you're staying for a while or just passing through, these Bangkok hotels offer a taste of everything the city has to offer.
items.text: These Bangkok Hotels Offer In-House Experiences, Beautiful Views, and Excellent Bang for Your Buck | Condé Nast Traveler Skip to main content Asia Chevron Thailand Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story After 14 years in Bangkok , I’ve watched the city evolve into one of the most electric destinations in Southeast Asia . It’s a city of duality—constantly on the move with new hotel openings, world-class restaurants, and an ever-changing shopping scene, but with tradition firmly at its core. There's something in Bangkok for every kind of traveler, no matter your age or budget . You can enjoy a lunch made by an 80-year-old auntie still serving the same streetside crab omelet she has for decades, or dine at the only three-Michelin-star restaurant in Thailand for dinner . Ancient golden temples stand alongside modern shopping centers, and old shophouses are being revived by the younger generation who want to preserve the city's heritage. When it comes to the hotel scene, this dichotomy is also in play. Guests can choose between historic boutique properties or glamorous new builds, and find every kind of amenity, design style, or cuisine under the sun. Just as captivating is the warmth and hospitality of the Thai people, something I’ve found to be unlike anywhere else in the world. Thailand is known as the “Land of Smiles,” and from my experience, it more than lives up to its name. The city reveals itself through small, thoughtful moments mixed with grand experiences, all set to an energetic pace that makes it one of my favorite destinations. If you're ready to see it all for yourself, read on for some of the best hotels in Thailand. —Megan Leon In this article: AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Top picks More editor-recommended hotels in Bangkok Frequently asked questions More Bangkok travel recommendations Our top picks: Best for families: Fairmont Bangkok Sukhumvit Best for couples: Dusit Thani Bangkok Best for business travelers: Kimpton Maa-Lai Best for a unique stay: Mustang Blu Best for large groups: Park Hyatt Bangkok Rosewood Bangkok Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Rosewood Bangkok Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Owen Raggett/Rosewood Bangkok Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Owen Raggett/Rosewood Bangkok Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Chevron Chevron Rosewood Bangkok Readers' Choice Readers' Choice Awards 2024 The 30-story tower that this hotel calls home cuts a striking figure in the Bangkok skyline, shaped as it is after the wai, a Thai gesture of greeting made by pressing one’s palms together—a fitting shape for a place that beautifully melds Thai hospitality with a hyper-polished service style. The staff here is supremely gracious: They remember names, press buttons for guests at the elevator banks, turn tables over quickly at breakfast, and happily fetch booster seats for little princes and princesses. And if that’s not enough to make you feel at home, perhaps the stylish rooms and common spaces will, designed as they are to offer a true sense of place. Modern sculptures and paintings by living Thai artists, and subtle design nods to the country’s silk-making history and garments worn by traditional Thai dancers, delight at every turn. — Matt Ortile Read Full Review Check Availability at Booking.com Check Availability at Expedia Courtesy The Peninsula Bangkok Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Virgile Simon Bertrand/Courtesy The Peninsula Bangkok Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Courtesy The Peninsula Hotels Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Courtesy The Peninsula Hotels Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Chevron Chevron The Peninsula Bangkok CNT Triple Crown CNT Triple Crown Readers' Choice Readers' Choice Awards 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2024 It feels like you might be in London when you're at The Peninsula in Bangkok's Thonburi neighborhood, thanks in part to the British racing vehicles parked out front. But the hotel's custom tuk-tuk reminds you that you're in Thailand, and rich, warm toffee tones carry throughout the lobby and lounges. The space offers grand views over the Chao Phraya and the Thai river homes across the water. The Peninsula swimming pool is among the best in the city; there's no better way to beat the heat in this famously hot capital than by taking a dip right on the river. —J.A. Read Full Review Check Availability at Booking.com Check Availability at Expedia Georg Roske Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Copyright 2564 Thanit Suvanish. All rights reserved. Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Georg Roske Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Chevron Chevron Capella Bangkok CNT Triple Crown CNT Triple Crown Hot List Hot List 2021 Gold List Gold List 2025 In a city where almost every high-end hotel brand has already made a mark, it takes something extra special to turn heads. Yet when Capella Bangkok finally opened after a seven-year tease, the city’s high-society set swooped in like magpies. Why? Capella’s first foray in Thailand is the only city hotel with villas right on the Chao Phraya River—multi-roomed retreats with private gardens and swimming pools lined with travertine marble. Suites in the main building—a blocky, low-slung affair with 101 rooms—come with plunge pools on their balconies, and the hotel tapped hot-shot chef Mauro Colagreco (of Mirazur in France ) to head its signature coastal Mediterranean restaurant, Côte. Crystalline coupes of private-label Champagne accompany check-in, brunches, and turn-down service, but that’s as flashy as it gets. The rest feels decidedly subdued. Service is hushed but switched-on, and the spa eschews New Age treatments for humble, age-old healing practices (tok sen hammer massages, luk pra kob herbal compresses) inspired by the historic Thai-Chinese community just outside its gates. —C.S. items.title: The Food Trends We’ll See in 2027, According to the World’s 50 Best Chefs
items.summary: What does the World's 50 Best Restaurants list tell us about the dining trends ahead? Top chefs weigh in.
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story On November 4, Lima, Peru , was a playground for global palates. Star chefs from across the world flocked to the culinary hotspot for the 50 Best Restaurants 2026, a prestigious awards ceremony that crowns the top restaurants around the globe based on anonymous nominations from over a thousand industry experts. Restaurant Asador Etxebarri , which is located in Spain's Basque Country, won top billing as the World’s Best Restaurant 2026 at the event held at the ornate Teatro Municipal de Lima. And before the winners took the stage, we were on the ground as Lima and its top restaurants buzzed with excitement all week. In addition to knowing which spots came out on top, we also wanted to understand what these results signaled about dining in the year ahead—so we asked chefs for their hot takes. After the plates, tastings, and pisco sours (so many pisco sours), these the top dining trends and places to look for in 2027, according to the world's best chefs. Read the full list of the 50 Best Restaurants in 2026 here. Lobster from Kjolle in Lima, which was just named No.7 on the World's 50 Best Restaurants list. Camila Novoa Traceability will be more essential than ever Chef-owner Pía León of Kjolle in Lima—a fine-dining wonder that showcases the megadiversity of the host nation with startlingly beautiful tasting odysseys—snagged the number seven spot this year, making it the top restaurant in the host country. With the global spotlight on her, León looks to the growing importance of knowing specifically where your food comes from, beyond just a vague sense of ‘local.’ “To me, traceability means understanding where each ingredient comes from, who produces it, and the knowledge behind it,” she told Condé Nast Traveler . “Many of the products we work with come from local producers and communities who have kept their techniques alive for many years. As cooks, we have a responsibility to recognize their work and the value of what they grow.” It’s a feeling that chef and co-owner Josh Niland of Sydney's Saint Peter (which also appeared on our 2025 Hot List of the best new restaurants in the world) emphasizes even further. The restaurant, founded by chef-owner Niland and his wife Julie Niland, focuses on whole-fish cookery and placed at number 50 this year, also earning the title of Best Restaurant in Oceania. “I think it [will be] ridiculous,” he says, if, in 10 years, restaurants are not telling us exactly on paper where things are from. “Like I think it's non-negotiable,” he said. “If you're writing a menu right now, let alone 10 years from now, I want to know why I'm paying $60, $70 for this chicken. Where is it from? That's how I feel about it. You know, we've got QR codes on the menu that you can scan and watch a fisherman pull a fish out of the water. Like, that's probably a very drastic leap, but I feel like that's where, to a degree, the premium end of dining needs to be. We need to be incredibly transparent about our labor, how we're paying people, like where things are from, all that.” Saint Peter in Sydney came in at No. 50 on the list, and was named the Best Restaurant in Oceania. Courtesy Saint Peter Expect menus to change more often as the climate does At New Nordic gem Kadeau in Copenhagen —number eight on the list and also recently awarded three Michelin stars this past June—head chef and co-owner Nicolai Nørregaard plays with time, drawing on both seasonal, hyper-local fresh produce, and preserved beauties from seasons past. Kadeau—where the team includes chef Francisco “Pancho” Cardenas supervising the kitchen, and Kyumin Hahn serving as partner—also won the Highest Climber award for jumping from number 41 in 2025 to its placement this year. So what, exactly, does “seasonality” mean when the seasons seem so different lately? Condé Nast Traveler asked Nørregaard just how climate change is impacting the menu, and what adjustments the team is making: “Some meals are shit,” Nørregaard said, “or some ingredients that we are relying on [are], so we need to change plans. But then maybe something else is in abundance, and then we just switch to that direction.” During Kadeau’s growing season, when it relies on produce from its garden on the Danish island of Bornholm and from what can be foraged nearby, adding more nutrients and water to the soil allows them to step in and give Mother Nature a helping hand, ensuring a better product. During the preservation season, in the colder months, the team showcases products like preserved onion that have been stored since spring and summer—but even that process is changing. Take the pine cone: A dry year might produce very few of the beauties, while a wet year will see abundance. “We sometimes need to think ahead and plan two years in advance,” he continued. “So we have to preserve something for more than one season because it might not come the next season.” Around the globe, more nimble menus—shifting ingredients, planning well ahead of time—are on the way to account for increasingly unpredictable weather. This is a further expression of adaptations already underway, including a reduced focus on meat, due to its environmental impacts, and broadened waste-reduction efforts. For diners, this means that no two tasting menus, even at the same restaurant, may be exactly the same; that talked-about dish may be swapped out for something else when the seasons or weather requires. But this commitment to the best, and the possibility for newness on menus, presents an arguably more interesting fine dining experience. Each menu, and dish, may represent a singular moment in time. The Sardine Pie at New Nordic gem Kadeau in Copenhagen , which placed number eight on the list. Soren Reed Kadeau was also recently awarded three Michelin stars this past June. Soren Reed Simplicity is the new luxury Sprawling menus as an indicator of abundance; dozens of items on a single plate—foams, sauces, sprigs of herbs placed

items.title: Micho - Gundry + Ducker
items.text: Micho - Gundry + Ducker Gundry + Ducker + Projects Studio News Commercial Practice Residential People Public Contact + Projects Studio News Contact Gundry + Ducker IMAGES HERE Micho Paris Text LOCATION : Paris France PHOTOGRAPHY : Roman Ricard Micho is a restaurant in Paris for the chef Julian Sebbag. It is located in a historic building in Central Paris. The design borrows from various classic interiors, such as 1950s English cafes, 1920s Vienesse Coffee houses, and New york Salt Beef bars. The common theme with these is that they are all informal and sociable places that form part of the life of the city and the street. December 2022 Filed under Commercial
credits: Roman Ricard Micho is a restaurant

items.title: Florence Street - Gundry + Ducker
items.text: Florence Street - Gundry + Ducker Gundry + Ducker + Projects Studio News Commercial Practice Residential People Public Contact + Projects Studio News Contact Gundry + Ducker Florence Street Text Location: Islington London Photography: Andrew Meredith Originally built as a flat backed house, the lower levels of this house had accumulated a variety of lean-to structures over the years, blocking the relationship with the garden. Conceived as a modern interpretation of the closet wing, the three-storey tower structure houses the various bathroom and utility spaces formerly accommodated within the main formal rooms of the house. The brick structure book-ends a two-storey conservatory-like structure providing space for a basement kitchen and an extension to the ground floor through-room. The sooty brick and mannered detail of the window arches and blind window are a playful interpretation of Victorian “house back” construction. The contrasting two-storey douglas fir-framed conservatory structure forms a visual and physical link between the garden and the original house. The formal ground floor living room retains its original shuttered window opening, which frames the view out. At lower ground floor level, the sliding door disappears into the wall structure to allow the basement to be opened up to the garden. Filed under residential

items.title: Temper - Gundry + Ducker
items.text: Temper - Gundry + Ducker Gundry + Ducker + Projects Studio News Commercial Practice Residential People Public Contact + Projects Studio News Contact Gundry + Ducker Temper Text Location: Soho London Photography: Hufton & Crow Temper is a 200-cover open Barbeque restaurant in Soho. The restaurant is centered around two ideas: A celebration of the preparation of often south-American inspired food prepared over flame and a continuation of the Soho late night tradition of atmospheric subterranean spaces. The two restaurant levels have different atmospheres, The smaller ground floor provides a shop window to see flour being milled and pressed into tacos by day and customers enjoying drinks by night, the basement is a large dark, theatrical space centred around a fire pit where the meat is cooked. Details and materials make reference to manufacturing and rural spaces and include engineering brick dark timber, concrete and terrazzo. Filed under commercial

items.title: The Good Egg Soho - Gundry + Ducker
items.text: The Good Egg Soho - Gundry + Ducker Gundry + Ducker + Projects Studio News Commercial Practice Residential People Public Contact + Projects Studio News Contact Gundry + Ducker IMAGES HERE The Good Egg Soho. Text Location: Soho London Photography: Andrew Meredith. We were asked to Re-cast “The Good Egg”, an independent daytime focused and well-loved Stoke Newington institution for the all day West End. Optimism, curiosity and enthusiasm, all in abundance in the kitchen, were encouraged, references from Montreal, New york, and Cinema explored. Simply reproducing the first site was never entertained. March 2018 Filed under commercial

items.title: Voodoo Rays - Gundry + Ducker
items.text: Voodoo Rays - Gundry + Ducker Gundry + Ducker + Projects Studio News Commercial Practice Residential People Public Contact + Projects Studio News Contact Gundry + Ducker Voodoo Rays Text Location: Hackney London Photography: Hufton & Crow Voodoo Rays is a pizza slice shop, and bar in Dalston East London. The client wanted to create a distinctive and characterful space that referenced both New York and London. Its neon signage and bright tiled interior is designed to be part of the night time street scene to sit within, and celebrate its location on Kingsland High Street. A long Pizza counter runs through the shopfront connecting the street with the interior. The interior is formed as a sequence of volumes clad in 6" ceramic tiles, reducing in scale and density to reveal the original building interior as you move towards the back of the shop. Each element is expressed in a different colour, the larger elements incorporating giant abstracted text. Filed under commercial
credits: Hufton & Crow Voodoo Rays is a pizza slice shop

items.title: Maggies Centre Manchester by Sir Norman Foster - Luke Hayes Photography
items.text: Maggies Centre Manchester by Sir Norman Foster - Luke Hayes Photography Maggie’s Manchester by Foster + Partners: ‘What matters is not to lose that joy of living in the fear of dying’ I was commissioned by The Architectural Review to document this beautiful calm project. The Maggie's Centres are a series of charitable architectural projects aimed at giving cancer sufferers a place to meet, talk and reflect away from the usual hospital environment. Due to the obvious sensitivities in taking photographs in such an environment, I decided to photograph as much of this project without the bulk and interference of using a tripod. Images published in AR Healthcare 2016 commended: architecture is deployed with great sensitivity to lift the spirits and help provide therapy. items.title: Design Museum - Luke Hayes Photography
items.text: Design Museum - Luke Hayes Photography I began working with the Design Museum in 2007 when I photographed a series of 'reinvented' footballs for an article in DAM magazine. Over the next decade I would document the museum's major exhibitions and key pieces from their archive collection. However The Design Museum is not just celebrating the past; it also looks to the future, showcasing new talent with the annual Designers in Residence show, and regular family days which aim to inspire the future generations of designers. The move to Kensington signifies the beginning of an exciting new era for the Design Museum; a larger building to build up the permanent collection and expansion of temporary exhibitions. items.title: Pierre Vives by Zaha Hadid Architects - Luke Hayes Photography
items.text: Pierre Vives by Zaha Hadid Architects - Luke Hayes Photography these images were taken on assignment for zaha hadid, during the opening day events at Pierre Vives. At one point during the evening Zaha sat down for a tv interview, and a crowd of people saw her and came over to get photos and autographs. I think she was really surprised and touched by the public response. She chatted and enjoyed listening to them, a side of Zaha rarely seen, and a privilege to capture. The Pierres Vives centre is a purpose-built government building in montpellier, france. designed by Zaha Hadid Architects, the glass and concrete building houses the multimedia library, public archive and sports department of the Herault regional government. items.text: thing — Dan|photo + chaussures + Wild Detectives + Black Ops Rare offering from Brooklyn Breweries. An imperial stout aged in bourbon barrels and bottle conditioned with champagne yeast. + Gyutoro 72 hour sous-vide wagyu shortrib, Thai basil and apple terrine, local farm greens, and spinach puree. Featured at Uchi Dallas. + nikka Thank you Tokyo. + Short ribs Home cooked meal of sous-vide short ribs, stewed winter root puree, and local wildflower honey roasted Romanesco. + Salud Whistle Pig 10 year rye whiskey—on the rocks. 100 proof, 100% Rye whiskey from an exceptional no-bullshit distillery out of Vermont. + Scapa 16 A beauty from the Orkney Islands. The barrels holding the scotch are continually buffeted for years by a salty sea mist. Any nectar that evaporates from the barrels is replaced by sea air and gradually infuses into the Scotch. So unlike other coastal whiskys, known for a powerfully smokey campfire character derived from kilning the malt with peat, Scapa is nuanced. Notes of a floral honey, saltwater taffy and the umami character of seaweed. + Aurelian Lure A 2013 vintage from Austin's Jester King Brewery. It's a sour ale initially fermented with a bouquet of wild yeasts and bacteria, then blended with fresh local apricots and refermented in oak barrels. + Hamachili Yellow tail sashimi, orange supremes, thai chili slivers, orange oil, golden tobiko, and micro greens. items.title: ater.architects
items.text: INTEGRAL LOCATION KYIV, UKRAINE TYPE SPORT AREA 100 SQ.M COMPLETION 2024 PHOTO MISHA LUKASHUK Nestled in the heart of Kyiv, Integral Yoga Studio is more than just a fitness space — it’s a haven where modern design meets the philosophy of mindful movement. The name "Integral" derives from the Latin word "holistic," perfectly capturing the essence of a space designed to foster inner harmony and balance. As the second studio in the network, this location embodies tranquility and intentional movement, brought to life by the creative vision of ater.architects . The 100-square-meter space seamlessly blends the warmth of natural materials, the tactile richness of textures, and a refined minimalism that reimagines traditional yoga studio design. Soft, rounded lines and muted warm tones create a soothing ambiance, while the brand’s signature gentle purple serves as a subtle yet striking accent. The interplay of light and form enhances the fluidity of the space, inviting guests to move effortlessly between zones while experiencing a profound sense of comfort and calm. The studio’s material palette is a refined fusion of natural elements designed to enhance sensory experience. Painted pine boards lend an airy lightness to the floors, while eco-friendly sand-colored marmoleum provides a seamless, sustainable surface. Rough-textured plaster on the walls and ceiling adds depth and character, contrasting beautifully with the softness of natural textiles. Enhanced by purple ambient lighting, this focal element immediately captivates visitors, setting the tone for the experience that awaits inside. The stainless steel reception desk and sleek metal wall sconces reflect warm, inviting light, creating depth and intimacy. Adjacent to the reception, a thoughtfully integrated retail display showcases the brand’s vibrant products on curved, built-in shelves that blend seamlessly into the space.
